lessons: Lesson 2.2: Approaching and Contacting a Suspect
Lesson 2.4: Behavioral Threat Assessment and Management
Lesson 3.6: Lost, Stolen, or Recovered Property
Lesson 5.1: Taking Custody of the Suspect
q: A recruit is asked to name the primary purposes of patrolling. Which answer matches the chapter?
Build partnerships, solve problems, and address the causes of crime
Maintain a public presence, enforce laws and ordinances, and deter crime
Inspect equipment, attend roll call, and learn the patrol area's boundaries
Respond to calls, take reports on recurring problems, and catch subjects
Patrol is the main daily activity of an officer; its primary purposes are keeping a public presence, enforcing laws and ordinances, and deterring crime.
Besides its primary purposes, what else does patrolling an assigned area include?
Recording BOLOs, extra-patrol addresses and officer safety bulletins
Identifying boundaries, major roads, landmarks and community resources
Checking the duty belt, the flashlight and the vehicle's maintenance
Developing resident and community contacts and giving residents information
Patrolling an area also means building a relationship with the community: developing resident and community contacts and giving residents information.
A burglary was reported five minutes ago, and the deputy races to the scene hoping to catch the subject. Which patrol strategy is this?
Reactive patrol
Proactive patrol
Community partnership
Problem solving
Reactive patrol deals with a crime after it happens; it calls for an immediate response to raise the chance of catching the subject.
In which policing model does the chapter place reactive patrol?
Problem-oriented policing, building long-term programs with partners
Community-oriented policing, working with residents on the causes of crime
Traditional policing, answering calls and taking reports on recurring problems
Proactive policing, traveling the area and speaking with people briefly
Reactive patrol belongs to traditional policing, where officers mainly respond to calls and write reports on problems that keep coming back.
A deputy keeps moving through her zone and stops for short talks with residents so they will later share information. Which strategy is she using?
Roll call
Reactive patrol
Proactive patrol
Directed response

Proactive patrol discourages crime through an officer's regular presence in the area. In proactive patrol the officer keeps moving through the area and talks briefly with people, building close ties with residents who can become future sources of information.
Which statement describes community-oriented policing?
It encourages the community to work with law enforcement on what causes crime
It responds immediately to a crime to catch the subject after it occurs
It is a brief meeting that shares current issues to keep in mind on patrol
It discourages crime by having an officer regularly present in the area
Community-oriented policing asks residents to join law enforcement in tackling the causes of crime and other neighborhood problems.
What is the goal of community policing, according to the chapter?
Develop long-term, proactive programs to address community problems
Maintain a public presence, enforce laws and ordinances, and deter crime
Increase understanding and trust between agencies and their communities
Study problems typical of certain neighborhoods and fight them with residents
Community policing aims to study problems common to particular neighborhoods and fight them together with residents.
Community-oriented policing has two main parts. Which pair is correct?
Identify, assess and manage persons of concern
Community partnerships and problem solving
Reactive patrol and proactive patrol
Contact officer and cover officer roles
Community-oriented policing rests on two main parts: community partnerships and problem solving.
What do community partnerships increase?
Visibility and access to the community through foot patrol
Understanding and trust between agencies and their communities
The accuracy and timeliness of records entered into FCIC
The likelihood of catching a subject after a crime occurs
Community partnerships build understanding and trust between agencies and the communities they serve.
Under the chapter's grouping of community partners, public housing and mental health agencies are which kind of representative?
Law enforcement representatives
Government representatives
Social service resources
Community representatives

Community partners include law enforcement representatives (elected, sworn or civilian), government representatives (public housing and mental health agencies) and community representatives (local businesses, professional groups and neighborhood leaders).
Which part of community-oriented policing lets an agency develop long-term, proactive programs?
Problem solving
Roll call
Community partnerships
Proactive patrol
Problem solving, the second part, uses partnerships to build long-term, proactive programs that address community problems.
Which example does the chapter give of building a community partnership?
Reporting a broken streetlight in the patrol area
Removing the door from a discarded refrigerator
Checking a car's interior light on at 2 a.m.
Stopping to play basketball with youth on patrol
Partnerships can start simply, such as chatting with a restaurant's owners and diners or stopping to play basketball with young people on patrol.
Positive, professional relationships with residents accomplish several things. Which is one of them?
They let only 24-hour agencies enter stolen property into FCIC
They inform the community about the methods agencies use to do their duties
They give dispatch your availability and location during the shift
They keep your patrol routine from being predicted by others in the area
Positive, professional relationships let officers learn about crime problems, form a bond with residents and show the community how the agency does its work.
At the start of a shift, what must you confirm about the items on your duty belt?
That the body camera data is stored correctly
That preventive maintenance is up to date
That all equipment is present and functional
That your devices are charged and on the right channel

Patrol equipment is vital to safety and effectiveness, so routinely confirm each item works and is stored safely. At the start of each shift, check every item on your duty belt is present and working, and carry a working flashlight every shift.
When inspecting a patrol vehicle, what does the chapter say to confirm?
Fire extinguishers, biohazard gear and first-aid kits work
Window controls and rear door handles are disabled
All duty belt items are present and the flashlight works
All equipment works and preventive maintenance is up to date
Inspect the patrol vehicle so all equipment works and its preventive maintenance is up to date.
A deputy skips checking the car's first-aid kit because the day shift 'always handles it.' What does the chapter say?
Only the body camera must be checked each shift
Never assume that others have maintained equipment
Emergency equipment is checked only at roll call
First-aid kits are the fleet manager's responsibility
Check emergency gear such as extinguishers, biohazard kits and first-aid kits on a regular basis, and never assume someone else kept it up.
If your agency requires a body camera, which topic does the chapter say you must know?
How long you must keep the data the camera records
Which channel to request for emergency traffic
How to patch radio channels during critical incidents
Which towing companies may receive lien information
Where a body camera is permitted or required, training covers its use, upkeep and storage, which activities you may or must record, and how long its data must be retained.
What is roll call?
A brief operational meeting before a shift that shares current issues
A meeting where you note addresses needing extra patrol
A broadcast describing a subject to help locate or apprehend them
A database search for wants, warrants or vehicle records
Roll call is a brief operational meeting before a shift that shares current issues to keep in mind on patrol.
Where does information shared at roll call come from?
Relatives, friends and close associates of persons of concern
Supervisors' oral instruction and records and reports from previous shifts
The alarm company's report of the alarm's cause to dispatch
Dispatchers' real-time checks of federal, state and local crime databases

Roll call information comes from supervisors' oral instructions and from records and reports of officers on earlier shifts; some agencies also broadcast it by computer, radio, telephone or other media.
What can cause a patrol officer's assigned area to change from day to day?
Weather, time of day, and school zones
Wind direction, traffic, and responder access
Staffing, call volume and individual assignments
Crowd mood, location, and direction of travel
One of the first things a patrol officer learns is the layout of the assigned area, district or jurisdiction; the area may change daily with staffing, call volume and assignments.
Before going on patrol, what should you identify first about your assigned area?
Its perimeter posts
Its deep corners
Its fatal funnels
Its boundaries
Before patrol, identify your area's boundaries and learn its major roads, landmarks and community resources so you can respond quickly.
What does the chapter say you should always have with you on patrol?
A map with important landmarks and patrol areas highlighted
A copy of every current computerized criminal history
A printed copy of each BOLO's cancellation message
A list of addresses where the alarm company is the key holder
Keep a map on hand that highlights key landmarks and patrol areas.
Which community resources does the chapter name for officers to be familiar with?
Animal control, FWC and nuisance animal trappers
Veterans Affairs, Children and Families and county clerks of court
Riot squad, SWAT, canine and mounted patrol
Shelters, social service agencies and internal agency resources
Know local resources such as shelters and social service agencies, plus resources inside your own agency.
During a shift your availability and location change several times. What does the chapter tell you to do?
Inform dispatch about each change
Note each change in your report
Tell your cover officer each time
Record it at the next roll call
Tell dispatch about any change in your availability or location during the shift.
How does the chapter define suspicious activity?
Any activity that a complainant reports to dispatch as unusual
Any activity that is abnormal for a specific area, whatever the time of day
Any activity that is goal-directed, premeditated and predatory
Any activity that is abnormal for a specific time of day in a particular area
Suspicious activity is any activity that is abnormal for that time of day in that particular area.
Patrolling a neighborhood at 2 a.m., a deputy sees a parked car's interior light on. What does the chapter say this could indicate?
A false alarm
A vehicle burglary
A chemical suicide
A self-help repossession
Knowing the law and the community and observing well help you decide whether suspicious activity is a crime in progress, such as a car's interior light on at 2 a.m. suggesting a vehicle burglary.
A deputy removes the door from a discarded refrigerator in a vacant lot. What kind of patrolling is this?
Problem solving through a long-term program
Community partnership that builds trust
Reactive patrolling that responds after a crime
Proactive patrolling that removes a potential hazard
Proactive patrol also clears public safety hazards, for example removing the door from an abandoned refrigerator or reporting a streetlight that is out.
What dictates which patrol method an officer uses?
The agency's call volume
The area being patrolled
The time of the shift
The officer's training level
The area being patrolled dictates which patrol method to use.
What disadvantages of vehicle patrol does the chapter name?
It makes your approach to calls easy to see at night
It limits the area you can cover and slows your response
It can isolate you from residents and divert your attention
It reduces your visibility and access to the community
Vehicle patrol covers larger areas but can isolate the officer from residents and divert attention.
Which advantage of foot patrol does the chapter describe?
You can keep a map and electronic mapping close at hand
You can use the PA system and spotlight to control a scene
You can closely look into concerns and watch specific areas
You can cover larger areas and respond to calls more quickly
Foot patrol makes the officer visible and accessible and lets the officer closely look into community concerns and watch specific areas.
How do daytime and nighttime foot patrol differ, according to the chapter?
Day hides your approach; night makes you highly visible to residents
Day covers larger areas; night lets you closely observe specific areas you choose
Day isolates you from residents; night diverts your attention
Day gives high visibility and access; night lets darkness conceal your approach
Daytime foot patrol makes you highly visible and gives greater access to the area, helping you notice minor details; at night, darkness can hide your approach to calls.
Why should you keep changing your patrol routine, day or night?
To keep others from predicting your patrol patterns
To cover a large area while observing specific areas
To learn the major roads, landmarks and resources
To keep the information from current BOLOs fresh
Day or night, keep changing your routine so others cannot predict your patrol pattern; combining vehicle and foot patrol covers a large area while still letting you watch specific spots.
A training officer says protecting the public starts with one thing. Which statement matches the chapter?
To protect the public, contact each suspect before backup arrives
To protect the public, rely on training and experience first
To protect the public, build community partnerships first
To properly protect the public, you must also keep yourself safe
To protect the public you must keep yourself safe; assess officer safety constantly, stay alert and keep situational awareness.
Which of these does the chapter list as a factor that impacts officer safety?
The color of the patrol vehicle's lights
Your ability to communicate with the PIO
Your ability to communicate with dispatch
The number of lessons in your training

Safety is also affected by the people you deal with, your view of the scene, your ability to reach dispatch and whether a suspect is armed or can reach a makeshift weapon; community partnerships can help keep you safe.
How can the community partnerships you build affect your own safety?
They replace the need for backup
They reduce the need to observe
They can help keep you safe
They build long-term programs

Safety is also affected by the people you deal with, your view of the scene, your ability to reach dispatch and whether a suspect is armed or can reach a makeshift weapon; community partnerships can help keep you safe.
How does the chapter define observation?
Narrowing of the field of view during a stressful event such as a foot chase or fight
Recognizing an occurrence using your senses by noticing people, things or circumstances
Collecting and analyzing behavioral information about a person of concern
Paying attention to what is going on around you so you stay alert and respond
Observation means using your senses to recognize what is happening by noticing people, things or circumstances.
How does the chapter suggest improving observational skills?
Mental rehearsal, firearm proficiency and first-aid skills training
Reviewing current BOLOs to keep the information fresh while patrolling
Scanning, controlled breathing and task-relevant self-talk under stress
Practice, such as memorizing descriptions of cars, people and scene details
Observation improves with practice, such as committing to memory the details of cars, people and scenes.
Arriving at a busy scene, a deputy fixes on one shouting man. What does the chapter say about observing a scene?
Do not get distracted by the whole scene; observe a few key elements first
Pick out cover and concealment first, then judge the shouting man alone
Watch only the hands of the closest person until backup arrives
Do not get distracted by a few elements; observe the entire scene before judging
Concentrate on behavior that matters to police work, including what is normal or out of place for an area, and take in the whole scene before deciding instead of fixing on a few details.
When should you identify cover and concealment at a scene?
Once a suspect is seen
After contacting dispatch
Immediately upon arrival
After separating witnesses
On arrival at a scene, immediately pick out cover and concealment from which to watch activity.
What is cover?
An area of containment surrounding the site of an incident of any size
A narrow space that restricts movement, typically a doorway or hallway
An object or group of objects that creates a visual barrier but may not stop a projectile
Anything that creates a bullet-resistant barrier between officer and threat
Cover is anything that puts a bullet-resistant barrier between you and a threat and protects you from gunfire.
You are advancing on an active shooter across a parking lot. How should you move, according to the chapter?
Straight to the suspect to end the threat quickly
From cover to cover to protect your head and body
Behind the cover officer while the contact officer speaks
In a low crouch along an indirect route to avoid detection
Move from cover to cover to protect your head and body when approaching or advancing on a shooter.
How does concealment differ from cover?
Concealment is preferred over cover when you need to observe
Concealment blocks the threat's view but may not stop gunfire
Concealment stops gunfire but does not block the threat's view
Concealment includes engine blocks, concrete and steel
Concealment is one or more objects that hide you from a threat's view but may not stop a bullet.
During a shooting, a deputy can stand behind either a dumpster or a wooden fence. Which statement fits the chapter?
Both are concealment because neither is listed in the chapter
A fence is concealment; use cover rather than concealment when possible
A fence is cover; it is preferred because it hides you from view
Both are cover because each one blocks the threat's line of sight
Examples of concealment: shrubs, fences, interior walls and other objects that hide you and give a position to observe from; cover is preferred over concealment.
Which sense does the chapter call often the starting point for observation?
Hearing
Sight
Touch
Smell
Sight is often the starting point of observation; nearsightedness or farsightedness without corrective lenses limits vision.
Which factors does the chapter say can affect your vision?
Weather conditions and your own health, plus strong odors such as ether
Lighting that distorts color, and dim objects blending into the background
Traffic, noises from nearby residences, and other environmental sounds
Selective hearing, rapid breathing and a narrowing of the field of view
Streetlights and fluorescent lamps can distort color perception, and dimly lit objects blend into the background.
What does the chapter say can stop you from recognizing sounds that show a crime in progress?
Lighting from streetlights or fluorescent lamps around the scene
Weather conditions or the state of your own health on that day
Strong odors such as gasoline or ether in the surrounding area
Background noises such as traffic, residences or the environment
Background noise such as traffic, household sounds or environmental sounds can keep you from hearing sounds that show a crime is in progress.
Why might a deputy fail to smell a dangerous substance outdoors?
Hazardous substances found outdoors are always easy to recognize by smell
Outdoor odors can hide smells, and strong odors can inhibit smelling
Background traffic noise can hide the sounds of a crime in progress
Dimly lit objects blend into the background and are hard to tell apart
Outdoor odors can hide other smells, and strong odors such as gasoline or ether can dull your sense of smell.
Which substance does the chapter say can be fatal if inhaled in a fine-powdered form and left untreated?
Chlorine gas
Ammonia
Ether
Fentanyl
Some easily identified hazardous materials, such as chlorine gas and ammonia, are harmful if inhaled, and fine-powder fentanyl can be fatal if inhaled and untreated.
A deputy finds a closed thermos in a suspect's car. What does the chapter say about identifying its contents?
Taste a small amount only if it appears to be a drug
Feel the container for heat as you would an engine
Use caution opening it and do not smell the contents
Smell it from a distance to judge if it is dangerous
Some hazardous substances are hard to recognize; open and close containers such as coolers, boxes and thermoses carefully, and never smell a container's contents, especially an unknown substance.
How can the sense of touch show that a vehicle was recently driven?
Touching the hood to check for fresh dirt
Touching the tires or engine to check for heat
Touching the windows to check for condensation
Touching the seats to check if they are warm
Touch helps identify items in a search or find clues, such as feeling tires or an engine for heat to tell if a vehicle was recently driven.
Why should you always wear gloves and PPE when using your sense of touch?
To prevent the suspect from feeling your hands during a pat down
To meet the rule that every arrestee must be searched twice
To avoid hazards like fentanyl-laced drugs and to avoid disturbing the scene
To keep your prints off any evidence that must go to the property clerk later
Always wear gloves and proper PPE when using touch, to avoid hazards like biohazards or fentanyl-laced drugs and to avoid disturbing a crime scene.
Which sense should never be used to identify an unknown substance?
Sight
Touch
Hearing
Taste
Never taste an unknown substance to identify it; if it is a drug or poison, you could become sick or die.
In the stress of a survival situation, what does the chapter say you will do?
Revert to your training
Depend on your partner
Rely on your mental rehearsal
Rely on your instincts
Under the stress of a survival situation you revert to your training.
How does the chapter say you can prepare for difficult situations?
By changing your patrol routine so others cannot predict it
By scanning your surroundings, breathing slowly and using self-talk
By studying, mentally rehearsing and regularly practicing safety procedures
By checking your equipment, charging devices and keeping all your gear clean
Mental conditioning, the will to survive, studying, mental rehearsal and regular practice of safety procedures prepare you to respond quickly and safely.
What decides which tactics you use in a situation?
Your agency's radio code system
The time since your last roll call
The circumstances of the situation
The number of officers on duty
The circumstances dictate the tactics; always stay alert and use observation to spot dangers.
How does the chapter define situational awareness?
The narrowing of the field of view during a stressful event
The ability to pay attention to what is going on around you
Recognizing an occurrence by noticing people, things or circumstances
Assessing a person's risk for future targeted violence

Situational awareness is the ability to pay attention to what is going on around you; assess surroundings, the number of people, the position of their hands and threats such as weapons or items usable as weapons.
What is tunnel vision?
The ability to pay attention to what is going on around you
Selective hearing caused by stress and fatigue in a pursuit
A space such as a doorway that restricts your movement
The narrowing of the field of view during a stressful event
Tunnel vision (also called funnel vision) is the narrowing of the field of view during a stressful event such as a pursuit, foot chase or armed confrontation, and can make you miss other dangers.
What is another name for tunnel vision?
Edging
Funnel vision
Fatal funnel
Deep corner
Tunnel vision (also called funnel vision) is the narrowing of the field of view during a stressful event such as a pursuit, foot chase or armed confrontation, and can make you miss other dangers.
What should you always do when confronting a suspect, according to the safety tips?
Identify yourself as an officer and ask for voluntary compliance first
Identify yourself as an officer and give detailed explanations of the law
Identify yourself as an officer and give direct commands such as 'stop'
Issue a threat to arrest right away so you gain control of the suspect
Always announce that you are a law enforcement officer and give short, direct commands such as 'stop' or 'don't move!' in a tone that fits the situation.
You believe a suspect is armed. What does the chapter say to do?
Call for backup and use tactics to contact, control and disarm the suspect
Ask the suspect to drop the weapon, then approach from concealment or shrubs
Holster your weapon and use verbal commands until backup arrives
Pat the suspect down right away before calling for backup
When you believe a suspect is armed, request backup and use tactics to contact, control and disarm the suspect, ideally disarming before you leave cover.
When possible, when should an armed suspect be disarmed?
Before leaving cover
Before calling dispatch
After handcuffing
After backup arrives
When you believe a suspect is armed, request backup and use tactics to contact, control and disarm the suspect, ideally disarming before you leave cover.
You have just shot an armed suspect who is down. What does the chapter say about approaching?
Do not rush to the suspect until no threat or other shooters remain
Do not rush to the suspect until you have told dispatch
Holster your weapon so you can handcuff the suspect quickly
Do not rush to the suspect until EMS and the supervisor arrive
After shooting a suspect, tell dispatch quickly; keep your weapon out and stay back until the suspect is no longer a threat and you are sure no other shooters or accomplices are around.
While parked, your patrol car is hit by rocks and a firebomb. What does the chapter say to do first?
Get away from the area immediately
Turn on the air conditioning to clear the air
Call for backup and hold your position
Abandon the vehicle and take cover
If your patrol vehicle is attacked with gunfire, firebombs, rocks or other projectiles, leave the area at once, roll up the windows and turn off the air conditioning to keep chemicals out.
Why does the chapter say to turn off the air conditioning during an attack on your patrol car?
To hear what is happening outside the vehicle
To prevent chemicals from getting into the vehicle
To save power for the radio and emergency lights
To keep the engine from overheating while fleeing
If your patrol vehicle is attacked with gunfire, firebombs, rocks or other projectiles, leave the area at once, roll up the windows and turn off the air conditioning to keep chemicals out.
When does the chapter say to abandon your patrol vehicle during an attack?
If the windows are broken by rocks or other projectiles
If it becomes disabled or chemicals get into the A/C
If there is another avenue of escape on foot
If it becomes disabled or there is no other avenue of escape
Abandon the vehicle if it is disabled or there is no other way to escape.
You are on foot when shots are fired at you. What does the chapter say to do?
Seek cover, call for assistance and plan a safe approach for responders
Abandon your vehicle, roll up its windows and leave the area right away
Seek concealment, call for assistance and plan a safe approach for responders
Identify yourself, give direct commands and approach the shooter directly
On foot under gunfire, take immediate cover, call for help and work out a safe approach for responding officers.
What does the chapter warn can happen if you do not use and maintain your equipment?
Your agency could lose access to the database system
It could break down and you could be seriously injured or killed
You could lose your FCIC/NCIC certification and access
You could be charged with a felony for unauthorized DAVID access
Check all equipment regularly, keep it clean and working, and keep electronic devices charged; equipment that breaks down from neglect can get you seriously hurt or killed.
What does the chapter say can happen if you do not keep your training updated?
You can lose the right to use the patrol vehicle's PA
You can be held liable for unfounded misconduct charges
You can be removed from the roll call distribution list
You can cause serious injury or death to you or others
Train regularly and know your equipment; letting training lapse can lead to serious injury or death for you or others.
Why does the chapter stress constant firearm training?
Firearm training replaces the need for physical fitness
Firearm proficiency is needed to enter FCIC data accurately and quickly
Firearm skills are required to use the CO2 extinguisher safely
You may fire only once in your career and must be fully prepared then
You may fire your weapon only once in your career and must be fully prepared to use it safely and effectively then; constant training builds the needed mindset.
What does the chapter include as part of fitness for duty?
Memorizing descriptions of cars and people
Knowing your agency's radio language fluently
Enough sleep and an exercise and wellness program
Keeping electronic devices charged at all times
Poor physical condition endangers you, other officers and the public; enough sleep and an exercise and wellness program are part of fitness for duty.
What does the chapter say can happen if you are busy or distracted on patrol?
You may miss danger signs and cause injury or death
You may be assigned a different patrol area
You may become too visible to the community
You may predict your own patrol patterns too easily
Being busy or distracted can make you miss danger signs and cause injury or death.
Which non-verbal cue does the chapter single out as most important to watch?
How fast a person is speaking
What a person is wearing
Whether a person makes eye contact
Where a person places their hands
Watch non-verbal cues: body language, where people place their hands and whether they lean toward or away from you; watching the hands may let you stop them from using a weapon.
Which cues does the chapter describe as non-verbal?
Signs and symbols on clothing and what a crowd is chanting
Hand placement and whether a person leans toward or away from you
Who the crowd rallies behind and who talks the loudest
A suspect pointing one way while saying they came from another
Watch non-verbal cues: body language, where people place their hands and whether they lean toward or away from you; watching the hands may let you stop them from using a weapon.
What does the chapter say about routine calls?
Never assume that a call is routine
Most calls are routine and need one officer
Routine calls can be handled without dispatch
Routine calls do not require situational awareness
Never assume a call is routine; going in without the right mindset breeds complacency in a potentially deadly situation.
When facing a dangerous situation, what should you rely on to perform your duties safely?
Your emotions and experience, not your training
The crowd's mood, not your agency's policies
Your training and experience, not emotional reactions
Your partner's judgment, not your own observations
In dangerous situations, lean on your training and experience rather than emotion to do the job safely.
What sets the rules on sharing electronic information obtained on duty?
Database access agreements and agency policies
The CJIS certification exam and background check
The FBI's security policy and public records law
The entering agency and its 24-hour operations
Database access agreements and agency policy set the rules for sharing electronic information.
Why must every text, email and radio message on duty be professional?
All transmissions must use the phonetic alphabet under the FBI's policy
All radio traffic is encrypted and reviewed by specialized units each week
All messages are logged by FDLE for driver reassessment requests
All computer activity is recorded and subject to review under public records law
Every computer action is logged under the FBI's security policy and can be reviewed under public records law, so keep texts, emails and radio traffic professional.
Why does the chapter tell officers to minimize mobile device use while driving?
To keep the radio clear
To prevent eavesdropping
To limit records requests
To avoid causing a crash
Mobile devices can distract you and reduce observation and safety; minimize their use while driving to avoid a crash.
Which is the most common communication device officers use?
The smartphone
The radio
The tablet
The laptop
The radio is the device officers use most; it carries vital information to and from dispatch and other officers, calls for backup and helps identify suspects or wanted persons.
During a multi-agency critical incident, what can dispatch do so different agencies can talk to each other?
Scramble the primary dispatch channel
Patch, or merge, radio channels
Designate a channel for emergency traffic only
Switch every unit to the talk around channel
Most agency radio systems have several channels, such as primary dispatch, talk around and specialized; during critical incidents dispatch can patch (merge) channels so different agencies can talk.
Radios differ by brand and model. Which controls and indicators do they generally share?
Channel selection, mileage, location and status
Power, volume, channel selection and transmission
Power, encryption, patching and emergency traffic
Volume, earpiece, phonetic codes and call signs
Radios come in many brands and models but generally have controls and indicators for power, volume, channel selection and transmission.
What is another name for public safety telecommunicators (PSTs)?
Intake officers
Booking officers
Recovery agents
Dispatchers
Public safety telecommunicators (PSTs), also known as dispatchers, are patrol officers' central point of contact.
Which describes most dispatchers, according to the chapter?
Correctional officers working at the county jail
Non-sworn personnel working in a centralized area
Sworn officers assigned to a patrol district
Non-sworn personnel working in each patrol car
Dispatchers are generally non-sworn personnel who run the radio and telecommunications systems from a centralized area with telephones and other resources.
How much privacy should you expect on the police radio?
No expectation of privacy at all
Privacy when using plain talk
Privacy on talk around channels
Privacy on encrypted channels only
Conduct all radio communication professionally and expect no privacy on the radio.
When may sensitive information or criminal history be sent over the radio?
Only on encrypted channels used by specialized units
Only after the dispatcher designates an emergency channel
Only when the suspect is out of hearing range
Only when there is an officer or public safety concern
Put sensitive details or criminal histories on the radio only when an officer or public safety concern requires it; specialized units may use scrambled or encrypted channels for security.
How loud should your portable radio be?
Turned down fully while responding to any call
Loud enough for others nearby to hear dispatch
Loud enough to hear but not so loud it is disruptive
Set to the agency's single standard volume level
Set your portable radio loud enough to hear but not so loud it disrupts; an earpiece helps prevent eavesdropping.
What can an earpiece help prevent?
Radio failure
Tunnel vision
Lost first words
Eavesdropping
Set your portable radio loud enough to hear but not so loud it disrupts; an earpiece helps prevent eavesdropping.
What is radio protocol?
The rules that set which agencies may enter stolen property data into FCIC
Speaking in a clear, concise, professional manner without signals or codes
Customs and regulations for constructing and transmitting radio messages
A system that uses numbers to stand for routine activities and requests
Radio protocol is the customs and regulations for building and sending radio messages, including codes and signals that can differ between agencies and regions.
What is plain talk?
Constructing and transmitting messages under set customs
Putting the number 10 before numbers that represent routine activities
Speaking clearly, concisely and professionally without signals or codes
Using English words to stand for letters in voice communication
Some agencies use phonetic-alphabet or uniform codes; others prefer plain talk, which is clear, concise, professional speech without signals or codes.
When does the chapter say to use the appropriate codes?
When the dispatcher requests it
When the radio channel is patched
When you are near a suspect
When you transmit road conditions

During a consensual encounter, the person suddenly runs away. Do you have grounds to pursue?
Yes, flight is probable cause
Only with a BOLO
No
Only with backup
If a person flees during a consensual encounter, you have no grounds to pursue.
What does a person's flight contribute to, according to the chapter?
Reasonable suspicion to detain for investigation
Exigent circumstances to enter a building
Grounds for a court to issue an injunction
Probable cause for an arrest on the spot
Flight alone is not probable cause to arrest but adds to reasonable suspicion to detain; with reasonable suspicion, you may lawfully pursue a fleeing suspect.
When do you have the legal authority to pursue a fleeing suspect?
When the person flees from a consensual encounter with you
With reasonable suspicion to detain, when the suspect flees
When the person is a crowd's loudest member
When the person refuses to answer your questions and walks off
Flight alone is not probable cause to arrest but adds to reasonable suspicion to detain; with reasonable suspicion, you may lawfully pursue a fleeing suspect.
Which resources does the chapter list among foot pursuit considerations?
Mounted patrol, riot squad or PIO
Victim advocate, chaplain or interpreter
Fire marshal, FWC or animal control
Canine, air support or SWAT
More factors: officers versus suspects, physical limits of each, available resources (canine, air support, SWAT), ability to secure the patrol car, and familiarity with the area.
You lose sight of a fleeing suspect. What should you be aware of?
The location of discarded items
The suspect's possible charges
The possibility of an ambush
The need to set a perimeter
Keep the suspect in sight; if you lose sight, expect a possible ambush.
A fleeing suspect tosses a bag over a fence. What should you do?
Note the location in your report after the pursuit ends
Stop and secure the bag yourself
Radio its location after the suspect is caught
Immediately alert assisting officers to its location by radio
Fleeing suspects often discard evidence or contraband; radio the location of discarded items right away.
What safety hazard does the chapter name for pursuing with a firearm in hand?
Tunnel vision setting in
Selective hearing from stress
An accidental shooting
A lost radio signal
Pursuing with a drawn firearm depends on circumstances and risks an accidental shooting; corners, fences, woods, pools and animals raise risk, so slow down and clear blind corners tactically.
Approaching a blind corner during a foot pursuit, what should you do?
Slow down and tactically clear the corner
Cut the pie at full speed
Knock and announce yourself at the blind corner
Slow down and request air support at the corner
Pursuing with a drawn firearm depends on circumstances and risks an accidental shooting; corners, fences, woods, pools and animals raise risk, so slow down and clear blind corners tactically.
You lose radio contact with dispatch during a foot pursuit. What should you do?
Reevaluate the decision to pursue
Switch to the talk around channel
End the pursuit immediately
Continue until contact returns
Losing radio contact with dispatch is a reason to reevaluate the pursuit.
When making a physical custody arrest, what must you tell the suspect?
That they are under arrest and the reason
The location of the bail hearing
Their Miranda rights before any search
Where they will be taken
For a physical custody arrest, tell suspects they are under arrest and why.
When should you handcuff, including double locking, during an arrest?
After telling the suspect the charges
After placing the suspect in the car
After searching for weapons or contraband
Before searching for weapons or contraband
Handcuff properly, including double locking, before searching for weapons or contraband, then do a custodial search with Defensive Tactics techniques.
When are Miranda requirements necessary?
Whenever you search an arrestee
Whenever you transport an arrestee
Whenever you make a physical arrest
Whenever you conduct an interrogation
Miranda requirements apply whenever you conduct an interrogation.
What must you separate from the arrestee's evidence and contraband?
Written statements
The arrest affidavit
Personal property
Booking photos
Keep the arrestee's personal property apart from evidence and contraband; agency or detention policy decides how personal property and contraband are handled.
What dictates what to do with an arrestee's personal property and contraband?
The victim's preference
The booking officer's preference
The PIO's media release
Agency or detention facility policy
Keep the arrestee's personal property apart from evidence and contraband; agency or detention policy decides how personal property and contraband are handled.
You find more evidence on or near the arrested person. What does the chapter say?
Additional charges may apply
It must be returned to the arrestee
It must be given to the booking officer
It is personal property, not evidence
Seize any evidence and process it per agency policy; other evidence found on or near the person may bring more charges.
Why provide general arrest information to victims, witnesses and family when reasonably possible?
This may be their only interaction with an officer
They must approve the release of information
They must be told the evidence collected
They are required to sign the booking forms
Victims, witnesses and the arrestee's family may have a direct interest; give general information whenever reasonably possible, since this may be their only contact with an officer.
What regulates what arrest information can be released to the public?
The arresting officer's judgment
The PIO, without regard to policy
State law and agency policies
The arrestee's family's wishes
What may be released to the public is governed by state law and agency policy.
Why must you not release information about evidence or potential witnesses after an arrest?
It is shared only with the arrestee's family
It may hinder the investigation or the arrestee's first appearance
It may hinder the investigation or make you subject to prosecution
It is entered into FCIC as recovered property before anything is released
The investigation may go on after the arrest; releasing details about evidence or witnesses can hurt it or even lead to your own criminal prosecution.
A bystander is recording your arrest on his phone. What does the chapter say?
It is a crime if he refuses to stop recording after a verbal command
It must be reported to the PIO before he posts it
It is allowed only if he is not a codefendant
It is not a crime; you cannot interfere unless he actively obstructs
People recording you on personal devices are not committing a crime, and you cannot interfere unless they are actively obstructing the investigation.
Reporters at a scene ask you detailed questions about the arrest. Who is usually responsible for releasing information to the media?
The cover officer at the scene
The public information officer
The arresting officer on scene
The booking officer at the jail
Most agencies have a public information officer (PIO) who releases information to the media and prepares responses to media requests.
Why must you keep physical control of the arrestee during the entire escort?
To ensure safety and prevent the arrestee from falling or fleeing
To keep the arrestee from recording the escort on a phone
To keep the arrestee away from codefendants at the detention facility
To meet the facility's weapon storage rules
Keep physical control of the arrestee during the whole escort, using Defensive Tactics escort techniques to prevent falls or flight.
Another officer hands you an arrestee and says he already searched him. What does the chapter say?
Pat him down only for weapons
Search again only when custody goes to booking
Search again every time custody is transferred
Search only if the arrestee seems nervous
Never assume the arrestee was already searched; every time custody passes from one officer to another, search again and secure property, evidence and contraband.
Why disable the rear window controls and door handles?
To protect you and the agency against misconduct claims
To prevent escape, injury and unfounded misconduct claims
To keep the seat belt secured
To prevent escape, injury, damage or destroyed evidence
Make sure rear window controls and door handles are disabled so they cannot open from inside, preventing escape, injury, damage or destruction of evidence.
Where does an arrestee typically ride in the transport vehicle?
The right rear passenger compartment
The front passenger seat
The left rear passenger compartment
The center of the rear seat
Help the arrestee into the vehicle, usually the right rear seat, and secure the seat belt.
Why do some agencies require audio or video recording of transports?
To confirm the beginning and ending mileage for the transport
To record the arrestee's Miranda warnings
To document the arrestee's statements for court
To protect you and your agency from unfounded misconduct charges
If required, give dispatch your destination and beginning and ending mileage; some agencies require audio or video recording of transports, which protects against unfounded misconduct claims.
When may a juvenile and an adult arrestee be transported in the same vehicle?
Only if the juvenile is emancipated
Only if a parent consents
Only if held under six hours
Only if they are codefendants
A juvenile may not be transported with an adult arrestee unless the two are codefendants.
You need an ambulance to transport an arrestee. What should you follow?
DCF's rules for juveniles
The Healthy Pregnancy Act's rules
Your agency's policies on accompanying the arrestee
The facility's medical intake rules
Notify dispatch when taking an arrestee to a medical facility or requesting EMS, and follow policy on accompanying an arrestee taken by ambulance.
An arrestee uses a motorized wheelchair. How should you adjust transport?
By releasing the arrestee on recognizance
By restraining in front only
In a way that doesn't compromise officer safety
By using an ambulance only
Adapt transport for an arrestee with a disability or special need, such as a service animal or motorized wheelchair, without giving up officer safety.
For a pregnant arrestee, where may you place restraints?
In the front of the arrestee
Behind the back, loosely
No restraints of any kind
Behind the back, double locked
For a pregnant arrestee, you may place restraints in front.
You cannot leave right after loading an arrestee on a hot day. What does the chapter say?
Move the arrestee to the front passenger seat for comfort
Enable the rear window controls so air can flow
Do not leave the arrestee in a hot car for an extended period
Report your beginning mileage while you wait
If you cannot leave right after loading, consider weather and temperature, and never leave an arrestee in a hot car for a long time.
An arrestee's size or medical condition makes transport difficult. What may you request?
The arrestee's family to drive them there
A larger transport vehicle or an ambulance
A juvenile-only transport vehicle
A second officer to ride in the back seat
The arrestee's size, health or medical condition may require a larger vehicle, an ambulance or a position change.
A person you arrest seems intoxicated and unsteady. What does the chapter tell you to check?
Whether he has pepper spray contamination
Whether the person has a call history
Whether he is a flight risk
Whether a medical condition may be causing it
If a person seems impaired or not in control of physical functions, check whether a medical condition may be the cause and get immediate medical attention if so.
Under the Healthy Pregnancy for Incarcerated Women Act, when may restraints be used on an incarcerated person in labor?
When she is combative during transport
When she is being moved to a medical facility by ambulance or car
When she is a substantial flight risk or an extraordinary circumstance exists
When she was charged or adjudicated as an adult in a felony court

The Healthy Pregnancy for Incarcerated Women Act bars restraining an incarcerated pregnant person during labor, delivery or postpartum recovery unless she is a substantial flight risk or another extraordinary medical or security reason requires it.
When you arrive at the destination, what should you report to dispatch?
The arrestee's pepper spray contamination
Your ending vehicle mileage
The arrestee's charges
The first appearance details
On arrival, notify dispatch with ending mileage, approach the drop-off point and get clearance to enter.
Where must you secure your weapons at a detention facility?
In the glove box, locked
With the arrestee's personal property bag
In the rear compartment of the patrol vehicle, out of view
In a locked location, such as the trunk or a weapons locker
At the detention facility, lock up your weapons in the patrol car trunk, a weapons locker or a lockbox at the drop-off point; the agency and facility set which places are acceptable.
When does your responsibility for the arrestee end?
When the arrest affidavit is signed
When the arrestee is fingerprinted
When facility staff receive the arrestee
When you get clearance at the drop-off point
You are responsible for the arrestee until facility staff receive them; watch for hazards such as codefendants or other arrestees.
After transporting an arrestee, what should you do with your vehicle?
Report the ending mileage and clear the call
Search the passenger compartment thoroughly as soon as practical
Disable the rear door handles again
Return to service and search the vehicle at the end of your shift
Give the facility the right documentation, and thoroughly search the vehicle's passenger compartment as soon as practical after transport.
How long may a juvenile be held in temporary custody in an adult jail's secure booking area?
No more than 30 days
No more than 24 hours
No more than 72 hours
No more than six hours

A juvenile may be kept in a jail's secure booking area or an adult jail for temporary custody of six hours or less, or for prints and photos, as long as adult arrestees cannot see or hear the juvenile.
What condition applies when a juvenile is held in an adult jail for fingerprints and photos?
They must be codefendants with an adult arrested on the same call
They must be out of sight and hearing of adult arrestees
They must be released within one hour
They must be released within six hours to a parent

A juvenile may be kept in a jail's secure booking area or an adult jail for temporary custody of six hours or less, or for prints and photos, as long as adult arrestees cannot see or hear the juvenile.
Until whom are you responsible for an arrested juvenile?
The booking officer at the county jail
DJJ, after confirming adult status
A parent, guardian or DCF representative
The state attorney's office handling the case
You are responsible for a juvenile with a medical condition, mental illness or substance effects, and until a parent, guardian or DCF representative takes responsibility.
When must you try to notify an arrested juvenile's parents?
Before the juvenile is questioned
After the first appearance
Within six hours of the arrest
Within a reasonable time after the arrest
Make a thorough effort to tell a juvenile's parents within a reasonable time after the arrest.
When custody of a juvenile is terminated, who may take custody?
Any adult the juvenile names, with no signature needed
The juvenile, released on their own recognizance
An adult relative, a qualified adult or an organization
DJJ, after confirming adult status
A juvenile cannot be released on their own recognizance; an adult relative, qualified adult or organization must take custody and sign booking forms or charging documents.
A dart-firing stun gun was used during an arrest. What must you do at booking?
Tell the PIO before the arrestee is booked
Tell the booking officer a conducted electric weapon was used
Note it only in the arrest affidavit, not at booking
Give the darts to the booking officer as personal property

Tell the booking officer the charges, any injuries, whether the arrestee is a juvenile, pepper spray contamination, any conducted electric weapon use, threats to self or others, and known medical conditions.
What must you not give the booking officer?
Injury information
The arrest affidavit
Personal property
Contraband or evidence
Give the booking officer the arrestee's personal property, but never contraband or evidence; then transfer custody.
Who must complete the arrest affidavit?
The intake officer
The arresting officer
The transporting officer
The booking officer
The arresting officer must fill out an arrest affidavit that goes with the arrestee to the booking officer.
Where does FCIC/NCIC receive criminal history data from?
Booking photos and personal property inventories
Fingerprint cards and arrest and correctional reports
Transaction logs and public records requests
Clerk of court and state attorney records
FCIC/NCIC builds criminal history data from fingerprint cards and arrest and correctional reports, so fill them out accurately.
What do many facilities do instead of taking new booking photos?
Use photos supplied by family members of the arrestee
Use DAVID license photos
Use security video stills
Access existing photos from past arrests
Booking photos give a visual record; many facilities can use photos from past arrests instead of taking new ones.
Why submit evidence using established procedures?
To maintain the chain of custody and reduce legal challenges
To let FCIC record it as recovered
To meet the found-property law
To allow the booking officer to inventory it with property
Process and package evidence and seized contraband per policy, and submit it by established procedure to keep the chain of custody and reduce legal challenges.
After turning over the arrestee and affidavit, what should you do?
Notify the arrestee's family of the bail amount
Inform dispatch of the call's completion and outcome
Request a hold order on the arrestee's property
Report your ending mileage
After turning over the arrestee and affidavit, tell dispatch the call is complete and its outcome.
What should your arrest documents clearly convey?
The witnesses' written statements only
The media summary prepared by the PIO
Investigative facts to assist in prosecution
The arrestee's account in his own words
Document arrests completely and accurately so the facts clearly support prosecution.
A field training officer asks you what patrol is to an officer's day and what it is mainly for. Which answer is accurate?
The main daily activity; mainly builds trust between agencies and the communities they serve
The main daily activity; mainly answers calls and takes reports on recurring problems
A brief daily meeting; shares current issues, BOLOs and safety concerns to keep in mind on shift
The main daily activity; keeps a public presence, enforces laws and ordinances, deters crime
Patrol is the main daily activity of an officer; its primary purposes are keeping a public presence, enforcing laws and ordinances, and deterring crime.
On patrol you stop to tell a neighborhood association about a string of car break-ins. Which part of patrolling is this?
Clearing a public safety hazard during proactive patrol
Recording roll call information that may affect the whole shift
Building a community relationship by giving residents information
Learning the area's community resources before patrol
Patrolling an area also means building a relationship with the community: developing resident and community contacts and giving residents information.
Which feature does the chapter tie to reactive patrol specifically?
Brief talks that turn residents into future sources of information
An officer's regular presence that discourages crime in the area
Long-term proactive programs built through community partnerships
An immediate response to raise the chance of catching the subject
Reactive patrol deals with a crime after it happens; it calls for an immediate response to raise the chance of catching the subject.
An agency's officers mostly answer calls and keep writing reports on the same recurring problems. Which model does the chapter link to this?
Problem solving
Traditional policing
Community partnership
Community-oriented policing
Reactive patrol belongs to traditional policing, where officers mainly respond to calls and write reports on problems that keep coming back.
Crime drops on a street simply because a deputy is seen there every day. Which strategy explains this?
Proactive patrol
Reactive patrol
Traditional policing
Civil standby
Proactive patrol discourages crime through an officer's regular presence in the area.
Why does a proactive patrol officer stop for short conversations while moving through the area?
To notify residents of addresses that need extra patrol attention
To confirm each resident's identity through DAVID and FCIC/NCIC queries
To take written statements that support probable cause for later arrests
To build close ties with residents who may become future sources of information
In proactive patrol the officer keeps moving through the area and talks briefly with people, building close ties with residents who can become future sources of information.
Residents and deputies meet monthly to tackle why burglaries keep happening on one block. Which approach is this?
A roll call briefing
Community-oriented policing
Proactive patrol of the block
Reactive patrol in traditional policing
Community-oriented policing asks residents to join law enforcement in tackling the causes of crime and other neighborhood problems.
What is the stated aim of community policing?
Building understanding and trust between agencies and the communities they serve
Responding immediately after a crime to raise the chance of catching the subject
Studying problems common to particular neighborhoods and fighting them with residents
Keeping a public presence, enforcing laws and ordinances and deterring crime
Community policing aims to study problems common to particular neighborhoods and fight them together with residents.
Which two parts does community-oriented policing rest on?
Community partnerships and problem solving
Roll call and equipment inspection
Observation and situational awareness
Community contacts and resident information
Community-oriented policing rests on two main parts: community partnerships and problem solving.
What does the chapter say community partnerships build?
A public presence that deters crime in an area
Understanding and trust between agencies and communities
Future sources of information through brief talks
Long-term, proactive programs that address problems
Community partnerships build understanding and trust between agencies and the communities they serve.
A public housing agency joins a task force with your sheriff's office. Which partner category is it?
Government representative
Community representative
Social service resource
Law enforcement representative

Community partners include law enforcement representatives (elected, sworn or civilian), government representatives (public housing and mental health agencies) and community representatives (local businesses, professional groups and neighborhood leaders).
Your agency and a church group launch a year-long after-school program to cut juvenile thefts. Which part of community policing is this?
Reactive patrol
Proactive patrol
Community partnership
Problem solving
Problem solving, the second part, uses partnerships to build long-term, proactive programs that address community problems.
Which example does the chapter give of a simple way to start a partnership?
Reporting a streetlight that is out to the city
Removing the door from an abandoned refrigerator
Playing basketball with young people while on patrol
Meeting mail carriers and sanitation workers
Partnerships can start simply, such as chatting with a restaurant's owners and diners or stopping to play basketball with young people on patrol.
Which benefit does the chapter list for positive, professional relationships with residents?
Showing the community how the agency does its work
Turning residents into future sources of information
Replacing the need for reactive patrol in the area
Giving residents access to criminal history records
Positive, professional relationships let officers learn about crime problems, form a bond with residents and show the community how the agency does its work.
Why should you routinely confirm that each piece of patrol equipment works and is stored safely?
Equipment is vital to your safety and effectiveness
Roll call supervisors inspect all equipment first
Preventive maintenance must be kept current
Neglected equipment must be logged at roll call
Patrol equipment is vital to safety and effectiveness, so routinely confirm each item works and is stored safely.
At the start of a shift, what does the chapter say to check on your duty belt?
That items are arranged by agency diagram
That every item is present and working
That it matches the previous shift's log
That devices are charged
At the start of each shift, check every item on your duty belt is present and working, and carry a working flashlight every shift.
When you inspect your patrol vehicle, what two things should you confirm?
The rear seat is searched and the doors cannot open inside
All equipment works and preventive maintenance is current
The rear seat is clear and the door handles are disabled
Emergency gear is stocked and the takedown lights work
Inspect the patrol vehicle so all equipment works and its preventive maintenance is up to date.
The first-aid kit in your assigned car looks full. What does the chapter say about emergency gear?
Check it only when preventive maintenance is due
Leave it to the agency, since gear is checked at roll call
Check it regularly; never assume someone else did
Check it at roll call; supervisors confirm it
Check emergency gear such as extinguishers, biohazard kits and first-aid kits on a regular basis, and never assume someone else kept it up.
Your agency issues body cameras. Which topic does the chapter say training covers?
How to release footage under public records law
How to request footage through the PIO
How to record a transport for misconduct claims
How long the camera's data must be kept
Where a body camera is permitted or required, training covers its use, upkeep and storage, which activities you may or must record, and how long its data must be retained.
What is roll call?
A supervisor's inspection of each officer's duty equipment
A list of addresses that need extra patrol during the shift
A brief operational meeting before a shift on current issues
A check-in that lets dispatch track your status
Roll call is a brief operational meeting before a shift that shares current issues to keep in mind on patrol.
Besides supervisors' oral instructions, where does roll call information come from?
Records and reports of officers on earlier shifts
Brief talks with residents during proactive patrol
Printed CCH copies from the previous shift
Dispatch's call history for each location

Roll call information comes from supervisors' oral instructions and from records and reports of officers on earlier shifts; some agencies also broadcast it by computer, radio, telephone or other media.
Why might your assigned patrol area be different from one day to the next?
Staffing, call volume and assignments change
The agency rotates areas to avoid complacency
Supervisors set areas at each roll call
Dispatch tracks your status as you check in
One of the first things a patrol officer learns is the layout of the assigned area, district or jurisdiction; the area may change daily with staffing, call volume and assignments.
Why should you learn your area's major roads, landmarks and community resources before patrol?
So you can map the boundaries
So you can vary your routine
So you can brief roll call
So you can respond quickly
Before patrol, identify your area's boundaries and learn its major roads, landmarks and community resources so you can respond quickly.
What does the chapter say your map should highlight?
Shelters and social service agencies
Recent crimes and BOLO locations
Key landmarks and patrol areas
Shelters and social services
Keep a map on hand that highlights key landmarks and patrol areas.
Besides shelters and social service agencies, which resources does the chapter say to know?
Landmarks and major roads
Mail carriers and utility workers
Resources inside your own agency
Neighborhood watches and businesses
Know local resources such as shelters and social service agencies, plus resources inside your own agency.
Mid-shift you stop for a meal outside your zone. What should you do?
Note it in your report at the end of shift
Tell dispatch about the change in your location
Tell your supervisor at the next roll call
Check out with dispatch only at the end of shift
Tell dispatch about any change in your availability or location during the shift.
How does the chapter define suspicious activity?
Activity abnormal for that time of day in that area
Activity reported by a resident to the dispatcher
Activity that matches a BOLO issued at roll call
Activity involving a person who flees from police
Suspicious activity is any activity that is abnormal for that time of day in that particular area.
At 2 a.m. you see a parked car's interior light on in a quiet lot. What crime does the chapter say this may suggest?
Vehicle burglary
Repair-shop dispute
Illegal repossession
Theft from a repair shop
Knowing the law and the community and observing well help you decide whether suspicious activity is a crime in progress, such as a car's interior light on at 2 a.m. suggesting a vehicle burglary.
You report a streetlight that is out. Which patrol activity is this an example of?
Community partnership building trust with residents
Proactive patrol clearing a public safety hazard
Roll call information to pass to the next shift
Reactive patrol responding to a call for service
Proactive patrol also clears public safety hazards, for example removing the door from an abandoned refrigerator or reporting a streetlight that is out.
What dictates which patrol method you use?
The time of day
The area being patrolled
The call volume
The time of the shift
The area being patrolled dictates which patrol method to use.
Which disadvantage does the chapter give for vehicle patrol?
It makes the officer predictable at night
It limits the area an officer can cover
It can isolate the officer from residents
It limits how closely you look into concerns
Vehicle patrol covers larger areas but can isolate the officer from residents and divert attention.
Which advantage does the chapter give for foot patrol?
Concealing every approach to every call
Visibility and accessibility to residents
Isolation from residents
Covering larger areas in less time overall
Foot patrol makes the officer visible and accessible and lets the officer closely look into community concerns and watch specific areas.
On night foot patrol, what advantage does darkness give you?
It makes you highly visible to residents
It gives greater access to the area
It can hide your approach to calls
It helps you notice minor details
Daytime foot patrol makes you highly visible and gives greater access to the area, helping you notice minor details; at night, darkness can hide your approach to calls.
How does the chapter suggest covering a large area while still watching specific spots?
Patrol by vehicle only at night
Vary your routine so you are unpredictable
Combine vehicle and foot patrol
Use specialized marine or mounted patrol
Day or night, keep changing your routine so others cannot predict your patrol pattern; combining vehicle and foot patrol covers a large area while still letting you watch specific spots.
What does the chapter say you must do in order to protect the public?
Patrol only by vehicle at night
Wait for backup on all calls
Avoid every armed suspect
Keep yourself safe
To protect the public you must keep yourself safe; assess officer safety constantly, stay alert and keep situational awareness.
Besides the people you deal with and your view of the scene, what else does the chapter say affects your safety?
Your ability to reach dispatch
Your vehicle's preventive maintenance
Your body camera's data retention
Your community partnerships

Safety is also affected by the people you deal with, your view of the scene, your ability to reach dispatch and whether a suspect is armed or can reach a makeshift weapon; community partnerships can help keep you safe.
What does observation mean in the chapter?
Practicing memorizing details of cars and people
Using your senses to recognize what is happening
Watching a scene from behind cover until backup
Scanning the scene to prevent tunnel vision
Observation means using your senses to recognize what is happening by noticing people, things or circumstances.
How can you improve your observation skills?
Focus on a few details instead of the whole scene
Rely on dispatch for each suspect description
Take in the whole scene before deciding
Practice memorizing details of cars, people and scenes
Observation improves with practice, such as committing to memory the details of cars, people and scenes.
A witness saw a robber. Which set of details does the chapter say to note when observing people?
Appearance, height, weight, hair, clothing and approximate age
Scars, tattoos, birthmarks and the driver license number
Tag, color, make and model of every vehicle involved
Name, race, date of birth and sex for a database query
When observing people, note appearance, height, weight, hair, clothing, approximate age and other personal details.
You arrive at a disturbance. What does the chapter say about forming a judgment?
Pick out cover first, then decide
Decide based on the first detail you see
Decide the incident type before arriving
Take in the whole scene before deciding
Concentrate on behavior that matters to police work, including what is normal or out of place for an area, and take in the whole scene before deciding instead of fixing on a few details.
What should you do immediately on arrival at a scene?
Separate witnesses before anything else
Approach the complainant's front door
Pick out cover and concealment to watch from
Tell dispatch you need backup at once
On arrival at a scene, immediately pick out cover and concealment from which to watch activity.
Which describes cover?
An area of containment around an incident
A shrub, fence or interior wall that blocks sight
A bullet-resistant barrier between you and a threat
An object that hides you from a threat's view only
Cover is anything that puts a bullet-resistant barrier between you and a threat and protects you from gunfire.
Shots ring out at a traffic stop. Which spot gives you cover?
Behind an interior wall
Behind the engine block
Behind a wooden privacy fence
Behind a hedge of shrubs
Examples of cover: engine blocks, brick walls, dirt embankments, concrete, steel and thick wood.
When advancing on a shooter, how does the chapter say to move?
From concealment to concealment
Through the deep corners
From cover to cover
In a low crouch, indirect route
Move from cover to cover to protect your head and body when approaching or advancing on a shooter.
What is the weakness of concealment?
It may not stop a bullet
It blocks only interior walls
It cannot hide you from view
It is less preferred only at night
Concealment is one or more objects that hide you from a threat's view but may not stop a bullet.
You must choose between a brick wall and a thick hedge. Which does the chapter prefer, and why?
The brick wall; cover is preferred over concealment
The brick wall; it hides you but may not stop a bullet
The hedge; it keeps the threat from seeing your approach
The hedge; concealment hides you and lets you observe
Examples of concealment: shrubs, fences, interior walls and other objects that hide you and give a position to observe from; cover is preferred over concealment.
At night under a streetlight, a witness says a car was green. Why might that be wrong?
Background noise affects the witness's memory
Streetlights can distort color perception
Uncorrected nearsightedness limits vision
Dim objects can look brighter under lamps
Streetlights and fluorescent lamps can distort color perception, and dimly lit objects blend into the background.
Why might you fail to hear a crime in progress?
Background noise from traffic or households
Streetlights distorting your perception
Strong odors dulling your other senses
Wearing an earpiece in your patrol radio
Background noise such as traffic, household sounds or environmental sounds can keep you from hearing sounds that show a crime is in progress.
Which substances does the chapter say smell can reveal?
Gasoline, natural gas and fentanyl
Fentanyl, chlorine and ammonia powder
Gasoline, petroleum products and ether
Gasoline, natural gas and gunpowder
Smell can reveal dangerous or illegal substances such as gasoline, petroleum products, natural gas or gunpowder, but weather and your health affect it.
What can dull your sense of smell?
Wearing gloves and other protective gear
Background traffic and household noise
Dim lighting from streetlights at night
Strong odors such as gasoline or ether
Outdoor odors can hide other smells, and strong odors such as gasoline or ether can dull your sense of smell.
Which substance does the chapter say can be fatal if inhaled and untreated?
Burnt gunpowder
Natural gas leaks
Gasoline vapor
Fine-powder fentanyl
Some easily identified hazardous materials, such as chlorine gas and ammonia, are harmful if inhaled, and fine-powder fentanyl can be fatal if inhaled and untreated.
During a search you find a closed thermos. What does the chapter say?
Feel it for heat to tell if it was recently used
Open it carefully and smell only from a distance
Open it carefully and never smell its contents
Open it quickly and never touch its contents
Some hazardous substances are hard to recognize; open and close containers such as coolers, boxes and thermoses carefully, and never smell a container's contents, especially an unknown substance.
How can touch tell you a vehicle was recently driven?
Checking the interior light at night
Watching for a running engine nearby
Feeling the tires or engine for heat
Noticing a usual car now missing
Touch helps identify items in a search or find clues, such as feeling tires or an engine for heat to tell if a vehicle was recently driven.
Why wear gloves and PPE when using touch?
To keep the chain of custody for all evidence collected
To avoid hazards and avoid disturbing a crime scene
To feel an engine for heat safely
To keep fentanyl from being inhaled
Always wear gloves and proper PPE when using touch, to avoid hazards like biohazards or fentanyl-laced drugs and to avoid disturbing a crime scene.
A suspect says a white powder is only sugar. What does the chapter say?
Never taste an unknown substance
Touch it only with gloves, then taste
Open it and inhale lightly
Never touch an unknown substance
Never taste an unknown substance to identify it; if it is a drug or poison, you could become sick or die.
Under the stress of a survival situation, what do you revert to?
Your emotions
Your training
Your backup
Your rehearsals
Under the stress of a survival situation you revert to your training.
Which practice does the chapter say prepares you to respond quickly and safely?
Funnel vision
Roll call
Plain talk
Mental rehearsal
Mental conditioning, the will to survive, studying, mental rehearsal and regular practice of safety procedures prepare you to respond quickly and safely.
What dictates the tactics you use?
Agency policy
The circumstances
Mental rehearsal
The area patrolled
The circumstances dictate the tactics; always stay alert and use observation to spot dangers.
Entering a crowded bar, what does situational awareness tell you to assess?
The radio channel used by the bar's security
The bar owner's lease and business license
Each person's name, race, date of birth and sex
The number of people and the position of their hands

Situational awareness is the ability to pay attention to what is going on around you; assess surroundings, the number of people, the position of their hands and threats such as weapons or items usable as weapons.
During a foot chase, your field of view narrows to the fleeing man. What is this?
Complacency
Fatal funnel
Cutting the pie
Tunnel vision
Tunnel vision (also called funnel vision) is the narrowing of the field of view during a stressful event such as a pursuit, foot chase or armed confrontation, and can make you miss other dangers.
What kind of commands does the chapter say to give a suspect?
Short, direct ones such as 'stop'
Polite requests repeated several times
Plain talk without codes
Coded signals the suspect cannot follow
Always announce that you are a law enforcement officer and give short, direct commands such as 'stop' or 'don't move!' in a tone that fits the situation.
You believe a suspect is armed. Ideally, when do you disarm him?
After he is handcuffed
Before you leave cover
During the escort
Once backup is on scene
When you believe a suspect is armed, request backup and use tactics to contact, control and disarm the suspect, ideally disarming before you leave cover.
After shooting a suspect, how long should you keep your weapon out and stay back?
Until you have told dispatch about the shooting
Until he is no threat and no accomplices remain
Until you have checked yourself for injuries
Until backup arrives and you approach
After shooting a suspect, tell dispatch quickly; keep your weapon out and stay back until the suspect is no longer a threat and you are sure no other shooters or accomplices are around.
After a shooting, when do you handcuff the suspect and give first aid?
Only after the suspect asks for help
After you check yourself for injuries
Before telling dispatch about the shooting
After backup arrives and you approach
After a shooting, check yourself for injuries, talk with arriving backup, stay behind cover and wait for backup before approaching; then handcuff when appropriate and give first aid as needed.
Rocks hit your patrol car during a riot. What does the chapter say to do?
Leave at once, roll up windows, turn off the A/C
Stop, take cover behind the engine block and call
Turn on the PA and order the crowd to disperse
Abandon the car and move to cover on foot
