If your patrol vehicle is attacked with gunfire, firebombs, rocks or other projectiles, leave the area at once, roll up the windows and turn off the air conditioning to keep chemicals out.
When does the chapter say to abandon your patrol vehicle under attack?
If it is disabled or there is no other escape
When chemicals get through the A/C system
As soon as the first projectile hits the car
When the A/C draws in chemicals
Abandon the vehicle if it is disabled or there is no other way to escape.
On foot, you come under gunfire. Besides taking cover and calling for help, what should you do?
Advance directly on the shooter's position
Return to your patrol car and leave the area
Work out a safe approach for responding officers
Roll up windows and turn off the A/C
On foot under gunfire, take immediate cover, call for help and work out a safe approach for responding officers.
What does the chapter warn about neglected equipment?
It voids your CJIS certification for the year
It must be listed in the officer safety bulletin
It voids preventive maintenance records
A breakdown can get you seriously hurt or killed
Check all equipment regularly, keep it clean and working, and keep electronic devices charged; equipment that breaks down from neglect can get you seriously hurt or killed.
What can result from letting your training lapse?
Serious injury or death for you or others
Mandatory reassessment through DAVID
Loss of CJIS certification to query FCIC
A felony for unauthorized database access
Train regularly and know your equipment; letting training lapse can lead to serious injury or death for you or others.
Why does the chapter stress constant firearm training even if you rarely shoot?
Letting training lapse risks only discipline
You may fire only once and must be ready then
Every computer action is logged and reviewable
Survival readiness includes first-aid skills
You may fire your weapon only once in your career and must be fully prepared to use it safely and effectively then; constant training builds the needed mindset.
Which does the chapter include in fitness for duty?
Enough sleep and a wellness program
A daily equipment inspection log
Firearm proficiency checks
A yearly medical review via DAVID
Poor physical condition endangers you, other officers and the public; enough sleep and an exercise and wellness program are part of fitness for duty.
You are reading messages while parked on a call. What risk does the chapter name?
Missing danger signs, causing injury or death
Creating logs reviewable as public records
Misusing your position with databases
Creating a public records law violation
Being busy or distracted can make you miss danger signs and cause injury or death.
Why should you watch where a person places their hands?
It shows inconsistencies in their story
It tells you their approximate age
It shows whether they are resisting without violence
You may stop them from using a weapon
Watch non-verbal cues: body language, where people place their hands and whether they lean toward or away from you; watching the hands may let you stop them from using a weapon.
Dispatch sends you to a simple noise complaint. What does the chapter say?
Use codes to save airtime
Never assume a call is routine
Treat it as non-life-threatening backup
Respond without backup by default
Never assume a call is routine; going in without the right mindset breeds complacency in a potentially deadly situation.
In a dangerous situation, what should you rely on?
Dispatch, to direct each of your moves
Training and experience, not emotion
Emotion and experience, not training
Instinct, since tactics vary by scene
In dangerous situations, lean on your training and experience rather than emotion to do the job safely.
Why does getting dispatch details on your mobile device help?
It encrypts sensitive data
It skips hit confirmation
It keeps the radio clear
It replaces checking in

Mobile devices give access to criminal records, driving history and agency records, and handle routine tasks such as checking in and out, viewing and receiving calls, getting dispatch details so the radio stays clear, and sending reports to a supervisor electronically.
What sets the rules for sharing electronic information?
CJIS certification and the certification exam
Database access agreements and agency policy
The FBI's security policy and public records law
Radio protocol and the agency's code system
Database access agreements and agency policy set the rules for sharing electronic information.
You text a sarcastic remark about a complainant from your patrol laptop. Why is this a problem?
Texts are broadcast to every unit on the channel
Every computer action is logged and can be reviewed
It violates the database's towing exception
The message is entered into the person's CCH
Every computer action is logged under the FBI's security policy and can be reviewed under public records law, so keep texts, emails and radio traffic professional.
What does the chapter say about mobile device use while driving?
Use it to check in and out
Minimize it to avoid a crash
Use it to keep the radio clear
Use it to send reports to supervisors
Mobile devices can distract you and reduce observation and safety; minimize their use while driving to avoid a crash.
During a multi-agency critical incident, how can dispatch let agencies talk to each other?
Patch (merge) channels
Use scrambled channels
Switch to talk around
Declare emergency traffic
Most agency radio systems have several channels, such as primary dispatch, talk around and specialized; during critical incidents dispatch can patch (merge) channels so different agencies can talk.
Which controls do radios generally have?
Patch, scramble, encrypt and emergency traffic
Talk around, primary, specialized and console
Spotlight, siren, PA and emergency lights
Power, volume, channel selection and transmission
Radios come in many brands and models but generally have controls and indicators for power, volume, channel selection and transmission.
Who is a patrol officer's central point of contact?
The booking officer at the jail
The public information officer
The public safety telecommunicator
The shift supervisor at roll call
Public safety telecommunicators (PSTs), also known as dispatchers, are patrol officers' central point of contact.
Which describes dispatchers in general?
Civilians who confirm hits for arresting officers
Supervisors who brief patrol at each roll call
Sworn officers assigned to a district station
Non-sworn staff working from a centralized area
Dispatchers are generally non-sworn personnel who run the radio and telecommunications systems from a centralized area with telephones and other resources.
Which duty belongs to dispatchers?
Confirming hits with the entering agency for you
Giving real-time information from crime databases
Deciding the level of backup each call requires
Releasing arrest information to the news media

Dispatchers answer, receive, transfer and dispatch 911 calls; they must dispatch officers; fire, rescue and EMS; and other public safety services, and give real-time information from federal, state and local crime databases.
How much privacy should you expect on the radio?
Full, on talk around
None, on any channel
Some, on encrypted channels
Some, with an earpiece
Conduct all radio communication professionally and expect no privacy on the radio.
When does the chapter say to put criminal histories on the radio?
Only when officer or public safety requires it
Whenever the channel is encrypted
Only on channels marked emergency traffic
Whenever you query a person on the computer
Put sensitive details or criminal histories on the radio only when an officer or public safety concern requires it; specialized units may use scrambled or encrypted channels for security.
How loud should your portable radio be?
Loud enough to hear but not disruptive
As loud as it goes, so no call is missed
Turned down only when telling dispatch you arrived
Loud enough for an earpiece-free scene
Set your portable radio loud enough to hear but not so loud it disrupts; an earpiece helps prevent eavesdropping.
How does the chapter define radio protocol?
Customs and rules for patching and scrambling channels
Customs and rules for building and sending messages
The certification exam required to use a radio
A list of channels dispatch can patch in an incident
Radio protocol is the customs and regulations for building and sending radio messages, including codes and signals that can differ between agencies and regions.
What is plain talk?
A system of 10-numbers for activities
A code that uses words for letters
Clear, concise speech without codes
A signal number for an armed person
Some agencies use phonetic-alphabet or uniform codes; others prefer plain talk, which is clear, concise, professional speech without signals or codes.
You are standing beside a suspect and need to tell dispatch something. Why use codes?
To get a channel set to emergency traffic only
To avoid exposing your actions
To keep the radio clear
To save airtime on the channel
Codes and signals save airtime, give exact meanings and keep radio traffic consistent and professional; use them near a suspect to avoid exposing your actions.
In the signals system, what does 'signal 0' commonly mean?
Armed person
Emergency traffic only
Emergency traffic
Prisoner in custody
The signals system says 'signal' before a number; 'signal 0' commonly means an armed person.
In the 10-code system, what does '10-15' commonly mean?
Prisoner in custody
Armed person on scene
Emergency traffic only
Officer ID and location
The numeric or 10-code system puts '10' in front of numbers that stand for activities; '10-15' commonly means prisoner in custody.
How is the tag 'RVB632' spoken in the alphanumeric system?
Romeo Victor Bravo Six Thirty-Two
Romeo Victor Bravo Signal Six Thirty-Two
Romeo Victor Bravo Six Three Two
Romeo Victor Baker Six Three Two
The alphanumeric system combines letters and numbers, such as call signs or tags; 'RVB632' is spoken 'Romeo Victor Bravo Six Three Two.'
Your new agency uses different radio codes than your academy taught. What does the chapter say?
Use the 10-code system, since it is statewide
You must become proficient in its own language
Use the 10-code system, which every agency shares
Use plain talk only, since codes vary
Your agency may use different codes and will train you; you must become proficient in its radio language.
Why should you hold the transmit button about one second before speaking?
Otherwise your tone will sound uneven
Otherwise eavesdroppers will hear you
Otherwise other traffic will be interrupted
Otherwise your first words will be lost
Before transmitting, listen for other radio traffic, then press and hold the transmit button about one second before speaking or your first words will be lost.
During a pursuit your voice rises and wavers on the radio. What does the chapter recommend?
Hold the radio farther from your mouth
Switch to plain talk and speak faster
Let dispatch take over all transmissions
Control your breathing and manage stress
Speak directly into the microphone in a clear, even tone; control your breathing and use stress management so your voice does not fluctuate under stress.
An officer on a high-priority call asks dispatch to restrict a channel. What is this called?
Patching the channels
Emergency traffic only
Talk around channel
A specialized channel
On high-priority calls officers may ask dispatch to make a channel emergency traffic only, and dispatch tells others not to transmit on it.
Why monitor other units' transmissions at all times?
In case they need backup
To confirm hits for them
To keep messages brief and accurate
In case they need to check out
Monitor other units' transmissions at all times in case they need backup.
Your radio dies during a shift. What does the chapter say to do?
Ask for emergency traffic only
Hold the transmit button longer
Check out of service on your mobile device
Use another way, such as calling dispatch
If your radio fails, use another way to communicate, such as switching channels or calling dispatch to report the failure.
Why does checking in and out with dispatch matter?
It keeps the radio clear for other units
It keeps you safer and lets them track you
It lets dispatch patch your channel
It enters your hours into FCIC for payroll
Agency policy may require telling dispatch when you start or end duty; checking in and out keeps you safer and lets dispatch send calls and track your status.
Dispatch calls your unit number. How should you answer?
Your call sign and the complaint type
Your assigned ID and current location
Your location and reason for the call
Your ID and the situation details
When dispatch calls you, answer with your assigned identification and current location.
Dispatch gives you a complaint type, location and suspect description. What should you do?
Ask dispatch to send it again on arrival
Keep it in memory so your eyes stay up
Write it down rather than relying on memory
Keep it in memory to save time en route
Write down what dispatch gives you rather than relying on memory, such as complaint type, location and suspect description; advise dispatch when you arrive and if you need backup or other resources.
Which elements does the chapter say a planned message to dispatch should contain?
Tag, color, make and model of every vehicle seen
Name, race, date of birth and sex of each subject
Complaint type, suspect description and your arrival
Officer ID, location, reason for call, situation details
Plan messages before sending; keep them brief and accurate with officer identification, current location, reason for the call and situation details.
You see a fight and stop on your own. Besides your ID and location, what does dispatch need first?
The radio channel you want patched to other agencies
The name, race, date of birth and sex for a query
What kind of situation it is and what help to send
The tag, make and model of any vehicle

When you start action on your own, give dispatch your ID and location, what kind of situation it is, what help you need, and descriptions of the people and vehicles involved (tag, color, make and model).
Which is another name for querying a database?
A BOLO broadcast to units
A wants and warrants check
A database hit
A CJIS certification review
Querying means running a database search for law enforcement purposes; it is also known as a vehicle check, records check or wants and warrants check.
Who may run a database query during your shift?
Only you, after CJIS training at each shift start
Only 24/7 agencies' records units
Only the entering agency's records unit
Dispatch, or you on your vehicle's computer
Dispatch may run queries for you, or you may run them yourself on your patrol vehicle's computer.
Where is FCIC housed?
At FDLE
At the FBI
At the clerk of court
At FLHSMV
FCIC (Florida Crime Information Center) is a database housed at FDLE with statewide information.
What is NCIC?
A national database maintained by the FBI
A network for state crime intelligence
An online driver database maintained by FLHSMV
A statewide database housed at FDLE
FCIC connects to NCIC (National Crime Information Center), a national database maintained by the FBI.
Besides all 50 states, where do NCIC records come from?
Canada, Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and D.C.
Mexico, Canada, Puerto Rico and also Guam
Canada, Mexico, Puerto Rico and D.C.
Interpol members, Canada and Puerto Rico
NCIC records come from all 50 states, Canada, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and the District of Columbia.
Why is CCH information always changing?
Officers edit it when they confirm a hit
FDLE reviews each submission before creating it
Several agencies can add charges and dispositions
The booking agency sends fingerprints to FDLE
A state attorney's office, a clerk of court and the Department of Corrections can add charges, arrests, dispositions and other information to a CCH, so CCH information is always changing.
You finish with a printed CCH. What should you do with it?
Give it to the tow company
Shred or burn it
Enter it as recovered
Keep it in the patrol car
Destroy printed CCH copies by shredding or burning after use.
What is needed for FCIC/NCIC entry?
The original report only, without supplements
A fingerprint check within 30 days
The original report and supplements
An agency that runs around the clock

Records are only reliable if entered accurately, so arrest reports and fingerprint cards must be correct, from suspects' name spellings to the laws violated; the original report and supplements are needed for FCIC/NCIC entry.
A small agency open only on weekdays wants to enter a stolen car into FCIC. What does the chapter say?
It must ask the FBI to enter it in NCIC
Agencies must run 24/7 to enter it
Any agency may enter it by day
It may enter it once CJIS-certified
Only agencies that operate around the clock, every day of the week, may enter stolen property and wanted or missing persons into FCIC.
Who must remove an FCIC record that is no longer needed?
The FBI
The entering agency
The agency that confirmed the hit
FDLE
The entering agency is responsible for its records' accuracy, timeliness and detail, and for removing them when no longer needed.
What must you do before accessing FCIC/NCIC?
Sign the towing company release agreement
Register with DAVID at FLHSMV
Register for DAVID ECI access
Complete CJIS training and pass the exam
Before accessing FCIC/NCIC you must complete CJIS certification training and pass the certification exam.
Within how many days of assignment to an FCIC terminal must you consent to a fingerprint background check?
60 days
30 days
six hours
90 days
Users must consent to a state and national fingerprint background check within 30 days of being hired or assigned to an FCIC terminal.
Your patrol computer has CJIS access. What must you do?
Share its data with tow companies only for liens
Share its data with tow companies
Physically secure it from unauthorized persons
Let only dispatch run its database queries
Computers with CJIS access must be physically secured from unauthorized persons.
A tow company asks you what a database shows about a car. What may you give it?
Nothing, under any circumstances at all
Registration and lien information
The owner's criminal history
Wanted person status
Database information is for law enforcement use only, with one exception: registration and lien information may be given to towing companies.
Which purpose does the chapter list for FCIC/NCIC transaction logs?
Public records requests
Public safety requests
Extradition decisions
Driver reassessments
FCIC/NCIC logs every user transaction; logs are used for compliance, criminal investigations, suspected misuse, public records requests and administrative purposes.
Which set of details does a person query need?
Name, driver license number and state
Name, race, date of birth and sex
Name, height, weight and scars
Name, SSN, tattoos and birthmarks
A person query needs the person's name, race, date of birth and sex.
To query a firearm, what do you give?
Serial number and manufacturer
The registration decal number
Model and caliber of the gun
Owner's name and home address on file
For a firearm, give the serial number and manufacturer; for a vehicle, the registration, VIN or registration decal number.
To query a vessel, which number may you use?
The hull identification number
The driver license number
The vehicle identification number
The firearm serial number
For a vessel, give the hull identification number (HIN), registration number or decal number; the reply describes the vehicle or vessel and gives the owner's name and address.
How do you query stolen property that is not a gun, vehicle or vessel?
Give category, manufacturer, description and markings
Give the owner's name, race, date of birth and sex
Give the VIN, hull number or registration decal
Give the serial number, model and caliber
For other stolen property, give the item category and manufacturer, a description, distinct markings, shape or other special identifiers.
Why might a query come back with several possible matches?
NCIC draws records from all 50 states and territories
It lists data the same as or similar to what you sent
It lists only data exactly the same as what you sent
Several agencies add to the same history
Query results list possible matches when data are the same as or similar to what was submitted.
Your query on a man returns a hit for a warrant. What must happen before you arrest him?
Run him through DAVID for a reassessment
Print his CCH and file it
Ask FDLE to remove the record
Confirm the hit with the entering agency
An exact database match is a hit, and you or your agency's designee must confirm it with the entering agency before arresting a wanted person or recovering a missing person or property.
Which problem does hit confirmation prevent?
A mistaken arrest on an expired warrant
A felony for unauthorized DAVID access
A record kept after it is not needed
A tow company getting criminal history
Hit confirmation makes sure the record is active and matches, avoids mistaken arrests on expired warrants or wrong data, and tells you what action to take, such as arrest or confiscation.
A hit says the entering agency will not extradite. What should you still do?
Remove the hit from FCIC yourself
Release the person and close the FCIC record
Hold the person for 24 hours anyway
Contact it in case it wants a follow-up report
Even if a hit says the entering agency will not extradite, contact that agency in case it wants a follow-up report.
What is extradition?
Surrender of a fugitive to a state or nation with jurisdiction
Return of recovered property to its rightful owner by the agency
Removal of a record by the entering agency when no longer needed
Transfer of an arrestee from patrol to booking officers
Extradition is the surrender of a fugitive to another state or nation that has jurisdiction.
Who maintains DAVID?
CJNet
FLHSMV
FDLE
The FBI
FLHSMV maintains DAVID (Driver and Vehicle Information Database), an online search database.
Which can you find in DAVID?
Computerized criminal histories (CCH)
Statewide crime intelligence (InSite)
Known or suspected terrorists files
Driver license photos and signatures

DAVID shows driver license applications, information, photos and signatures; state ID cards; identification documents of non-citizens; driving and vehicle history; insurance information; and Florida vehicle and vessel registrations.
Through DAVID, what can you request for a driver?
A license reassessment or medical review
A criminal history from FALCON
A state and national fingerprint check
A criminal history check through FALCON
Through DAVID you can ask for a driver to be reassessed for a license or a medical review, and a DAVID registration query also checks FCIC/NCIC for stolen vehicles or vessels.
Which database on CJNet is Florida's Integrated Criminal History System?
DAVID
InSite
FALCON
CART

CJNet (Criminal Justice Network) gives access to databases such as InSite (statewide crime intelligence), FALCON (Florida's Integrated Criminal History System), CART (Child Abduction Response Team) and the Florida Sexual Offender and Predator database.
A friend asks you to run her ex-boyfriend's tag in DAVID. What does Florida law say?
It is allowed for registration and lien data
It is allowed if you are on duty
It is a civil infraction only
Unauthorized access is a felony
Under Florida law it is a felony to willfully and knowingly access, or let someone access, any criminal justice computer, system or network such as DAVID or FCIC/NCIC without authorization.
A call comes in. What does the chapter say about the steps you use?
Weigh time of day only for the route
Use the same basic steps for every call
Let the dispatcher set the steps for each call type
Use different steps for criminal and civil calls
Judge each call by the information dispatch gives you, use the same basic steps for every call and tell dispatch you are on your way.
What does the chapter say about electronic mapping?
Use it, keep it updated, and keep paper maps too
Use it only to identify your area's boundaries
Use it to highlight active BOLO locations
Avoid it near a scene, since screens backlight you
Pick the safest response for you, other officers and the public; use electronic mapping but keep it updated and keep paper maps in the car.
Why might the most direct route not be the quickest?
Construction, street closings or special events
Dispatch must first patch the channels
School zones only matter during the summer
Weapons or hazards may be at the scene
Choose the safest and quickest route; the most direct route may not be quickest because of construction, street closings or special events.
Besides risks in the area, what may dispatch tell you about the call?
Whether anyone is injured
Where to park your car
Which route is the quickest
Which officer will be contact
Use personal knowledge or dispatch information to identify risks in the area; dispatch may also say if anyone is injured.
Dispatch reports a man with a knife and a fire at the scene. What do these threats help decide?
Which BOLO format to use
Whether to use plain talk or codes
Who becomes the PIO
How many officers respond
These threats help decide how many officers respond.
Responding at night to a robbery in progress, what might policy let you do near the scene?
Use the siren so the suspects scatter and flee
Use lights and siren to the door
Turn off your headlights to avoid detection
Turn off your headlights to signal backup
You may not always use lights and siren; depending on the call and policy, you may turn off headlights at night near a scene, such as a robbery in progress, to avoid detection.
When should you turn down your radio?
When dispatch gives you a BOLO
When transmitting road conditions
When telling dispatch you have arrived
When monitoring other units' traffic
Slow down near the scene so you do not pass the address or alert suspects, and turn down your radio when you tell dispatch you have arrived.
Two units respond to the same alarm. What should they coordinate?
Which direction each will arrive from
Which officer will be contact and cover
Which unit will request emergency traffic
Which officer will relay the BOLO
Stop a short distance from the address, and coordinate with other responding units which direction each will arrive from.
Pulling up to a burglary call, you see a car parked with its engine running down the block. Why does it matter?
It may belong to a lookout or a getaway driver
It means a usual car is now missing
It means the car's interior light is on
It shows the car was recently driven
Check the area around the car and report suspicious vehicles or people leaving; watch for parked cars with engines running and hidden suspects or a lookout accomplice.
Which observation does the chapter give as an obvious clue?
A streetlight that has burned out
A usual car now missing from its spot
Mail piling up in the box
Flies at a window
Look for obvious clues, such as a car sitting in a lot that is usually empty at that hour, or a car that is usually there and now is not.
While waiting for backup at a building, what should you do?
Knock and announce right away
Take and keep the best tactical position
Take the best position in the doorway
Check every entry point for tampering

While approaching, take and keep the best tactical position (especially while waiting for backup), walk up to suspicious vehicles to check for occupants, feel the hood for heat, and close in on buildings using cars, fences, trash cans or shrubs.
Which approach lowers the chance of detection?
A low crouch and an indirect route
A route past the swimming pool
A low crouch and a direct route
A route through the fatal funnel
A low crouch and an indirect route lower the chance of detection; keep scanning entrances and surroundings.
Which hand should hold your flashlight?
Support hand, held over the firearm
Support hand, held away from the body
Support hand, held against the vest
Support hand, held at the center of the body
Carry the flashlight in your support (non-dominant) hand, held away from your body, and move to a new position right after using it.
Why should you know where to aim before switching on a flashlight?
It temporarily impairs your night vision
It reveals deep corners first
It backlights other officers
It temporarily impairs suspects' night vision
Know where other officers are and do not light them up; know where to aim before switching on, since a flashlight temporarily impairs night vision.
As soon as possible after arriving, what should you decide?
Whether the matter is civil or criminal
Whether to issue a BOLO right away for the suspect
The incident type and whether a BOLO is needed
The incident type and whether backup is needed
As soon as possible, decide the incident type and whether backup is needed, check for injuries, give first aid, request medical help and preserve the scene if needed.
How should you treat suspects, victims and witnesses?
All with dignity, in one group
All with dignity and respect
Suspects as threats, victims as witnesses
Suspects firmly, victims gently
Identify everyone involved (complainants, victims, witnesses and suspects) and treat them all with dignity and respect.
What do initial contacts let you decide?
Civil, criminal, felony or misdemeanor
Hostile, non-hostile or passive crowd
Reactive, proactive or community patrol
Low, high or life-threatening risk
Initial contacts let you decide the type of complaint: civil, criminal, felony or misdemeanor.
The suspect left an hour ago and can't readily be pursued. What do you do?
Interview victims and witnesses to identify him
Set a perimeter and wait for a canine
Issue a statewide BOLO before doing any interviews
Run his name through DAVID
Find out how much time has passed; if the suspect left and cannot readily be pursued, interview victims and witnesses for information to identify the suspect.
How does the chapter say to build rapport with the people you interview?
Introduce yourself by badge number
Explain the charges with empathy
Give them a mediation referral and a resource list
Introduce yourself by name and use theirs
Ask for identification and personal and contact information, introduce yourself by name and use the person's name to build rapport.
Why separate witnesses and have each describe what happened?
It lets them check each other's facts
It lets you decide civil or criminal
It helps establish probable cause
It confirms the suspect's identity
Separate everyone, have each describe what happened, ask follow-up questions, get a suspect description and ask if they would identify the suspect later; this helps establish probable cause.
Why get written statements when required?
They replace your detailed notes
They help establish probable cause
They classify the complaint for you
They let the PIO release witness names
Get written statements when required, since they help establish probable cause for an arrest.
What does a BOLO do?
Confirms a database hit with an agency
Restricts a radio channel to one call
Describes the subject to help locate them
Requests a driver's medical reassessment
A BOLO (be on the lookout) describes the subject, gives the name and other details that help locate or apprehend them.
What does the chapter say about BOLO formats?
There is no standard format or content
They must be printed and handed out
They must be issued by a state agency
They must include a recent photograph
BOLOs have no standard format or content and may be printed, photographs, verbal reports, electronic messages or internet postings.
What should you do with current BOLOs?
Cancel them after one shift
Note the major points and review them
File them once your shift has ended
Delete them after a day on patrol
Note the major points of each BOLO and review current ones to keep the information fresh on patrol.
A BOLO is needed immediately at your scene. What should you do?
Gather and verify information for a written BOLO
Relay all significant information to dispatch
Run database checks for the suspect's warrants
Write the BOLO and get supervisor approval
Follow agency policy to start a BOLO; if one is needed immediately at a scene, relay all significant information to dispatch.
No immediate BOLO is needed and suspect information is thin. What should you do?
Run database checks for warrants and history
Relay all significant information to dispatch
Issue a Blue Alert for the suspect
Cancel the BOLO request through dispatch
If no immediate BOLO is needed, keep gathering and verifying information for a written BOLO, and run database checks for warrants and history if suspect information is thin.
A missing teen has been found. Who makes sure the BOLO is canceled?
Only the entering agency
You, another officer or dispatch
Only the PIO for the agency
Only the agency that issued it originally
Cancel a BOLO when the subject is found or it is no longer needed; you, another officer or dispatch makes sure the cancellation goes through the proper messaging system.
When planning contact with a suspect, what decision comes first in the chapter's list?
Whether to approach now or wait for backup
Whether to ask the suspect for consent to search
Whether to run the suspect through DAVID
Whether to handcuff at the start of contact
When planning contact, decide whether to approach the suspect now or wait for backup, pick a suitable location and identify hazards.
Which factors does the chapter say to weigh about the suspect before contact?
Criminal history, behavior and possible weapons
Age, height, weight and clothing description
Name, date of birth, address and Social Security number
Mode of travel, direction and last location
Weigh the suspect's criminal history, behavior and possible weapons, and keep watching hands and body language.
A suspect says he came from the store to the north while pointing south. What is this?
A form of giving false identification
An inconsistency to watch for
A sign of resisting without violence
A form of resisting with violence
Watch for inconsistencies, such as saying they came from one direction while pointing another.
Three suspects stand together at a gas station. What does the chapter stress?
Coordinating backup and suspect control is critical
Handcuff all three of them before any conversation starts
Separate and interview the leader first
Let the cover officer interview the other two
Be aware of other people present and the suspect's escape routes; multiple suspects add extreme risk, so coordinating backup and suspect control is critical.
Who does all the talking with the suspect?
The cover officer
The contact officer
The contact and cover officers
The backup officer
The contact officer is usually the primary officer; this officer leads the approach and does all the talking with the suspect, including commands and interviews.
Why should only one officer do the talking during a contact?
It lets the contact watch for crowds
It frees the cover to run queries
It builds a non-custodial atmosphere
The person focuses on one voice
Having one officer talk lets the suspect focus on one voice instead of several officers giving different directions.
During a contact, a hostile crowd gathers. Whose job is watching it?
The PIO's
The backup's alone
The cover officer's
The contact officer's
The cover officer handles officer safety only: watching the contact officer's interaction and hazards like hostile crowds, traffic or escape routes.
A third officer arrives at a two-officer contact. What does the chapter say this officer does?
Takes over the talking from the contact officer
Watches crowds instead of the cover
Gives the commands as a second voice
Shares cover duties and assists as requested
Additional officers share cover duties and assist the contact officer as requested.
Approaching a suspect, what does the chapter say to keep scanning for?
Inconsistencies
Exits only
Weapons
Witnesses

Moving toward a suspect: approach carefully, keep your eyes on the suspect, keep a safe distance, stay alert for resistance, watch position and movements for signs of flight or assault, and keep scanning for weapons.
How do you verify a suspect's identity?
Ask him for his Social Security number only
Accept his answers if they are consistent
Compare database results with his answers
Use DAVID ECI to reach his family
Ask for name, date of birth, address, SSN and legal ID, and verify identity through criminal justice databases by comparing results with what the suspect said.
FCIC shows an out-of-county warrant for your suspect. What may you do next?
Hold him until the warrant and extradition check out
Hold him until the warrant and booking check out
Pat him down and release him with a warning
Release him and ask the issuing agency to pick him up
A warrant found in a database such as FCIC/NCIC lets you hold the suspect while the warrant and extradition are confirmed; once confirmed, arrest and transport the suspect.
The issuing agency waives extradition. What must happen?
Release him and document it
Hold him for six hours
Hold him while extradition is confirmed
Transport him to that agency
If the agency that issued the warrant waives extradition, the suspect must be released; document what you did per policy.
You think a suspect has a dangerous weapon. What may you do?
A building search
A pat down
A handcuffing
A hit confirmation
With a justifiable reason to think the suspect is a threat or may run, you may handcuff at the start of contact; if you think the suspect has a dangerous weapon, do a pat down.
A detained man is cleared as a suspect. What happens to the handcuffs?
Leave them on until transport
Remove them after the hit is confirmed
Remove them now
Remove them once transport arrives
Remove handcuffs if the person is no longer a threat or no longer a suspect.
How can a relaxed, non-custodial atmosphere be useful?
It keeps the suspect focused on one voice
It can keep him focused on one voice
It can help get consent to transport
It can help get consent to search
Share current suspect information with backup; building rapport and a non-custodial atmosphere can help other efforts, such as getting consent to search.
A man refuses to give identification when lawfully detained. What is this?
Resisting without violence
Giving false identification
Resisting with violence
Breach of the peace
Resisting without violence is non-violently resisting, obstructing or opposing an officer doing legal duties, such as ignoring lawful commands, refusing handcuffs or refusing to give identification.
A handcuffed man kicks at you. What does the chapter call this?
Resisting with violence
Disorderly conduct
Giving false information
Resisting without violence

Resisting with violence is knowingly resisting or obstructing an officer by committing or offering to commit violence against the officer during legal duties, such as fighting while being handcuffed; a person can resist with violence while already in handcuffs.
A suspect seems calm. What does the chapter say?
Remove any handcuffs at once
Never assume he is compliant
Pat him down only if he moves
Let the cover officer leave
Never assume a person is compliant; be ready for violent resistance and use Defensive Tactics to stay safe and gain control.
How do officers end up as backup?
Only when dispatch assigns them
Called by others, or on their own decision
Only when a supervisor orders it
Only on life-threatening calls for service
Officers are often called to back up others, or decide on their own to back up based on the circumstances.
A suspect is still on scene at a disturbance. Which backup level is this?
Officer-initiated
Non-life-threatening
Life-threatening
High-risk
High-risk backup includes helping serve a warrant, joining a vehicle pursuit or going to a scene where the suspect is still there.
You are responding code to an emergency backup call when the suspect is arrested. What should you do?
Upgrade your response
Downgrade your response
Request more units
Request emergency traffic only
Stay in visual and verbal contact with the requesting officer and adjust as information arrives, such as downgrading an emergency response once the suspect is arrested and the scene is under control.
Arriving as backup at night, how should you use your flashlight?
Minimize it to stay hidden from the primary
Hold it close to your body
Use it to show the primary your location
Minimize it to keep others safe
On arrival, survey the scene, keep situational awareness and minimize flashlight use to keep others safe.
What does the second unit do on arrival at a call?
Do all the talking to the suspect
Take over as contact officer
Set up a perimeter on arrival
Whatever the primary officer needs
Make visual or verbal contact with the primary officer to find out what is needed, stay alert and avoid distractions such as your phone; the backup does whatever the primary officer needs.
What trend in targeted violence does the chapter describe?
More frequent and deadlier, as overall crime rose
Less frequent, following the drop in overall violent crime
Rising only in schools, while workplaces have declined
More frequent and more deadly, even as overall crime fell
Overall violent crime has dropped over three decades, yet targeted violence, including mass events such as active shooter incidents, has recently become more frequent and more deadly.
What does targeted violence involve?
A person of concern making a direct threat to police
A crowd leader inciting a hostile, agitated group
A person of concern intending to harm a known target
A random attack on people who happen to be nearby
Targeted violence involves an identifiable person of concern (perpetrator) with the intent and capability to physically harm an identifiable target (intended victim).
Which agencies' studies produced the key findings on targeted violence?
DJJ and the Department of Children and Families
FWC and local animal control
FDLE, FLHSMV and the clerk of court
The U.S. Secret Service, the FBI and others
Studies by the U.S. Secret Service, the FBI and other government agencies produced several key findings on targeted violence.
What does the chapter say about predicting violent behavior?
It can be predicted from a person's mental health history
It cannot be prevented once a threat is communicated
It cannot be predicted reliably but can be prevented
It can be predicted reliably using a demographic profile
Violent behavior cannot be predicted reliably, but it can be prevented.
A coworker matches the 'typical shooter' type from the news. What does the chapter say?
Profiles help but need a communicated threat
There is no profile, so profiling is not useful
Profiles work if the person has a weapon
Profiles work only with mental health records
There is no psychological or demographic profile of an active shooter or targeted attacker, so profiling is not useful for preventing targeted violence.
Why can others notice targeted violence before it happens?
It is usually caused by mental illness
It grows from planning and preparation
It follows a known demographic profile
It follows a single demographic profile
Targeted violence is rarely impulsive or random; it grows from organized thinking and behavior, such as planning and preparation, that others can notice and report.
What is the role of mental health problems in targeted violence?
The basis of the profile
The reason attacks are impulsive
The usual main cause
Seldom the main cause
Mental health problems are seldom the main cause of targeted violence.
What is the difference the chapter draws about threats?
Threats must be made to the target
Posing a threat requires a stated threat
Threats are made to police before attacks
Making a threat differs from posing a threat
Communicated threats should never be ignored, but persons of concern often do not threaten the target or police before attacking; making a threat differs from posing a threat.
What kind of process is BTAM?
Proactive and investigative
Reactive and punitive
Random and impulsive in nature
Reactive and investigative
BTAM is a proactive, investigative process for identifying, assessing and managing the risk of targeted violence from an identified or identifiable person.
What does BTAM apply to collect and analyze behavioral information?
The law enforcement intelligence cycle
The proactive patrol strategy
The community problem-solving model
The identify, assess and manage functions
BTAM applies the law enforcement intelligence cycle to collect and analyze behavioral information, including observable attack-related behaviors that suggest someone is on a 'pathway to violence.'
Who mainly handles the assess stage investigation?
The first patrol officer
Relatives and close associates
Trained BTAM professionals
The agency's PIO
Assess is the core of BTAM: collecting and analyzing behavioral information from all sources, including your observations; trained BTAM professionals mainly handle this investigation.
Who are often the best sources of information for a BTAM assessment?
Relatives, friends and close associates
The person's demographic profile
Trained BTAM professionals
Mental health records and diagnoses alone
The quantity and quality of reported information directly affect the accuracy of the assessment; relatives, friends and close associates are often the best sources.
Why report what you see about a person on a pathway to violence promptly?
Patrol officers lead the assessment
Violent behavior can be reliably predicted
You may be the only officer to see it
Arrest is the only management strategy
You may be the only officer to see critical information about a person moving along a pathway to violence, so report it promptly and accurately.
What range of requests do non-criminal calls cover?
Civil standbys to riots and unlawful assemblies
Lost property reports to felony warrant service
Specific information to building security checks
Animal calls to vehicle fires
Non-criminal calls range from requests for specific information to requests for a building security check.
How should your command presence fit a non-criminal call?
Lowered, since civil calls need no backup
Set to the crowd's threat level
Adjusted to fit the situation
Set by dispatch before you arrive
Every call needs a professional response with command presence adjusted to fit the situation.
Residents think an officer's orders were unfair. What does the chapter warn may follow?
They may become future information sources
They may form a community partnership
They may ask for a civil standby
They may not cooperate
Public trust depends on whether people see your authority as appropriate, proper and just; if they do not see it as legitimate, they may not cooperate.
A neighbor dispute starts calmly. Why keep your composure and proceed safely?
Every computer action is logged
Boundary disputes need a recent survey
The complainant may need a referral
A simple incident can quickly turn criminal
A simple incident can quickly turn criminal, so keep composure, show emotional intelligence and proceed safely.
A driver locked out of her car calls 911 for an officer. What does the chapter suggest?
Show empathy and explain why it isn't a police matter
Provide a civil standby
Force entry as you would for a well-being check
Refer her to the county clerk of court office
When you cannot give the service expected, use interpersonal skills to show understanding and empathy and explain why; power outages and locked-out drivers, for example, do not need police.
When do you usually need bystanders' help?
During a death notification
In civil standbys, like a custody exchange
In emergencies, like a rescue
When serving a writ of replevin
You may need bystanders' help, usually in emergencies such as rescuing a victim, giving first aid or overcoming a suspect's resistance.
Before ordering bystanders to assist, what should you do?
Check whether they are under arrest
Introduce yourself and listen
Size up the scene to judge what help is needed
Run each bystander through FCIC
Size up the scene to decide what kind of help you need and how much.
In which case may Florida law let you order the public to help?
Holding a perimeter post
Holding a person for breach of the peace
Executing a writ of replevin
Clearing rooms with the buttonhook

Florida law lets officers order members of the public to help in certain cases, such as catching or holding a person for breach of the peace, or the rescue or escape of someone arrested on civil process.
Which order to a bystander does the chapter forbid?
One given after sizing up the scene
One about first aid
One that is unsafe for them
One that is clear and specific
Never direct a member of the public to help in a way that is unlawful, beyond their ability or unsafe for them.
A neighbor asks for a well-being check. What should dispatch check?
The property's lien and registration records
The subject's call history in DAVID
The subject's call history at the location
The subject's DAVID emergency contacts
A person with medical issues may ask for routine well-being checks; neighbors or relatives may also request one, and dispatch should check the subject's call history at the location.
On arrival at a well-being check, what should you tell dispatch?
Your ending mileage
Any vehicles at the location
The flies at the windows
The mail piling up in the box
On arrival, tell dispatch about any vehicles there and take a quick look for signs of forced entry or inactivity, such as mail piling up in the box.
No one answers. Which next step does the chapter suggest?
Force entry right away to check inside
Issue a Purple Alert for the resident
Ask neighbors about whereabouts or a key
Leave a business card and clear the call
If appropriate, contact the owner or management about the person and access; find out if the person is in a medical facility or under arrest; ask neighbors about whereabouts or a key.
You can't reach the person and see no distress signs. What do you do?
Request backup for forced entry
Leave without a report, since nothing was found
Contact dispatch or record actions; follow policy
Force entry, since no answer means danger
If you cannot reach the person and see no immediate signs of distress, contact dispatch or record your actions on the in-vehicle computer and follow policy on notifying the chain of command.
Through a window you see a man collapsed on the floor. What may you do?
Follow policy, force entry and search
Wait for the landlord to bring a key
Request a death notification from the agency
Update the requester first
When you reasonably believe a person is in immediate danger, follow policy; you may force entry and search the premises.
You started a well-being check on your own. What should you find out afterward?
Whom to contact for follow-up
Whom to update on the outcome
Whether to notify next of kin
Whether to file a Silver Alert
When appropriate, update the person who asked for the check on the outcome and recommend future action; if you started the check, find out whom to contact for follow-up.
Who may start a security check?
Only the owner or property agent
A resident, you or dispatch
A resident, you or the alarm company
Only the alarm company
Security checks of homes, buildings or grounds may be requested by residents or started by you or dispatch.
Where should you park on a security check?
Close, to give foam access
Upwind, out of traffic
At a distance, watching the area
At the main entrance, spotlight on
Notify dispatch on arrival and park at a distance from the building while watching the area.
Walking a building's perimeter, what should you check?
Every hydrant for access
Every vehicle's hood for rain or dew
Every swimming pool for hazards
Every entry point for tampering
Run a vehicle check on suspicious vehicles and check every entry point for tampering while walking the perimeter.
You find a forced back door. How can you find the owner?
Posted contacts, neighbors or dispatch
The property clerk's storage logs for the area
Pawnshop records or FCIC queries
A DAVID emergency contact query

If something is suspicious, find the owner by posted contact information, witnesses and neighbors, or dispatch, and ask about circumstances; begin investigative action if there are signs of crime, damage or loss.
When might you be assigned to tell a family a relative has died?
Your agency investigates the death, or another jurisdiction asks
Only when DAVID ECI lists an emergency contact for them
Only after a 24/7 agency enters the death into FCIC
Your agency investigates the death, or the family asks
You may be assigned a death notification when your agency runs a death investigation or another jurisdiction asks.
How do you find the next of kin's contact details?
Through criminal justice databases
Through FALCON criminal history
Through a BOLO to other agencies
Through pawnshop records
Find the next of kin's name, address and phone through criminal justice databases.
You want to use DAVID ECI to find a burglary suspect's mother. What does the chapter say?
ECI may be used through CJNet
ECI may be used for any law enforcement purpose
ECI is open to tow companies
ECI is for emergencies, never investigations
DAVID emergency contact information (ECI) may be used only for emergencies, never as an investigative tool; follow agency policy when using it.
The family speaks little English. Who may help with the notification?
A booking officer
A wildlife rehabilitator
A public information officer from the agency
An interpreter, advocate or chaplain
Be sensitive to cultural and religious issues and identify language or cultural barriers first; a victim advocate, agency chaplain or interpreter may help.
The deceased's closest relative lives in Georgia. What should you do?
Call the family by telephone right away
Ask a chaplain to call them
Use DAVID ECI to call them
Ask the local agency there to notify
If the next of kin is in another town or state, ask the local law enforcement agency there to notify; get its number from dispatch, the internet or FCIC/NCIC queries.
When is a telephone death notification acceptable?
Only when the family has no local agency
Only when there is no other option
Whenever the family is out of state
Only after 24 hours have passed
Telephone notification is acceptable but least preferred; use it only when there is no other option, and then call as soon as possible.
Which statement should you avoid in a death notification?
'Here is a support referral'
'I know how you feel'
'Your relative is dead'
'Your relative has died'
Avoid statements such as 'I know how you feel' or 'God never gives us more than we can handle.'
A resident reports a monitor lizard in her yard. How does the chapter classify it?
Wildlife
Exotic animal
Livestock
Domestic animal
An exotic animal is one that is not native to Florida, such as a python, parrot or monitor lizard.
On arrival at an animal call, what do you identify first?
Whether it is wildlife or exotic
Whether FWC should be called
Whether it is loose or contained
Immediate threats and injuries
On arrival, identify immediate threats and injuries needing first aid and call EMS as needed.
What do you find out about the animal?
Alligator, snake, bear or raccoon
Python, parrot or monitor lizard
Loose, contained, injured or aggressive
Native, exotic, domestic or livestock
Find out whether the animal is loose, contained, injured or aggressive.
Who may you call to handle an alligator?
The local fire marshal
The agency property clerk
FWC or animal control
A licensed recovery agent
Next you may try to capture it or call animal control or the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC), weighing your experience and training before handling any animal.
When may you use force on an animal?
If it endangers safety or is exotic
If it is loose and exotic
If it endangers safety or is badly injured
If it is loose in a neighborhood
Use appropriate equipment and force if an animal endangers personal or public safety or is badly injured.
You discover a house fire with neighbors close by. Besides calling dispatch, what may you need to do?
Clear each room with a buttonhook entry
Set up a perimeter with natural barriers
Contact a supervisor; follow evacuation procedure
Set flares around the house for a perimeter
When you find a fire, tell dispatch right away and request help; nearby occupants may need to leave, so contact a supervisor and follow agency evacuation procedure.
Once firefighters arrive, what is your primary role?
Fight the fire alongside firefighters with gear
Lead the fire investigation and interview witnesses
Help investigators; control crowds and traffic
Lead the fire investigation
After the fire department arrives, the officer's primary role is to help firefighters and the fire marshal investigate and to keep crowd and traffic control.
Dispatch sends you to a vehicle fire. What should you ask?
Whether anyone is trapped
Whether downed lines are nearby
What the wind direction is
Whether hazmat is present
For a vehicle fire, ask dispatch what is known: where it is, what is burning, whether anyone is trapped and whether fire rescue was notified; notify dispatch on arrival.
Parking at a vehicle fire, what does the chapter say to consider?
Cones and flares
Downed lines
Wind direction and traffic flow
Wind direction and speed
When parking, consider wind direction and speed, traffic and safe access for other responders, and use your vehicle to block traffic and protect the work area.
How do you size the perimeter at a vehicle fire?
By the number of trapped victims
By the need to preserve evidence after a crash
By its nearness to traffic, property and people
By the wind direction and speed
Use cones or flares to set a perimeter, sized by the fire's nearness to traffic, property, victims and witnesses; move people, including the injured, away if possible.
Victims are trapped beyond your ability to rescue. What should you do?
Secure the scene for fire personnel
Preserve the scene for the fire investigator
Move highly flammable items away from the vehicle
Make every reasonable effort to put out the fire
If victims are trapped beyond your ability to rescue, make every reasonable effort to put out the fire immediately; extinguishers may help reach trapped victims.
Which extinguisher is better for a gasoline fire?
Water
CO2
Foam, for liquids
Foam
Foam extinguishers work best on paper or wood fires, while CO2 extinguishers are better for flammable liquids.
A crash caused a vehicle fire. What does the chapter say?
The scene must be preserved for the PIO
The scene must be preserved for evidence
It is a false alarm of fire
The scene goes to the fire marshal
You may be asked to give incident details, control traffic, hold a perimeter or give first aid; a fire caused by a crash must be preserved for evidence.
An alarm sounds because of a faulty sensor. Is it an offense?
Yes; it is a breach of the peace under state law
No; only intentional false alarms are crimes
Yes, if it sounds twice
Yes; every false alarm is a crime
A malfunctioning alarm is not an offense, but intentionally causing one is a crime.
To charge a person for a fake fire alarm, what must you document?
The alarm was caused by a power outage
The suspect spread it without reasonable cause
The suspect was a flight risk
The alarm system was inspected and found faulty
To charge false alarm of fire, document that the suspect spread a false fire alarm without reasonable cause.
Which detail best aids recovery of lost property?
The property clerk's log number
The pawnshop where it was sold
Unique identifiers like scratches
The owner's name, race and sex
Document lost property on a general information report with a description and estimated value; precise descriptions and unique identifiers like scratches or unique parts aid recovery.
After recording a lost item's serial number, what should you query?
FCIC/NCIC and a local pawn shop system
DAVID and FLHSMV records
CJNet's InSite and FALCON databases
The clerk's repair-bond records

Record serial or unique numbers in the report and enter them into FCIC/NCIC, then query FCIC/NCIC and a local system that searches pawn shops for recovered items; lost property may turn into stolen property.
You recover a stolen laptop listed in FCIC. What may you ask the entering agency?
To send a writ of replevin
To issue a hold order
To photograph the item
To remove the entry

Handling stolen property can include verifying it as stolen in FCIC/NCIC and local databases, asking the entering agency to remove the entry, and finding the owner or original report to add a supplement.
A stolen item has forensic value. What should you do?
Place a 90-day hold order on it
Enter it as found property
Submit it as evidence
Return it to the owner

It also includes photographing the item, processing it for latent prints and touch DNA, returning it to the owner if it has no forensic value (and documenting that), or submitting it as evidence if the owner cannot be found or it has forensic value.
Where do you send a suspect identified through recovered property?
The clerk of court for a bond
The property clerk for storage
The BTAM team for assessment
The right department for follow-up
Forward any suspect or item identification to the right department for follow-up investigation.
How long may a pawnbroker hold order last unless a court extends it?
No more than six hours
No more than 30 days
No more than 60 days
No more than 90 days
With probable cause that a pawnbroker's property is misappropriated, an official may place a written hold order of no more than 90 days unless a court extends it.
How many hold orders may be placed on the same pawned property?
Only one
Up to two
One per agency
No limit
The official may rescind a hold order in writing, and only one hold order may be placed on the property.
A deputy turns in a bike she located after a theft report. How is it entered into FCIC/NCIC?
As seized
As recovered
As stolen
As lost
Try to identify the owner or whether it is evidence; return non-evidence property per policy, treat stolen items as stolen property, and enter recovered property into FCIC/NCIC as recovered.
An aquarium finds an unclaimed phone after 30 days. What may it do?
Enter it into FCIC as recovered
Dispose of it or donate it to charity
Sell it in its gift shop to cover costs
Place it under a hold order
They must keep a record and hold the property at least 30 days; if unclaimed they may not sell it but must dispose of it or donate it to a charitable institution.
Two neighbors argue over who owns a strip where a hedge was planted. What do the owners need?
A writ of possession from county court
A certificate from the property clerk
A recent survey of the land
An injunction from the clerk of court
Property disputes between neighbors are usually civil; owners need a recent survey to show who owns the land in question, such as where trees were planted.
Where should you refer parties in a boundary dispute?
The property clerk
Civil court
The state attorney
County jail intake
Boundary disputes are civil matters handled outside the criminal justice process; refer the parties to civil court.
A landlord wants a nonpaying tenant out without the tenant's consent. What is the only legal way?
Changing the locks after written notice
A writ of replevin from the circuit court
An eviction proceeding in county court
Asking an officer to remove the tenant
Under the Act, the only legal way for a landlord to recover the home without the tenant's consent is an eviction proceeding in the county court where the home is located.
After a landlord wins an eviction, who receives the writ of possession?
The sheriff
The landlord
The clerk of court
The recovery agent
If the landlord wins, the court sends a writ of possession to the sheriff, who may remove the tenant and give the landlord possession after a set notice period.
A landlord changed the locks while the tenant was at work. What does the chapter say?
The tenant may enter until legally evicted
The tenant must get a writ of replevin to reenter
The officer should arrest the tenant for trespass
The landlord may do so once rent is 30 days late
A tenant keeps the right to enter until legally evicted, and the landlord may not lock the tenant out by changing the locks.
Without a writ of possession, you tell a tenant she'll be arrested if she doesn't leave. What is this likely to be?
Writ of replevin
Self-help repossession
Wrongful eviction
Civil standby
You may physically evict a tenant only after a writ of possession; removing a tenant or belongings without one, or suggesting the tenant will be arrested for not leaving, is likely wrongful eviction.
What may a creditor who leases property to a borrower get by contract?
A pawn hold order
A court injunction
A security interest or lien
A writ of possession from court
A creditor (owed money) who sells or leases property to a borrower may get a security interest or lien through a contract or security agreement.
What court order lets a creditor take collateral?
An injunction
A hold order
A writ of replevin
A writ of possession
The contract lets the creditor take the property as collateral when the borrower defaults; a writ of replevin is the court order that lets the creditor take that collateral.
When does Florida allow an agent to repossess with no court order?
Only after posting a bond with the clerk
Only after a hold order expires
Only without a breach of the peace
Only with a writ of possession
Without a court order, Florida allows self-help repossession only if it can be done without a breach of the peace.
A borrower asks you whether the agent can really take his truck. What does the chapter say?
Keep the peace; give no legal advice
Explain whether a breach occurred
Advise the borrower to post a bond
Tell the agent to come back with a writ
In a repossession dispute the officer keeps the peace and may not give legal advice to either side.
The car is hooked to the tow truck and ready to go when the owner runs out. What does the chapter say?
The owner may take the car back by posting a bond
The officer must check FCIC for a lien first
The agent must unhook it because the owner objects
The repossession is complete; let the agent leave
If the vehicle is already hooked to the tow truck ready for transport, or the agent is behind the wheel ready to drive, the repossession is complete and the agent should be allowed to leave.
The owner and the agent start shoving. What does the chapter say about taking the car?
The agent may not lawfully take it
The owner must post a bond to keep it
The officer must issue a hold order
The agent may take it with an officer
If a breach of the peace occurs, the recovery agent may not lawfully take the vehicle.
A car owner disputes a repair bill. How can he get the car back under Florida law?
Post a bond for the invoice plus storage
Ask an officer to stand by while he takes it
Get a writ of replevin from the county court
Get a hold order from the clerk
Florida law lets an owner who will not pay a repair bill get the vehicle back by posting a bond with the clerk of court for the invoice amount, storage fees included.
An owner drives his car off the repair lot without paying or posting a bond. What should happen?
Refer him to civil court
Let him go; it is a civil matter
Issue him a 90-day hold order
Investigate him for theft
An owner who refuses to pay and takes the vehicle without posting a bond should be investigated for theft.
Which civil calls does the chapter say can become highly confrontational?
Landlord-tenant disputes and child custody issues
Boundary disputes and auto repair bill disputes
Landlord-tenant disputes and repossessions
Repossessions and civil standbys
Civil calls such as landlord-tenant disputes or child custody issues can become highly confrontational.
How do you gauge the threat at a civil disturbance?
Dispatch details, call history, what you know and see
The crowd's mood, size, location and direction
The incident type and time elapsed
Whether the call is non-life-threatening
Gauge the threat from dispatch information, the address's call history, what you know about the people and what you see; stay alert and request backup to match the threat.
At a civil disturbance, what should you query FCIC/NCIC for?
Concealed weapon licenses
Injunctions or warrants
Liens or registrations
Hold orders or pawns
Query FCIC/NCIC for injunctions or warrants.
A court orders a man to stay away from his ex-wife. What is this order?
A writ of replevin
An injunction
A writ of possession
A hold order
An injunction is a court order that requires someone to do or not do certain things, such as stay away from a former spouse or a domestic violence victim.
Once a disturbance is found to be civil, what should you do?
Give information and resources like mediation
Serve a writ of possession on the tenant
Lock the tenant out until court
Refer them to the state attorney
Once a disturbance is found to be civil, give information and resources, such as referring a landlord-tenant dispute to civil court or mediation.
Tension rises during a civil standby. Which option does the chapter give?
Give one party legal advice
Serve a writ of replevin
Refer both to civil court
Suggest one or both parties leave

A civil standby usually needs little action because your presence keeps things calm; if tension rises, separate the parties, suggest one or both leave, or have them contact the clerk of court or their lawyers.
How should you act during a civil disturbance?
On the side of the court order holder
Impartially, using conflict management
On the side of the property owner
As mediator, giving legal advice
Remain impartial and use conflict management skills so the situation does not escalate.
Must a court order exist before a civil standby?
No, a hold order is used
It depends on agency policy
Yes, a writ of replevin
Only for pretrial release
Agencies differ on whether a court order must exist before a civil standby, so know your agency's policy.
Before a special event detail, what does the agency brief you on?
The command post, enforcement level and banned items
The leader's name and the group's chants
The crowd's mood, size and direction of travel
The crowd leader and the instigator
The agency briefs you on the command post, how strictly to enforce, safety concerns, banned items and other issues; know where other officers are and stay highly alert.
When does law enforcement step in to resolve an assembly?
When it is no longer peaceful
When it lacks a permit
When the crowd's direction changes
When it is protected by the First Amendment
The First Amendment protects peaceful assembly; when an assembly is no longer peaceful, law enforcement resolves the disturbance.
Who decides whether a gathering is lawful?
The fire department, by occupancy limits
The event organizer, under the permit
The crowd's leader, by agreement
You, under state law and local ordinances
People may gather if they cause no disturbance and stay within the law; you decide whether a gathering is lawful under state law and county and city ordinances.
Where might a sudden crowd come from?
Scheduled sporting events downtown
Permitted fairs and concerts
Bars closing or venues letting out
Planned fairs and outdoor concerts
Florida may require permits for planned events expecting large crowds; sudden crowds can come from bars closing or venues letting out.
Some members of a crowd are wearing gang colors and symbols. What does the chapter say to identify?
Whether it is organized and who leads it
Whether it needs a special event detail
Whether it is hostile, non-hostile or passive
Whether a rooftop vantage is free
Identify whether the crowd is organized and whether anyone is leading or agitating it; some crowds involve gang members displaying colors, symbols and weapons.
Which vantage point does the chapter suggest for monitoring a crowd?
A doorway
Inside the crowd
An attic
A rooftop
Monitor from the best vantage point, such as a patrol car, rooftop or video monitoring system.
What should you relay often to dispatch about a crowd?
The leader's name and the group's chants
The command post and banned items
Size, movement, weapons and property damage
The underage drinking you have ignored
Relay information often to dispatch or assisting agencies: crowd size and movement, weapons such as broken bottles, property damage and any escalation or de-escalation.
What is the first consideration when engaging a crowd?
Officer safety
Separating the leader
Finding a vantage point
Showing force

Any large gathering can be dangerous; officer safety is the first consideration when engaging a crowd. Sheer numbers can overwhelm responding officers and make it hard to remove or arrest members of a large group, so call for help and wait for backup.
Why keep an exit strategy around a crowd?
Attacks can come from any direction
Crowds always turn hostile
The crowd's leader may be the instigator
Attacks usually come from the front
A crowd's anonymity can provoke aggressive individuals; attacks can come from any direction, so keep an exit strategy and do not let the crowd corner you.
What can help settle a crowd?
Threatening arrest at first contact
Showing force or threatening arrest
Showing force or presence in numbers
Moving into the center of the crowd
Showing force or presence in numbers can help settle a crowd.
How can you learn why a group gathered?
The crowd's mood and location
The crowd's size and direction of travel
Signs and symbols on clothing, and chants
Whom the crowd rallies behind
Learn why the group gathered by looking at signs and symbols on clothing and listening to what people say or chant.
How can you identify a crowd's leader?
Watch the crowd's direction of travel
Listen to the group's chants
Read the signs and symbols on clothing
See whom it rallies behind and who talks
Identify the leader or instigator by watching how the crowd interacts: whom it rallies behind, who does the talking, who stands out loudest and prompts activity.
After backup arrives, what do you do with the leader?
Arrest the leader in front of all
Threaten arrest to gain control
Ignore the leader to avoid conflict
Separate and interview the leader
After backup arrives, separate the leader from the crowd and interview the leader without the group's influence.
What can threatening arrest at first contact do?
Identify the instigator quickly
Show presence in numbers
Turn a peaceful event violent
Settle a hostile crowd
Threatening arrest at first contact can turn a peaceful event violent.
You see underage drinking in a large crowd. What does the chapter say?
Use discretion; have enough backup first
Ignore it until the event ends for the night
Threaten arrest at first contact
Ignore it to keep the peace
Separate crimes inside a crowd, such as underage drinking or drug use, must be dealt with, but use discretion for safety and have enough backup before making a physical arrest.
What do your alarm-call tactics depend on?
The number of officers required
The weather and the time of day
The key holder's response time
The alarm's type and location
Some alarms are false; your response and tactics depend on the alarm's type and location, considering threats to life, danger to the public or major property loss.
Who may tell dispatch why a building's system went off?
The booking officer
The wildlife rehabilitator
The canine handler
The alarm company
Dispatch may learn the cause of the alarm from the alarm company.
A silent robbery alarm comes in from a bank. How should you arrive?
Using a stealth approach
Lights and siren to the door
Parking upwind of the bank
Knock and announce at the door
Alarms may be audible or silent, so match your response (lights and siren or a stealth approach) and stay aware of unknown risks.
How many officers do some agencies require on alarm calls?
A canine team
At least two
At least three
One, plus the key holder
Some agencies require at least two officers on alarm calls; others send a second officer in certain circumstances or on request.
Arriving at an alarm, what should you have dispatch do?
Check the subject's call history
Issue a BOLO for any suspects
Run the tags of vehicles there
Restrict the channel to emergency traffic

Park a safe distance away (up the road or several doors down, for example), have dispatch run the tags of vehicles there, size up the location and report signs of forced entry like broken glass or open doors.
A crime occurred long ago and no suspects are found. What do you do?
Begin an investigation
Clear the call as false
Plan a two-officer building search
Set a perimeter, starting large
If a crime occurred and no suspects are present, secure the scene; if much time has passed and no suspects are found, begin an investigation.
Suspects are inside after an alarm. What do you decide while planning?
Whether the call is non-life-threatening
Whether to cut the pie or buttonhook
Whether they know police are there
Whether the alarm was a false alarm
If suspects are present, plan to apprehend them: decide on a perimeter, whether they know police are there, whether a building search is needed and whether to call a canine or tactical team.
A medical alert alarm sounds. What should you do until EMS arrives?
Search the whole building for possible suspects
Run the tags of vehicles there
Assist with first aid and safety functions
Wait in your car for the key holder to arrive
For fire, medical or unknown alarms, identify the issue, notify the right agency and assist with crowd control, witness statements, safety functions and first aid until EMS arrives.
Which calls can lead to a building search?
Well-being checks, civil standbys and security checks
Special event details and riots
Lost property and found property calls
Alarms, open doors, burglaries and trespassing
Building searches follow alarms, open doors, burglaries and trespassing calls and can turn high-risk.
Before you go in to look for a suspect, what must you determine?
That the alarm company has a key
That entry is legally allowed
That the owner has been notified by phone
That a perimeter is set
Determine that a building search is legally allowed first, recalling the exigent circumstances that justify warrantless entry.
How should you get access to a building for a search?
Through a writ of possession issued to the sheriff
Through the most direct doorway
By forcing entry as on a well-being check
Through the owner or a property agent if possible
Secure the exterior with a perimeter if needed, direct uninvolved people to safety and get access through the owner or a property agent if possible.
You are the only unit at a warehouse with an open door. What does the chapter say?
Knock and announce, then search
Cut the pie at each door alone
Never search one without the owner
Never search one alone
Never search a building alone; use other officers and a canine if available, and plan with your partner how to search and secure it.
Why secure your keys and change before a building search?
They impair night vision
They create crossfire risk
Jingling reveals where you are
They backlight other officers
Jingling keys, change, phones and radios can reveal where you are, so secure loose items and lower volumes; never put your flashlight beam on other officers.
Why use hand signals and stay together while searching?
To save airtime like radio codes
To track which rooms have been cleared
To cover each other and save radio airtime
To cover each other and lower crossfire risk
Use hand signals, work together and stay together so you cover each other and lower the risk of crossfire.
What is the biggest danger in a building search?
An animal locked in a closet
A fatal funnel such as a hallway
A hidden, possibly armed suspect
Losing radio contact with dispatch
