In a building search the biggest danger is a hidden, possibly armed suspect, so search carefully and completely.
After you finish the first sweep, what should you consider?
Releasing the canine unit
Returning the building to the owner
Setting a second, smaller perimeter
Swapping areas for a second pass
After the first search, consider swapping areas with your partner for a secondary search.
How do you tell which way a door opens?
Cut the pie
Knock and announce
Find the hinges
Edge it
Decide how to enter by how doors and windows open, for example finding the hinges to see which way a door opens; most entries are through doorways.
Before going into a building, what does the chapter say to do?
Get an emergency channel and draw
Turn your radio up to full volume
Knock loudly and wait for an answer
Cut the pie at every window
Before going in, ask dispatch for an emergency radio channel and draw your firearm.
At 2 p.m. you find a home's door open on a security check. What may you do?
Edge the door
Buttonhook in
Knock and announce
Cut the pie
You may knock and announce to let people leave or suspects surrender, such as at a 2 p.m. security check of a home with an open door.
What does 'stop, look and listen' remind you to do?
Keep track of cleared rooms
Never rush in without a plan
Scan to avoid tunnel vision
Listen before transmitting
Have a plan before going in and never rush: stop, look and listen, and watch for anyone behind doors.
During a pair search, you spot a threat. What should you do?
Use a hand signal only
Request an emergency channel
Use a hand signal
Give loud verbal commands
In pairs, keep visual contact, communicate, never assume your partner sees and hears what you do, and give loud verbal commands at any threat to alert your partner.
Which is a fatal funnel?
An attic
A closet
A deep corner
A doorway
Fatal funnels are narrow spaces that restrict movement, usually doorways, hallways and windows.
Entering a room, which area must you clear first?
The deep corners
The closets inside
The doorway
The windows
Deep corners cannot be seen from the doorway and must be cleared first on entry; also watch for people in shadows and dark areas.
What governs tactics for stairways, attics and locked doors?
The circumstances
Agency policy
The fatal funnel
The partner plan
Stairways, locked doors, closets, attics and other barriers affect tactics; follow agency policy for them.
Standing beside a door and scanning the room before entering is called what?
Buttonhook
Crisscross
The fatal funnel
Cutting the pie
Cutting the pie (edging) means standing to one side of a door and scanning as much of the room as possible before entering; then enter deliberately.
When clearing rooms, what should each officer state?
Their ID and location
Their entry method
Their area of responsibility
The rooms already cleared
Clear rooms of immediate threats starting with deep corners, stay together and search each room fully before moving on, stating each officer's area of responsibility while keeping firearm safety.
What is a building search limited to?
Finding persons and evidence
Finding contraband
Finding persons
Finding recovered property
The search is limited to finding persons; after each room, close the door or keep it under observation, and return the building to the responsible person once cleared.
What is a perimeter?
A search of open ground with a partner
A natural barrier like a canal or fence line that blocks escape
An area of containment around an incident site
A show of force or presence in numbers
A perimeter is an area of containment around an incident site; its size and scope depend on the incident, and it may use natural or artificial barriers.
How big should a perimeter start?
Set by time elapsed
Sized by incident type
Large, then adjusted
Large, then fixed
Start with a large perimeter and adjust it as the situation changes; the primary officer or a supervisor decides the need and resources from knowledge of the area.
How many officers does a basic perimeter usually need?
One
Two
Four
Six
A basic perimeter can be set with minimal resources, usually two officers, and can use headlights, spotlights, barricades and natural boundaries.
What determines which resources you use at a perimeter?
Incident type, time elapsed and geography
The suspect's possible charges
The suspect's mood, size and direction of travel
The availability of air support
Use resources to protect the public while limiting contained suspects' movement; choice depends on incident type, time elapsed and geography, and may include more staff, a helicopter or canines.
At your perimeter post, a man matching the suspect walks by. What do you do?
Report it at relief
Act only if he runs
Report it and act immediately
Report it and leave your post

At an assigned post, keep the perimeter intact by constant observation, keep contact with other officers, report notable information such as anyone matching the suspect, and act immediately if someone tries to enter or leave.
How long do you stay at your perimeter post?
Until the helicopter arrives
Until six hours have passed since the incident began
Until relieved, relocated or resolved
Until the canine unit arrives
Stay at your post until relieved or relocated or the situation is resolved; good planning and positioning make perimeters work even with limited resources.
A suspect flees into a neighborhood. What comes first?
Search the business area first
Note the low-light spots
Safety: chase before backup
Safety: ask for backup and resources
Suspects often escape into open areas, building grounds, neighborhoods or business areas; safety comes first, so ask for backup and resources such as aviation or canine.
Searching open ground, how fast should you move?
As fast as the canine moves
Only as fast as the canine
Only as fast as is safe
Only as fast as your partner
Ground search techniques: work with a partner, do not expose yourself, use cover and concealment, mind your noise and move only as fast as is safe, coordinate to avoid crossfire.
During a ground search you hear dogs barking two yards away. Why does it matter?
It may point to a nuisance animal
It may point to a wildlife call
It may point to the suspect's location
It may point to a false alarm
Listen for sounds such as barking dogs or alarms that may point to the suspect's location or direction, and note riskier areas such as low light or hiding spots.
Compared with building searches, how are exterior ground searches different?
They are harder to plan
They are harder to contain
They need no perimeter
They need no partner
Exterior ground searches are harder to contain than building searches; fences, pools, vehicles, dead ends and barriers affect tactics.
A cleaner appears during your search. How do you treat her?
As a key holder for access
As a bystander to send to safety
As a crowd leader to interview
As a potential threat until confirmed
You may meet people with a legitimate reason to be there, such as employees, residents or cleaners; treat anyone as a potential threat until their status is confirmed.
Searching a bedroom for a suspect, may you open the dresser drawers?
No; a person could not be there
Yes, under exigent circumstances
No; drawers are fatal funnels
Yes; contraband may be inside
You are searching for a suspect, not evidence, so you may not search places a person could not reasonably be, such as dresser drawers.
You meet an unverified man during a search. What should you do?
Command him to assist you
Direct him to safety until confirmed
Detain him until backup arrives
Contact and detain him until confirmed
An encountered person may have information; contact and detain an unverified subject until identity and status are confirmed.
You find a suspect hiding. What does the chapter say?
Keep searching and clearing the area
Remove the perimeter right away
Keep searching and release the perimeter
Have everyone stand down and clear
Even after finding a suspect, keep searching and clearing the area, consider a secondary search, and proceed with caution if you find a suspect hiding.
A man walks away from a consensual conversation. May you pursue?
Yes; it adds reasonable suspicion
No; there are no grounds
Yes, since flight is probable cause
Yes; flight is probable cause
If a person flees during a consensual encounter, you have no grounds to pursue.
What does flight add to?
Grounds for a pat down
Probable cause to make an arrest
Reasonable suspicion to detain
Grounds for a consensual encounter
Flight alone is not probable cause to arrest but adds to reasonable suspicion to detain; with reasonable suspicion, you may lawfully pursue a fleeing suspect.
Which is a pursuit factor about the patrol car?
Its preventive maintenance
Ability to secure it
Its takedown lights
Its rear door handles
More factors: officers versus suspects, physical limits of each, available resources (canine, air support, SWAT), ability to secure the patrol car, and familiarity with the area.
You lose sight of the fleeing suspect. What should you expect?
A possible surrender
A possible ambush
Air support
A dropped bag
Keep the suspect in sight; if you lose sight, expect a possible ambush.
The suspect tosses a bag while running. What should you do?
Mark it with a cone
Hold it for a hold order
Radio its location right away
Radio its location after the chase
Fleeing suspects often discard evidence or contraband; radio the location of discarded items right away.
Which effects of stress and fatigue does the chapter list?
Distorted color under streetlights
Strong odors dulling your smell
Selective hearing, tunnel vision, rapid breaths
Dim objects blending into the background at night
Reassess safety constantly; stress and fatigue cause selective hearing, tunnel vision and rapid breathing.
Why is pursuing with a drawn firearm risky?
It backlights other officers
It reveals your location
It causes tunnel vision
It risks an accidental shooting
Pursuing with a drawn firearm depends on circumstances and risks an accidental shooting; corners, fences, woods, pools and animals raise risk, so slow down and clear blind corners tactically.
Chasing a man on foot, you lose radio contact with dispatch. What should you do?
Reevaluate the chase
Request emergency traffic
Switch to codes
Ask a bystander to call 911
Losing radio contact with dispatch is a reason to reevaluate the pursuit.
Taking a suspect into physical custody, what must you tell him?
That he is under arrest and why
His first appearance information
Where he will be taken
His bail procedures
For a physical custody arrest, tell suspects they are under arrest and why.
When do Miranda requirements apply?
Whenever you conduct an interrogation
Whenever you place handcuffs on any person
Whenever you begin a transport to jail
Whenever a juvenile is taken into custody
Miranda requirements apply whenever you conduct an interrogation.
How should you handle an arrestee's wallet and the drugs found on him?
Place both under a hold order
Keep them apart, per agency and jail policy
Keep them together, per agency policy
Enter both in FCIC as recovered
Keep the arrestee's personal property apart from evidence and contraband; agency or detention policy decides how personal property and contraband are handled.
Searching an arrestee, you find a second bag of pills nearby. What may this bring?
A civil referral
A Miranda warning
More charges
A hold order
Seize any evidence and process it per agency policy; other evidence found on or near the person may bring more charges.
The arrestee's mother asks what is happening. Why give her general information?
She must sign the arrest affidavit
She must be told the witnesses
This may be her only contact with an officer
She must be told the witnesses' names
Victims, witnesses and the arrestee's family may have a direct interest; give general information whenever reasonably possible, since this may be their only contact with an officer.
What governs what you may release to the public about an arrest?
The First Amendment
The PIO's preference
State law and agency policy
The CJIS security policy
What may be released to the public is governed by state law and agency policy.
A reporter asks you who the witnesses were. What risk does the chapter describe?
Harming the case or even your own prosecution
Breaching the peace
Committing a felony under DAVID law
Misusing your position with criminal databases
The investigation may go on after the arrest; releasing details about evidence or witnesses can hurt it or even lead to your own criminal prosecution.
A bystander films your arrest from the sidewalk. What may you do?
Refer him to the PIO for footage rules
Nothing, unless he actively obstructs
Arrest him for resisting without violence
Command him to help with the arrest
People recording you on personal devices are not committing a crime, and you cannot interfere unless they are actively obstructing the investigation.
Who prepares responses to media requests?
The contact officer on the scene
The dispatcher
The BTAM team
The public information officer
Most agencies have a public information officer (PIO) who releases information to the media and prepares responses to media requests.
During the escort to the patrol car, why keep physical control?
To check for weapons again
To show presence in numbers
To prevent falls or flight
To keep codefendants apart
Keep physical control of the arrestee during the whole escort, using Defensive Tactics escort techniques to prevent falls or flight.
A deputy hands you an arrestee he says he searched. What do you do?
Pat him down only
Search him again at the jail
Search him again yourself
Search only his pockets
Never assume the arrestee was already searched; every time custody passes from one officer to another, search again and secure property, evidence and contraband.
Before loading an arrestee, why are the rear window controls and handles disabled?
To prevent escape, injury or evidence destruction
To keep the arrestee out of a hot car
To prevent escape, injury or misconduct claims
To allow the transport to be recorded
Make sure rear window controls and door handles are disabled so they cannot open from inside, preventing escape, injury, damage or destruction of evidence.
Where do you usually seat an arrestee?
The right rear seat
The left rear seat
The right front seat
Behind the driver
Help the arrestee into the vehicle, usually the right rear seat, and secure the seat belt.
Why do some agencies record transports?
It protects against unfounded misconduct claims
It reports the ending mileage
It replaces the need to report beginning and ending mileage
It records the ending mileage
If required, give dispatch your destination and beginning and ending mileage; some agencies require audio or video recording of transports, which protects against unfounded misconduct claims.
You arrest a 16-year-old and an unrelated adult at the same scene. May they ride together?
No, unless held under six hours
No, unless they are codefendants
Yes, if under six hours
Yes, if kept out of sight and hearing
A juvenile may not be transported with an adult arrestee unless the two are codefendants.
Your arrestee needs EMS. What must you do?
Pull over somewhere safe and call your supervisor
Report the ending mileage to dispatch
Notify dispatch and follow policy on riding along
Restrain him in front for the ride
Notify dispatch when taking an arrestee to a medical facility or requesting EMS, and follow policy on accompanying an arrestee taken by ambulance.
An arrestee uses a motorized wheelchair. What does the chapter say?
Seat him in the right front
Use a larger vehicle or an ambulance every time
Adapt transport without giving up safety
Adapt transport without giving up the chair
Adapt transport for an arrestee with a disability or special need, such as a service animal or motorized wheelchair, without giving up officer safety.
How may you restrain a pregnant arrestee?
Behind the back
In front, only during labor
In front
Behind, double locked
For a pregnant arrestee, you may place restraints in front.
You can't leave right after loading on a hot afternoon. What does the chapter warn?
Enable the rear window controls so air can flow in
Report beginning mileage
Never leave an arrestee in a hot car long
Move him to the left rear seat
If you cannot leave right after loading, consider weather and temperature, and never leave an arrestee in a hot car for a long time.
A very large arrestee won't fit safely in your car. What may be required?
Front restraints for the trip
A civil standby at the jail
A larger vehicle or a second officer
A larger vehicle or an ambulance
The arrestee's size, health or medical condition may require a larger vehicle, an ambulance or a position change.
An arrestee seems impaired. What should you check?
Whether he is a codefendant
Whether he has a service animal needing accommodation
Whether a medical condition is the cause
Whether he has a call history
If a person seems impaired or not in control of physical functions, check whether a medical condition may be the cause and get immediate medical attention if so.
Under the Healthy Pregnancy for Incarcerated Women Act, when may a person in labor be restrained?
Flight risk or a medical reason
Flight risk or an extraordinary reason
When charged or adjudicated as an adult
Substantial danger or flight risk

The Healthy Pregnancy for Incarcerated Women Act bars restraining an incarcerated pregnant person during labor, delivery or postpartum recovery unless she is a substantial flight risk or another extraordinary medical or security reason requires it.
Arriving at the jail, what do you give dispatch?
The pepper spray use
The arrestee's property list
The arrestee's charges
Your ending mileage
On arrival, notify dispatch with ending mileage, approach the drop-off point and get clearance to enter.
Where may you secure your firearm at the jail?
In your holster, strap fastened
Trunk, weapons locker or lockbox
Rear compartment, out of view
With the arrestee's property
At the detention facility, lock up your weapons in the patrol car trunk, a weapons locker or a lockbox at the drop-off point; the agency and facility set which places are acceptable.
When does responsibility for an arrestee pass from you?
When you get clearance to enter the drop-off point
When facility staff receive the arrestee
When you report ending mileage
When the affidavit is signed
You are responsible for the arrestee until facility staff receive them; watch for hazards such as codefendants or other arrestees.
When should you search your car's passenger compartment after a transport?
Before the next shift
As soon as practical
Only if the arrestee was combative
As soon as booking ends
Give the facility the right documentation, and thoroughly search the vehicle's passenger compartment as soon as practical after transport.
For how long may a juvenile be held in an adult jail for temporary custody?
Six hours or less
Thirty days
Thirty days or less
Until DCF arrives

A juvenile may be kept in a jail's secure booking area or an adult jail for temporary custody of six hours or less, or for prints and photos, as long as adult arrestees cannot see or hear the juvenile.
Which juveniles are exceptions to adult-jail limits?
Those awaiting transport to detention
Those in pre-court holding areas
Those who are codefendants
Those charged or adjudicated as adults
Most juveniles in adult jails or lockups are awaiting transport or in pre- or post-court holding; exceptions are juveniles charged as adults or emancipated or adjudicated as adults.
How can you confirm a juvenile's legal adult status?
DAVID emergency contact information records
DJJ, court records or criminal histories
The arrest affidavit
FALCON criminal histories only
Confirm a juvenile's legal adult status with the Department of Juvenile Justice, court records or criminal histories.
Until when are you responsible for a juvenile with a medical condition?
Until booking receives the affidavit
Until DJJ confirms adult status
Until six hours pass
Until a parent, guardian or DCF takes it
You are responsible for a juvenile with a medical condition, mental illness or substance effects, and until a parent, guardian or DCF representative takes responsibility.
When should you try to tell a juvenile's parents?
Within a reasonable time after arrest
Before Miranda warnings
Only if DCF is involved or taking custody
Within six hours
Make a thorough effort to tell a juvenile's parents within a reasonable time after the arrest.
Can a juvenile be released on their own recognizance?
No; a qualified adult must take custody
Yes, if held under six hours
Yes, if emancipated
No; juveniles are always held for court
A juvenile cannot be released on their own recognizance; an adult relative, qualified adult or organization must take custody and sign booking forms or charging documents.
What do you give the booking officer before transferring custody?
Personal property, never evidence or contraband
Your weapons, for safekeeping
Personal property and evidence, never contraband
Evidence, after a hold order
Give the booking officer the arrestee's personal property, but never contraband or evidence; then transfer custody.
Who fills out the arrest affidavit?
The state attorney
The arresting officer
The booking officer
The transporting officer's supervisor
The arresting officer must fill out an arrest affidavit that goes with the arrestee to the booking officer.
Which data do you record about an arrestee?
Name, race, sex, DOB, SSN, charges, case no.
Mode and direction of travel at arrest
Tag, color, make and model of the car
Height, weight, scars, tattoos and any birthmarks
Record the arrestee's name, race, sex, date of birth, SSN, criminal charges and case number.
Why fill out fingerprint cards and arrest reports accurately?
DAVID uses them for reassessments
FCIC/NCIC builds histories from them
They let booking reuse photos
They set the chain of custody
FCIC/NCIC builds criminal history data from fingerprint cards and arrest and correctional reports, so fill them out accurately.
What may many facilities use instead of a new booking photo?
Security video stills
Driver license photos
Photos from past arrests
Photos from family members
Booking photos give a visual record; many facilities can use photos from past arrests instead of taking new ones.
Why submit evidence by established procedure?
To keep the chain of command
To support a hold order
To keep the chain of custody
To enter it as recovered
Process and package evidence and seized contraband per policy, and submit it by established procedure to keep the chain of custody and reduce legal challenges.
After turning over the arrestee and affidavit, what do you tell dispatch?
The call is complete and its outcome
The pepper spray use
The arrestee's charges and the case number
Your ending mileage
After turning over the arrestee and affidavit, tell dispatch the call is complete and its outcome.
Why document arrests completely and accurately?
So the facts clearly support prosecution
So the facts clearly support release
So FDLE can create the arrestee's CCH
So the chain of custody holds
Document arrests completely and accurately so the facts clearly support prosecution.
Which device is clipped near an officer's collar to talk without lifting the radio?
A scrambled earpiece
A vehicle-mounted radio
A dispatch base station
A shoulder microphone
Radio equipment shown in the chapter includes a handheld radio, a vehicle radio and a shoulder microphone.
A deputy finds a records system the chapter never names. May the agency use it?
Yes; agencies may use other databases
No; only FCIC, NCIC and DAVID
Only for agencies that run 24 hours a day
Only through CJNet
Agencies may use other criminal justice databases beyond those the chapter lists.
What does the chapter call improperly managing criminal justice databases?
A wrongful eviction
Resisting without violence
A breach of the peace
Misuse of your position
Mismanaging criminal databases is misuse of your position.
A witness finishes describing the robbery. What does the chapter say you should do?
Ask her for a written statement only
Take detailed notes of the account
Take brief notes of the account
Relay it as a BOLO right away
Take detailed notes of each account.
Which reason for a BOLO does the chapter list?
A tenant needing eviction
An area needing extra patrol
A hit needing confirmation
A driver needing reassessment
Local, state or national agencies issue BOLOs for missing or wanted persons, stolen property, suspicious activity or areas needing extra patrol.
What makes a safe approach to a suspect, per the chapter?
A backup officer who takes command
One officer who talks and one who searches
A contact and a cover officer, each with a role
Several officers giving commands at once
A safe approach is teamwork between a contact officer and a backup or cover officer, each with a separate role.
On a call, a man says something that worries you about future violence. What is critical?
Comparing him to a shooter profile
Collecting and reporting it per policy
Arresting him under BTAM on the spot
Waiting to see if he makes a threat
Identify: on calls you may see or hear something that identifies a person of concern; collecting and reporting it per agency policy is critical to prevention.
No one answers the door at a well-being check. Where else does the chapter say to look?
At the windows for flies
In the car for a parking pass
At the mailbox for piled-up mail
In the windows for signs of distress
Try to reach the person by knocking or phoning, and look in the windows for the person's status or signs of distress.
You need immediate access for a well-being check. What may you request?
A hold order from the property's owner or manager
Backup or other resources for forced entry
An injunction from the clerk of court
A writ of possession from the county court
If you need immediate access, call for backup or other resources to help with forced entry; give first aid, relay the person's status to dispatch or request more emergency resources.
Which gear does the chapter name for security checks?
Gloves, masks and biohazard kits
Spotlights, flashlights and radios
Cones, flares and portable barricades
Extinguishers and first-aid kits
Use gear such as spotlights, flashlights and radios on security checks.
You finish a security check. What do you do?
Swap areas with backup for a secondary search
Set a perimeter with two officers
Begin a building search alone
Report necessary information to dispatch
After a security check, report the necessary information to dispatch.
Relatives are located nearby. How does the chapter say to notify them?
Through a chaplain alone
In person if possible
Through their local agency
By telephone right away
Once relatives are located, visit the family in person if possible.
How does the chapter describe the risk on an in-person death notification?
Life-threatening, like a serious crash
High-risk, like serving a warrant
It never needs a second officer present
Usually calm, but practice officer safety
You may request a backup officer for an in-person notification; it is normally non-confrontational, but practice officer safety.
The family asks how the death happened, but the case is open. What should you do?
Say 'I know how you feel'
Share the witnesses' names
Refer them to the county clerk of court's office
Explain the investigation limits answers
Answer the family's questions about the deceased's location and the circumstances; if the investigation does not allow answers, explain that.
Besides FWC and animal control, whom may you request on an animal call?
Local fire marshals
Agency property clerks
Wildlife rehabilitators
Licensed recovery agents
You may request wildlife rehabilitators or nuisance animal trappers.
Your extinguisher can't knock down a burning car. What should you do?
Request the fire marshal
Switch to a foam extinguisher
Call the fire marshal only
Request fire rescue
Judge fire intensity and request fire rescue if you cannot put it out; survey for victims and hazards such as hazmat and downed power lines.
At a vehicle fire, someone may be inside. What do you do first?
Ask about wind direction
Move flammable items away from the burning car
Check if it is occupied; start rescue
Set cones and flares for the perimeter
Check if the vehicle is occupied; begin rescue, move victims to safety and give first aid.
With every victim out and no immediate threat, what comes next?
Move flammable items before victims
Release the scene to the owner
Secure the scene for fire personnel
Secure the scene for the fire marshal
Once victims are out and there is no immediate threat, secure the scene for fire personnel and evaluate and move highly flammable or combustible items if practical.
How does the chapter define a false alarm of fire?
An activation with no sign of a real threat
An alarm triggered by a power outage
An alarm spread without reasonable cause
An alarm caused by weather or animals
A false alarm of fire is an alarm activation with no evidence of a reasonable threat; it may be intentional or a malfunction.
A man turns in a bag of someone else's prescription pills. What does the chapter say to follow?
Replevin law
Found-property law
Hold-order law
Agency policy
Examples: a lost cell phone, a burglary victim finding stolen items at a pawn shop, or someone turning in prescription drugs or valuables; follow agency policy.
Which is a way stolen property may come to your attention?
A resident tells you about it
A landlord changes the locks
A clerk issues a certificate
A clerk issues a release certificate
Stolen property may surface on routine patrol, at traffic stops or arrests, or from a resident.
Where does the chapter say stolen property is often sold?
To theme parks
To repair shops
To recovery agents
To pawnbrokers
Stolen property is often sold to pawnbrokers.
Which places does Florida law let dispose of found property?
Hotels and motels
Theme parks, zoos and museums
Pawnbrokers and the clerk
Property clerks and the sheriff
Florida law lets theme parks, entertainment complexes, zoos, museums, aquariums, public food service and public lodging establishments dispose of or donate lost or abandoned property found on site.
At a landlord-tenant disturbance, what does the chapter say you need?

A writ of replevin from the landlord
A writ of possession in hand
A recent land survey
You need a general idea of what action, if any, you can take at landlord-tenant disturbances.
Where do arguments over unpaid mechanic bills usually arise?
At pawnbroker shops
At mobile home parks
At RV parks and campgrounds
At auto repair shops
Disputes over repair bills arise at auto repair shops.
At a civil disturbance, how do you decide whether a crime occurred?
The FCIC query results alone
A recent survey of the land
Assessment, interviews and observing
Whether a court order exists for a civil standby
Separate, identify and interview everyone involved and verify through assessment, interviews and observation whether a crime was committed.
What is a civil standby?
Holding pawned property 90 days
Mediating a boundary dispute
Serving an eviction writ by yourself alone
Keeping the peace through presence
A civil standby is when an officer keeps the peace through presence while a court order is served or a call is handled.
During a civil standby, when do you separate and question the parties?
Only after the PIO arrives
When needed, to decide on enforcement
Only after a writ is shown
Never; give legal advice instead
When needed, separate and question the parties to decide whether to take enforcement action.
Which assignment does the chapter call a special event detail?
A civil standby
Holding a perimeter post
A building search
Security at a concert
Special event details include security for sporting events, concerts, fairs and political rallies, and for event facilities, attendees and employees.
A non-hostile crowd has been passive all night. What does the chapter warn?
Release the specialized units
Stay complacent but alert
Never become complacent
Release the exit strategy
Non-hostile crowds are more passive, but never become complacent because things change fast.
How should you speak to a crowd's leader?
Firmly, with an arrest warning
Through the event's command post
Professionally, in front of the group
Professionally, with respect
Speak professionally with dignity and respect, tell the leader why officers are there, and ask the leader to comply with the law; the leader's cooperation is a major factor.
How can you learn an alarm's cause?
Observing, interviewing and dispatch information
Resetting the panel to see if it repeats
Observing, interviewing and the key holder only
Running the alarm company through FCIC
Find the alarm's cause by observing, interviewing people present and getting dispatch information such as a suspect description, false alarm notice or the key holder's response.
As you move through a building, what must you keep track of?
Your partner's entry method
Fatal funnels you have crossed
Deep corners in each room
Rooms or areas already cleared
Search systematically and keep track of cleared rooms or areas.
Which pair does the chapter call the two common room-entry methods?
Fatal funnel and deep corner
Edging and cutting the pie
Knock and announce, then enter
Crisscross and buttonhook
Two common room-entry methods are crisscross and buttonhook; coordinate with other officers whichever you use.
At which points in transport should you treat an arrestee with dignity?
At every point
Only when cuffed in front
Only during the escort
Only at the facility
Treat the arrestee with dignity and respect at every stage of transport.
What must the rear compartment be clear of before loading?
Seat belts and restraints
Seat belts and restraint straps
Window and door controls
Drugs, weapons and equipment
Make sure the rear compartment is clear of drugs, weapons and equipment.
When do you take the handcuffed arrestee's property and contraband?
At the jail, during booking
Immediately, before the search
Immediately after a thorough search
At the car, after loading
Search the handcuffed arrestee thoroughly and immediately take all property, evidence and contraband.
How do you keep control of the arrestee inside the facility?
Leaving the arrestee in the car first
Restraining him in front
Verbal commands and physical direction
Hand signals to your partner
Gather the arrestee's property, remove the arrestee safely and keep physical control into the facility with verbal commands and physical direction.
Who processes arrestees at many county jails?
Dispatchers on the radio
Public information officers
Booking or intake officers
Recovery agents for creditors
Many agencies have booking or intake officers (law enforcement or correctional) at the county jail, and you must know and follow their policies.
A detained man gives a fake name. Which of the chapter's two common non-cooperation forms is this?
Resisting an officer with violence
Breach of the peace in public
Resisting an officer without violence
Giving false information while detained
Two common forms of non-cooperation are resisting an officer (with or without violence) and giving false information while arrested or lawfully detained.
A lawfully detained woman gives her sister's name and date of birth. What is this?

Resisting with violence
Refusing identification
Resisting without violence
Giving false identification happens when someone under arrest or lawful detention gives the officer a false name or otherwise lies about who they are.
Which aspect of a person of concern does the chapter list for BTAM to consider?

Race and ethnicity
Age and gender
Shooter profile match
Consider the person's current life circumstances, intimate relationships and close associations, financial status and resources, education and training, and mental and physical health.
In BTAM's manage stage, where do the strategies come from?
A demographic profile
The identification report
The first patrol report
The assessment
Manage: agencies choose strategies from the assessment to prevent or reduce violence, and patrol officers may be asked to help BTAM investigators.
Mid-chase, your radio goes silent and dispatch can't hear you. What does the chapter call this?
A reason to holster your firearm
A reason to draw your firearm
A reason to reevaluate the pursuit
A reason to drop the perimeter
Losing radio contact with dispatch is a reason to reevaluate the pursuit.
Who may end a foot pursuit?
You or a supervisor, at any time
Only you, once the suspect is caught
Only a supervisor, by radio
You or dispatch, at any time

You or a supervisor may end a pursuit at any time, including when the suspect's location is unknown, you cannot continue from injury, fatigue or unfamiliarity, or the suspect is identified and no longer a threat.
Which topic does the chapter list for explaining to an arrestee's family?
The written statements
First appearance information
The evidence collected so far
The names of the witnesses
Be empathetic while explaining the charges, where the arrestee will be taken, bail procedures and first appearance information.
A dim figure seems to vanish against a dark wall. Which sense does the chapter call the usual starting point of observation, and what limits it here?
Smell; strong odors dull the other senses
Touch; gloves dull what you can feel
Hearing; background noise masks movement
Sight; dim objects blend into the background
Sight is often the starting point of observation; nearsightedness or farsightedness without corrective lenses limits vision.
Officers rely on laptops, tablets and smartphones. Which device does the chapter say they use most?
The laptop
The body camera
The radio
The tablet
The radio is the device officers use most; it carries vital information to and from dispatch and other officers, calls for backup and helps identify suspects or wanted persons.
Which term means: Dealing with a crime after it happens by responding right away to improve the chance of catching the subject?

Community partnerships
Community-oriented policing
Proactive patrol
Reactive patrol deals with a crime after it happens; it calls for an immediate response to raise the chance of catching the subject.
Which term means: Discouraging crime through an officer's regular presence, moving through the area and talking briefly with people?
Proactive patrol
Community-oriented policing
Suspicious activity
Reactive patrol
Proactive patrol discourages crime through an officer's regular presence in the area.
Which term means: Residents and law enforcement working together on the causes of crime and other neighborhood problems?
Reactive patrol
Community partnerships
Community-oriented policing
Proactive patrol
Community-oriented policing asks residents to join law enforcement in tackling the causes of crime and other neighborhood problems.
Which term means: The part of community policing that builds understanding and trust between an agency and its community?
Problem solving
Community partnerships
Proactive patrol
Community-oriented policing
Community partnerships build understanding and trust between agencies and the communities they serve.
Which term means: The part of community policing that uses partnerships to build long-term, proactive programs?
Community partnerships
Community-oriented policing
Problem solving
Proactive patrol
Problem solving, the second part, uses partnerships to build long-term, proactive programs that address community problems.
Which term means: A brief operational meeting before a shift that passes on current issues to watch for on patrol?
Community-oriented policing
Community partnerships
Roll call
Proactive patrol
Roll call is a brief operational meeting before a shift that shares current issues to keep in mind on patrol.
Which term means: Anything happening that is abnormal for that time of day in that particular area?
Community-oriented policing
Community partnerships
Proactive patrol
Suspicious activity
Suspicious activity is any activity that is abnormal for that time of day in that particular area.
Which term means: Using your senses to recognize what is happening by noticing people, things or circumstances?
Concealment
Cover
Observation
Situational awareness
Observation means using your senses to recognize what is happening by noticing people, things or circumstances.
Which term means: Anything that puts a bullet-resistant barrier between you and a threat?
Observation
Cover
Non-verbal cues
Concealment
Cover is anything that puts a bullet-resistant barrier between you and a threat and protects you from gunfire.
Which term means: One or more objects that hide you from a threat's view but may not stop a bullet?
Non-verbal cues
Concealment
Tunnel vision (funnel vision)
Cover
Concealment is one or more objects that hide you from a threat's view but may not stop a bullet.
Which term means: Staying alert to what is happening around you so you can react to it?
Concealment
Observation
Situational awareness
Cover

Situational awareness is the ability to pay attention to what is going on around you; assess surroundings, the number of people, the position of their hands and threats such as weapons or items usable as weapons.
Which term means: A field of view that narrows under stress, as in a pursuit or armed confrontation?
Cover
Non-verbal cues
Concealment
Tunnel vision (funnel vision)
Tunnel vision (also called funnel vision) is the narrowing of the field of view during a stressful event such as a pursuit, foot chase or armed confrontation, and can make you miss other dangers.
Which term means: Body language, such as where a person places their hands and whether they lean toward or away from you?
Cover
Tunnel vision (funnel vision)
Non-verbal cues
Concealment
Watch non-verbal cues: body language, where people place their hands and whether they lean toward or away from you; watching the hands may let you stop them from using a weapon.
Which term means: Another name for a dispatcher, the hub of contact for patrol officers?
Plain talk
Patching
Public safety telecommunicator (PST)
Radio protocol
Public safety telecommunicators (PSTs), also known as dispatchers, are patrol officers' central point of contact.

Radio protocol
Public safety telecommunicator (PST)
Patching

Which term means: Clear, concise, professional speech on the radio without signals or codes?
Public safety telecommunicator (PST)
Plain talk
Radio protocol
Patching
Some agencies use phonetic-alphabet or uniform codes; others prefer plain talk, which is clear, concise, professional speech without signals or codes.
Which term means: Merging radio channels during critical incidents so several agencies can communicate?
Plain talk
Public safety telecommunicator (PST)
Radio protocol
Patching
Most agency radio systems have several channels, such as primary dispatch, talk around and specialized; during critical incidents dispatch can patch (merge) channels so different agencies can talk.
Which term means: Running a database search for law enforcement purposes; also called a vehicle, records or wants and warrants check?
Querying
CJNet
FCIC
DAVID
Querying means running a database search for law enforcement purposes; it is also known as a vehicle check, records check or wants and warrants check.
Which term means: A statewide database housed at FDLE?
DAVID
FCIC
Computerized criminal history (CCH)
NCIC
FCIC (Florida Crime Information Center) is a database housed at FDLE with statewide information.
Which term means: A national database maintained by the FBI?
CJNet
FCIC
DAVID
NCIC
FCIC connects to NCIC (National Crime Information Center), a national database maintained by the FBI.
Which term means: The record FDLE creates in FCIC from arrest information and fingerprints?
DAVID
Computerized criminal history (CCH)
CJNet
NCIC

FCIC
CJNet
DAVID

Which term means: Handing a fugitive over to another state or nation with jurisdiction?
DAVID
Extradition
CJNet
Computerized criminal history (CCH)
Extradition is the surrender of a fugitive to another state or nation that has jurisdiction.
Which term means: The online driver and vehicle database maintained by FLHSMV?
NCIC
FCIC
Querying
DAVID
FLHSMV maintains DAVID (Driver and Vehicle Information Database), an online search database.
Which term means: The network that gives access to InSite, FALCON, CART and the sexual offender and predator database?
Computerized criminal history (CCH)
Hit
DAVID
CJNet

Which term means: A description of a subject and other details that help locate or apprehend them?
Contact officer
Computerized criminal history (CCH)
BOLO
CJNet
A BOLO (be on the lookout) describes the subject, gives the name and other details that help locate or apprehend them.
Which term means: Usually the primary officer; leads the approach and does all the talking with the suspect?
Resisting an officer without violence
Resisting an officer with violence
Cover officer
Contact officer
The contact officer is usually the primary officer; this officer leads the approach and does all the talking with the suspect, including commands and interviews.
Which term means: The backup officer, responsible only for officer safety at the scene?
Contact officer
Cover officer
Resisting an officer without violence
Resisting an officer with violence
The cover officer handles officer safety only: watching the contact officer's interaction and hazards like hostile crowds, traffic or escape routes.
Which term means: Non-violently resisting, obstructing or opposing an officer doing legal duties?
Cover officer
Resisting an officer without violence
Contact officer
Resisting an officer with violence
Resisting without violence is non-violently resisting, obstructing or opposing an officer doing legal duties, such as ignoring lawful commands, refusing handcuffs or refusing to give identification.
Which term means: Knowingly resisting or obstructing an officer by committing or offering violence during legal duties?
Cover officer
Resisting an officer with violence
Contact officer
Resisting an officer without violence

Resisting with violence is knowingly resisting or obstructing an officer by committing or offering to commit violence against the officer during legal duties, such as fighting while being handcuffed; a person can resist with violence while already in handcuffs.
Which term means: A person arrested or lawfully detained stating a fake name or otherwise lying about who they are?
Resisting an officer with violence
Giving false identification
Cover officer
Contact officer
Giving false identification happens when someone under arrest or lawful detention gives the officer a false name or otherwise lies about who they are.
Which term means: Violence by an identifiable person of concern with intent and capability to harm an identifiable target?
Behavioral threat assessment and management (BTAM)
Pathway to violence
Targeted violence
Giving false identification
Targeted violence involves an identifiable person of concern (perpetrator) with the intent and capability to physically harm an identifiable target (intended victim).
Which term means: A proactive, investigative process for finding, judging and reducing the risk that a person will commit targeted violence?
Contact officer
Resisting an officer with violence
Behavioral threat assessment and management (BTAM)
Pathway to violence
BTAM is a proactive, investigative process for identifying, assessing and managing the risk of targeted violence from an identified or identifiable person.
Which term means: Observable, attack-related behaviors suggesting a person may be heading toward targeted violence?

Resisting an officer with violence
Behavioral threat assessment and management (BTAM)
Pathway to violence
BTAM applies the law enforcement intelligence cycle to collect and analyze behavioral information, including observable attack-related behaviors that suggest someone is on a 'pathway to violence.'
Which term means: Any creature that is not native to Florida?
Exotic animal
Borrower
Hold order
False alarm of fire

Which term means: An activation with no evidence of a reasonable threat, by malfunction or on purpose?
Hold order
Borrower
False alarm of fire
Exotic animal
A false alarm of fire is an alarm activation with no evidence of a reasonable threat; it may be intentional or a malfunction.
Which term means: A written notice freezing pawned property believed misappropriated for up to 90 days?

Writ of possession
Writ of replevin
Self-help repossession

Writ of replevin
Self-help repossession
Writ of possession

Creditor
Self-help repossession
Wrongful eviction

Which term means: The person or company that is owed money?
Borrower
Creditor
Writ of possession
Self-help repossession

Which term means: The person who takes out a loan?
Writ of possession
Creditor
Self-help repossession
Borrower
A creditor (owed money) who sells or leases property to a borrower may get a security interest or lien through a contract or security agreement.

Wrongful eviction
Writ of replevin
Self-help repossession

Writ of replevin

Which term means: A court order requiring a person to do or not do specific acts, such as stay away from someone?

Civil standby

Which term means: Keeping the peace through officer presence while a court order is served or a call is handled?

Writ of possession
Self-help repossession
Injunction
A civil standby is when an officer keeps the peace through presence while a court order is served or a call is handled.
Which term means: A narrow space that restricts movement, usually a doorway, hallway or window?
Buttonhook (wraparound) technique
Fatal funnel
Crisscross technique
Deep corner

Which term means: A spot you cannot see from the doorway, so it is checked first when you go in?

Deep corner
Crisscross technique

Which term means: Standing to one side of a door and scanning as much of the room as possible before entering?
