Keeping electronic devices charged and clean
Poor physical condition endangers you, other officers and the public; enough sleep and an exercise and wellness program are part of fitness for duty.
A child is badly hurt at a scene and a deputy feels overwhelmed. What does the chapter say to rely on?
Training and experience rather than emotion
Emotion rather than training and experience
Training and emotion rather than experience
Experience and emotion rather than training
In dangerous situations, lean on your training and experience rather than emotion to do the job safely.
You want to run a driver's history and send a report to your supervisor without tying up the radio. Which device does the chapter say handles this?
Your vehicle radio
Your shoulder microphone
Your handheld radio
Your mobile device

Mobile devices give access to criminal records, driving history and agency records, and handle routine tasks such as checking in and out, viewing and receiving calls, getting dispatch details so the radio stays clear, and sending reports to a supervisor electronically.
Another agency's officer asks you to email him records from a database. What sets the rules for sharing this information?
Database access agreements and your supervisor
Database access agreements and agency policy
FDLE and the requesting agency's own policy
Agency policy and the requesting officer's agency
Database access agreements and agency policy set the rules for sharing electronic information.
A deputy reads call notes on her laptop while driving to a call. What does the chapter warn?
Minimize device use while driving to avoid a crash
Minimize radio use while driving to avoid a crash
Never use a mobile device while on patrol
Use the device only to view and receive calls
Mobile devices can distract you and reduce observation and safety; minimize their use while driving to avoid a crash.
A deputy needs backup right now. Which device does the chapter say officers use most to call for it?
The radio
The mobile device
The mobile laptop
The base station
The radio is the device officers use most; it carries vital information to and from dispatch and other officers, calls for backup and helps identify suspects or wanted persons.
A deputy wants to talk to dispatch without taking her radio off her belt. Which equipment shown in the chapter helps?
A base station
A shoulder microphone
A mobile laptop
A vehicle radio
Radio equipment shown in the chapter includes a handheld radio, a vehicle radio and a shoulder microphone.
A trainee asks who runs the radio and telecommunications systems. What does the chapter say about dispatchers?
Generally non-sworn personnel in each patrol district
Generally non-sworn personnel in a centralized area
Generally sworn personnel in each patrol district
Generally sworn personnel in a centralized area
Dispatchers are generally non-sworn personnel who run the radio and telecommunications systems from a centralized area with telephones and other resources.
During a crash call a dispatcher sends fire rescue and checks a driver's record. Which duties does this show?
Patching radio channels so several agencies can talk
Dispatching services and giving crime database information
Recording roll call information for the next shift
Creating computerized criminal histories from arrests

Dispatchers answer, receive, transfer and dispatch 911 calls; they must dispatch officers; fire, rescue and EMS; and other public safety services, and give real-time information from federal, state and local crime databases.
A deputy jokes about a citizen over the radio, thinking only her squad is listening. What does the chapter say?
Be professional, though the radio is private to you
Be professional and expect no privacy on the radio
Jokes are fine on a scrambled or encrypted channel
Be professional only on scrambled or encrypted channels
Conduct all radio communication professionally and expect no privacy on the radio.
A deputy wants to broadcast a suspect's full criminal history on the radio. When does the chapter allow this?
Only after you check in with dispatch for the shift
Only when an officer or public safety concern requires it
Only when a specialized unit requests the information
Only on a scrambled or encrypted channel for security
Put sensitive details or criminal histories on the radio only when an officer or public safety concern requires it; specialized units may use scrambled or encrypted channels for security.
Your portable radio is so loud that people across the room can hear it. What does the chapter suggest?
Switch to a scrambled or encrypted channel
Keep it loud so you never miss a call for backup
Set it loud enough to hear and use a shoulder mic
Set it loud enough to hear and use an earpiece
Set your portable radio loud enough to hear but not so loud it disrupts; an earpiece helps prevent eavesdropping.
You are on a report call while another unit is on a traffic stop. What does the chapter say about their radio traffic?
Monitor it only when dispatch calls your unit number
Switch channels so your call isn't interrupted
Turn your volume down until your report is done
Monitor it at all times in case they need backup
Monitor other units' transmissions at all times in case they need backup.
You are starting your shift. Why does the chapter say checking in with dispatch matters?
It keeps dispatch safer and lets you receive calls and track them
It keeps you safer and lets supervisors track your overtime
It lets dispatch send calls and replaces attending roll call
It keeps you safer and lets dispatch send calls and track you
Agency policy may require telling dispatch when you start or end duty; checking in and out keeps you safer and lets dispatch send calls and track your status.
Dispatch calls your unit number while you are on patrol. How should you answer?
With your assigned identification and current location
With your assigned identification and your destination
With your name and your current location on patrol
With your call sign and the location of your last call
When dispatch calls you, answer with your assigned identification and current location.
You want to check whether a man you stopped holds a Florida concealed weapon license. Which database does the chapter say holds this?
NCIC
FCIC
DAVID
CJNet

FCIC holds information on people and property; driver licenses and registrations; wanted and missing persons; stolen guns, vehicles, securities and other property; status files and computerized criminal histories; and concealed weapon licenses.
A man you stopped may have an active protection order filed in another state. Which database does the chapter say holds those files?
FALCON
NCIC
DAVID
FCIC

NCIC contains stolen, abandoned and recovered property, wanted and missing persons, the National Sex Offender Registry, and files on people on supervised release, with active protection orders, foreign fugitives, immigration violators and known or suspected terrorists or gang members.
A hit returns from NCIC on a record entered in Puerto Rico. Where does the chapter say NCIC records come from?
All 50 states, Canada, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and D.C.
All 50 states, Canada, the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico only
All 50 states, Canada, Guam, Puerto Rico and the District of Columbia
All 50 states, Mexico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and D.C.
NCIC records come from all 50 states, Canada, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and the District of Columbia.
A deputy misspells an arrestee's last name on the fingerprint card. Why does the chapter say this matters?
Records are only reliable if entered accurately
Records are only reliable if logged by FCIC
Records are only reliable if FDLE enters them
Records are only reliable if entered within 30 days

Records are only reliable if entered accurately, so arrest reports and fingerprint cards must be correct, from suspects' name spellings to the laws violated; the original report and supplements are needed for FCIC/NCIC entry.
Your agency entered a stolen car that has since been returned to its owner. Who must remove the record?
The arresting agency
The recovering agency
The FDLE records unit
The entering agency
The entering agency is responsible for its records' accuracy, timeliness and detail, and for removing them when no longer needed.
A new deputy wants to run a tag through FCIC on her first day. What must she complete first?
CJIS certification training and a fingerprint check
CJIS certification training and DAVID access training
CJIS certification training and the certification exam
DAVID certification training and the certification exam
Before accessing FCIC/NCIC you must complete CJIS certification training and pass the certification exam.
An employee was just assigned to an FCIC terminal. By when must he consent to a fingerprint background check?
Before his first query on the terminal
Within 60 days of being hired or assigned
Within 30 days of being hired or assigned
Within 30 days of passing the CJIS exam
Users must consent to a state and national fingerprint background check within 30 days of being hired or assigned to an FCIC terminal.
A deputy leaves her CJIS-connected laptop open in a public lobby. Which rule does this break?
Users must consent to a fingerprint background check
Records must be removed when no longer needed
Computers with CJIS access must be physically secured
Every user transaction must be logged by FCIC/NCIC
Computers with CJIS access must be physically secured from unauthorized persons.
A deputy runs her ex-boyfriend's new partner through FCIC out of curiosity. What can result, according to the chapter?
Discipline, retraining and criminal charges
Loss of certification and loss of DAVID access
Discipline, loss of certification and a civil fine
Discipline, loss of certification and criminal charges
Using FCIC/NCIC outside your duties can bring discipline, loss of certification and criminal charges, and the agency may be held liable and lose system access.
A public records request asks for queries run on a person. Which FCIC/NCIC feature makes this possible?
Every user transaction is logged
Every hit must be confirmed first
Every record lists the entering agency
Every query returns possible matches
FCIC/NCIC logs every user transaction; logs are used for compliance, criminal investigations, suspected misuse, public records requests and administrative purposes.
You are entering a stolen pistol into FCIC. What does the chapter say to give?
The serial number and caliber
The manufacturer and description
The VIN or registration decal
The serial number and manufacturer
For a firearm, give the serial number and manufacturer; for a vehicle, the registration, VIN or registration decal number.
A victim's stolen bicycle has a custom paint job. Which details does the chapter say to give for property like this?
Serial number and manufacturer only, like a firearm
Manufacturer, VIN, description and registration decal
Category, serial number, value and distinct markings
Category, manufacturer, description and distinct markings
For other stolen property, give the item category and manufacturer, a description, distinct markings, shape or other special identifiers.
Your name query comes back with three people who are not exact matches. Why?
Results list every record entered by your own agency
Results list records the same as or similar to what you sent
Results list records from all 50 states, Canada and territories
Results list each record that hit confirmation verified
Query results list possible matches when data are the same as or similar to what was submitted.
Dispatch confirms a warrant hit is no longer active. What has hit confirmation done here?
Waived extradition for the issuing agency
Avoided a mistaken arrest on an expired warrant
Created a computerized criminal history record
Checked the driver for a medical review
Hit confirmation makes sure the record is active and matches, avoids mistaken arrests on expired warrants or wrong data, and tells you what action to take, such as arrest or confiscation.
You need a driver's photo and signature to confirm who you stopped. Which system does the chapter say shows them?
NCIC
DAVID
CJNet
FCIC

DAVID shows driver license applications, information, photos and signatures; state ID cards; identification documents of non-citizens; driving and vehicle history; insurance information; and Florida vehicle and vessel registrations.
After a crash, a driver seems unable to drive safely due to a medical issue. What can you do through DAVID?
Ask for the driver's photos and signature from DAVID
Run a registration query that also checks FCIC/NCIC
Ask for the driver to be reassessed or get a medical review
Ask for a driver's insurance history to be reviewed
Through DAVID you can ask for a driver to be reassessed for a license or a medical review, and a DAVID registration query also checks FCIC/NCIC for stolen vehicles or vessels.
A deputy lets a friend read FCIC results on her screen. What does the chapter call mismanaging databases like this?
Unauthorized disclosure
A breach of contract
Misuse of your position
An access violation
Mismanaging criminal databases is misuse of your position.
Dispatch sends you to a call; the direct route passes a street fair. What does the chapter say about your route?
The most direct route is always the safest
The quickest route may not be the safest
The safest route may not be the most direct
The most direct route may not be the quickest
Choose the safest and quickest route; the most direct route may not be quickest because of construction, street closings or special events.
Responding to a disturbance, you don't know the neighborhood. How can you identify risks in the area?
Use dispatch information, which may say if anyone is hurt
Use dispatch information, which may say if anyone is armed
Wait at the scene for the complainant to brief you
Ask the alarm company for its key holder list
Use personal knowledge or dispatch information to identify risks in the area; dispatch may also say if anyone is injured.
Arriving at a burglary call, you see a car idling nearby with someone inside. What does the chapter say to watch for?
A victim who has returned home after the crime
A neighbor who called in the suspicious activity
A witness waiting to give a written statement
A lookout accomplice in a car with its engine running
Check the area around the car and report suspicious vehicles or people leaving; watch for parked cars with engines running and hidden suspects or a lookout accomplice.
At 3 a.m. a car sits in a business lot that is always empty overnight. What does the chapter call this?
An obvious clue
A routine sign
A minor detail
A hidden clue
Look for obvious clues, such as a car sitting in a lot that is usually empty at that hour, or a car that is usually there and now is not.
You approach a suspicious car at a burglary scene. What does the chapter say to check?
Wait for backup before going within sight of the car
Shine your spotlight into the car from your patrol unit
Walk up to look for occupants and feel the hood for heat
Run the tag through DAVID before getting out of your car

While approaching, take and keep the best tactical position (especially while waiting for backup), walk up to suspicious vehicles to check for occupants, feel the hood for heat, and close in on buildings using cars, fences, trash cans or shrubs.
Approaching a building at night where a burglar may be inside, how does the chapter say to lower your chance of detection?
An upright walk and the direct route
A low crouch and an indirect route
An upright walk and an indirect route
A low crouch and the direct route
A low crouch and an indirect route lower the chance of detection; keep scanning entrances and surroundings.
Searching outside a building at night with another deputy, you want to use your flashlight. What does the chapter warn?
Point the light at the ground so suspects can't see it
Don't light up other officers, and know where to aim first
Use the light only after backup has entered the building
Keep the light on at all times so officers see each other
Know where other officers are and do not light them up; know where to aim before switching on, since a flashlight temporarily impairs night vision.
You begin talking with a witness at a robbery. How does the chapter say to build rapport?
Separate the witness from everyone else first
Introduce yourself by name and use the person's name
Ask right away whether the suspect was armed or violent
Get a written statement before asking any questions
Ask for identification and personal and contact information, introduce yourself by name and use the person's name to build rapport.
Three witnesses saw a robbery. What does the chapter say to do to help establish probable cause?
Keep them together and have each describe what happened
Separate them and have each describe what happened
Separate them and get only written statements
Separate them and have one describe what happened
Separate everyone, have each describe what happened, ask follow-up questions, get a suspect description and ask if they would identify the suspect later; this helps establish probable cause.
Policy requires a written statement from a robbery victim. Why does the chapter say it matters?
It helps establish the BOLO's last known location
It helps establish rapport with the victim
It helps establish the suspect's direction of travel
It helps establish probable cause for an arrest
Get written statements when required, since they help establish probable cause for an arrest.
A local agency wants all units to watch a park after several car break-ins. Which BOLO reason does the chapter list for this?
Suspicious activity seen
Areas needing extra patrol
Missing persons last seen
Stolen property recovered
Local, state or national agencies issue BOLOs for missing or wanted persons, stolen property, suspicious activity or areas needing extra patrol.
You are writing a BOLO for a robbery suspect who fled on foot. What does the chapter say to include?
Direction of travel and the reporting officer
Last known location and the victim's name
Last known location and direction of travel
Incident location and the witnesses' names

A BOLO should include as much as possible: the subject's name and identifiers, incident location, reason for the BOLO, alleged violation, last known location and direction of travel, and a description or photo of the person, vehicle or property.
Five BOLOs were read at roll call. What does the chapter say to do with them on patrol?
Memorize every detail word for word at once
Note the major points and review current ones
Wait for dispatch to repeat them when needed
Keep them until the next roll call, then discard
Note the major points of each BOLO and review current ones to keep the information fresh on patrol.
You spot a wanted man walking into a crowded store. When planning contact, what does the chapter say to decide?
Whether to confirm the warrant before contact
Whether to issue a BOLO now or after contact
Whether to handcuff now or after backup arrives
Whether to approach now or wait for backup
When planning contact, decide whether to approach the suspect now or wait for backup, pick a suitable location and identify hazards.
A man you plan to contact has a record of assaulting officers. What does the chapter say to weigh?
Criminal history, behavior and possible weapons
Criminal history, behavior and backup
Behavior, hazards and possible weapons
Criminal history, location and possible weapons
Weigh the suspect's criminal history, behavior and possible weapons, and keep watching hands and body language.
Three deputies surround a suspect and all start shouting orders. What does the chapter recommend?
One officer talks so backup hears one voice
Each officer talks so all directions are heard
One officer talks so the suspect hears one voice
The senior officer talks by radio to backup
Having one officer talk lets the suspect focus on one voice instead of several officers giving different directions.
You are walking toward a suspect who keeps glancing at an alley. What does the chapter say to watch for?
Signs of flight or assault in tone and word choice
Signs of flight or assault in his hands only
Signs of flight or assault in position and movements
Signs of resistance in position and movements

Moving toward a suspect: approach carefully, keep your eyes on the suspect, keep a safe distance, stay alert for resistance, watch position and movements for signs of flight or assault, and keep scanning for weapons.
An FCIC/NCIC check shows a warrant for the man you stopped. What may you do while it is confirmed?
Release him and ask the issuing agency to pick him up
Hold the suspect while the warrant and extradition are confirmed
Arrest and transport him before confirmation comes back
Issue a BOLO and let him leave until it is confirmed
A warrant found in a database such as FCIC/NCIC lets you hold the suspect while the warrant and extradition are confirmed; once confirmed, arrest and transport the suspect.
The agency that issued an out-of-county warrant says it will not extradite. What must you do?
Release the suspect and document per policy
Release the suspect and enter a BOLO
Arrest the suspect and confirm extradition
Hold the suspect and document per policy
If the agency that issued the warrant waives extradition, the suspect must be released; document what you did per policy.
A suspect you are about to question keeps reaching toward his waistband. What does the chapter allow?
A full search of his car before any questioning
Handcuffing only after a full custodial search
Handcuffing at the start, and a pat down for a weapon
A pat down only after he consents to a search
With a justifiable reason to think the suspect is a threat or may run, you may handcuff at the start of contact; if you think the suspect has a dangerous weapon, do a pat down.
Backup arrives while you are talking with a suspect. What does the chapter say to do?
Have backup start a search for consent later
Let backup take over talking with the suspect
Share current suspect information with dispatch
Share current suspect information with backup
Share current suspect information with backup; building rapport and a non-custodial atmosphere can help other efforts, such as getting consent to search.
You hear a deputy run a traffic stop near you on a dark road. What does the chapter say about backing up?
Officers may decide on their own to back up
Officers back up only when dispatch sends them
Officers may back up only after the primary asks
Officers back up only when asked by radio
Officers are often called to back up others, or decide on their own to back up based on the circumstances.
You arrive as backup on a traffic stop. What does the chapter say to do first?
Contact your supervisor to find out what is needed
Contact the driver to find out what is needed
Contact dispatch to find out what is needed
Contact the primary officer to find out what is needed
Make visual or verbal contact with the primary officer to find out what is needed, stay alert and avoid distractions such as your phone; the backup does whatever the primary officer needs.
A recruit says violence is rising everywhere. What does the chapter say about trends?
Violent crime rose, while targeted violence dropped
Violent crime and targeted violence have both dropped
Violent crime dropped, but targeted violence has risen
Violent crime and targeted violence have both risen
Overall violent crime has dropped over three decades, yet targeted violence, including mass events such as active shooter incidents, has recently become more frequent and more deadly.
A trainer cites research behind BTAM. Who does the chapter say studied targeted violence?
The U.S. Secret Service and FDLE only
The U.S. Marshals, the FBI and others
The U.S. Secret Service, the FBI and others
FDLE, the FBI and other state agencies
Studies by the U.S. Secret Service, the FBI and other government agencies produced several key findings on targeted violence.
A parent asks if police can tell who will commit a school shooting. What does the chapter say?
Violent behavior can't be predicted or prevented reliably
Violent behavior can be predicted by mental health records
Violent behavior can be predicted reliably and then prevented
Violent behavior can't be predicted reliably but can be prevented
Violent behavior cannot be predicted reliably, but it can be prevented.
A student has been mapping out his school and researching guns. What does the chapter say about targeted violence like this?
It is usually impulsive and comes without warning
It is random and can't be noticed beforehand
It grows from planning that others can notice
It is usually driven by mental illness alone
Targeted violence is rarely impulsive or random; it grows from organized thinking and behavior, such as planning and preparation, that others can notice and report.
A deputy says a person of concern must be mentally ill. What does the chapter say?
Mental health problems are usually the main cause
Mental health records alone predict violence
Mental health problems are the only cause
Mental health problems are seldom the main cause
Mental health problems are seldom the main cause of targeted violence.
You are reporting a person of concern you met on a call. What does the chapter say the report should include?
A prediction of when the person might act
A detailed description of the person's diagnosis
A detailed description of the encounter
A list of the person's criminal history
Information for identifying a person of concern includes a detailed description of the encounter, your reasons for concern, and personally identifiable information for the person and witnesses.
You report a person of concern. Who mainly handles the assessment investigation?
The reporting patrol officer
The responding patrol supervisor
The FDLE threat assessment unit
Trained BTAM professionals
Assess is the core of BTAM: collecting and analyzing behavioral information from all sources, including your observations; trained BTAM professionals mainly handle this investigation.
A BTAM investigator wants to learn more about a person of concern. Who does the chapter say are often the best sources?
Friends, coworkers and the patrol officer
Mental health records and diagnoses
Relatives, friends and close associates
Relatives, teachers and close associates
The quantity and quality of reported information directly affect the accuracy of the assessment; relatives, friends and close associates are often the best sources.
A person of concern told a friend he wants revenge and keeps a rifle at home. Which critical information does this show?
Motive shared with others and the target's schedule
Criminal history and the target's vulnerabilities
Mental health history and immediate access to firearms
Motive shared with others and immediate access to firearms

Critical information includes motive and intent shared with others, ability and means to act (above all immediate access to firearms or other weapons), access to the target, and the target's vulnerabilities.
A BTAM team asks you to make regular contact with a person of concern. Which BTAM step is this?
Assess
Identify
Manage
Report
Manage: agencies choose strategies from the assessment to prevent or reduce violence, and patrol officers may be asked to help BTAM investigators.
On a call, you see signs a man is moving toward violence. Why does the chapter say to report it promptly?
You may be the only one who can arrest him
You must make the assessment yourself
You must report it before writing a BOLO
You may be the only officer who sees it
You may be the only officer to see critical information about a person moving along a pathway to violence, so report it promptly and accurately.
Your shift has a caller asking for directions and a business asking for a building check. How does the chapter describe calls like these?
Civil calls, from landlord disputes to child custody issues
Non-criminal calls, from information requests to security checks
Non-criminal calls, from information requests to civil standbys
Civil calls, from information requests to security checks
Non-criminal calls range from requests for specific information to requests for a building security check.
A deputy treats a lost-dog call with the same stern manner she uses at a fight. What does the chapter say about command presence?
Save command presence for criminal calls only
Adjust command presence to fit the situation
Drop command presence on non-criminal calls
Use the same command presence on every call
Every call needs a professional response with command presence adjusted to fit the situation.
Residents on a block refuse to talk with deputies after a rough arrest. What does the chapter say about public trust?
People may not cooperate if they don't see authority as legitimate
People may not cooperate if officers use plain talk on the radio
People may not cooperate if officers refuse to give a referral
People may not cooperate if they don't see officers on foot patrol
Public trust depends on whether people see your authority as appropriate, proper and just; if they do not see it as legitimate, they may not cooperate.
At a crash, you need help pulling a driver from a burning car. When does the chapter say you may need bystanders' help?
Usually in civil standbys such as moving property
Usually in emergencies such as finding witnesses
Usually in emergencies such as directing traffic
Usually in emergencies such as rescuing a victim
You may need bystanders' help, usually in emergencies such as rescuing a victim, giving first aid or overcoming a suspect's resistance.
A man arrested on civil process breaks away and a neighbor is nearby. What does Florida law let you do?
Order the neighbor to help only with first aid
Ask the neighbor to help only if he volunteers
Order the neighbor to help only after backup arrives
Order the neighbor to help recapture him

Florida law lets officers order members of the public to help in certain cases, such as catching or holding a person for breach of the peace, or the rescue or escape of someone arrested on civil process.
You need help at a scene and a bystander offers to tackle an armed man. What does the chapter say?
Never direct help that is unsafe for them
Direct help only in a breach of the peace
Never direct help without a written order
Direct help only from people who volunteer
Never direct a member of the public to help in a way that is unlawful, beyond their ability or unsafe for them.
A mail carrier calls about a home with mail piling up. Which sign does the chapter list as needing a well-being check?
An open door or a car parked in the driveway
A barking dog or an abnormal presence of flies
A bad odor or a car parked in the driveway
A bad odor or an abnormal presence of flies
Signs needing a well-being check include a bad odor from a home or an abnormal presence of flies showing lack of activity.
A resident leaving on vacation asks you to check her home. Who does the chapter say may start a security check?
Residents or dispatch only
Residents or the owner only
Supervisors or dispatch only
Residents, you or dispatch
Security checks of homes, buildings or grounds may be requested by residents or started by you or dispatch.
A neighboring county asks your agency to notify a family of a death. When does the chapter say you may be assigned?
When your agency investigates or another jurisdiction asks
Only when your agency runs the death investigation
Only after a 24/7 agency enters the death into FCIC
Only when DAVID lists an emergency contact for them
You may be assigned a death notification when your agency runs a death investigation or another jurisdiction asks.
You are about to deliver a death notification in person. What does the chapter say about backup?
Backup is never needed since it's non-confrontational
Backup is required on every notification
You may request backup; practice officer safety
Bring a chaplain instead of a backup officer
You may request a backup officer for an in-person notification; it is normally non-confrontational, but practice officer safety.
The next of kin lives in another state and no agency there can help. What does the chapter say about telephoning?
It's acceptable only if a chaplain makes the call
It's preferred when the family lives in another state
It's never allowed; ask the other state to visit
It's least preferred; use it only when there is no other option
Telephone notification is acceptable but least preferred; use it only when there is no other option, and then call as soon as possible.
The family asks how their son died, but the case is still open. What does the chapter say to do?
Explain that the investigation does not allow answers
Refer them to the public information officer for answers
Give every detail since the family has a right to know
Answer only questions about the deceased's location
Answer the family's questions about the deceased's location and the circumstances; if the investigation does not allow answers, explain that.
A grieving mother is crying after a notification. Which statement does the chapter tell you to avoid?
He is in a better place
He died at the hospital
He was taken to the hospital
I know how you feel
Avoid statements such as 'I know how you feel' or 'God never gives us more than we can handle.'
An alligator is in a backyard pool. After assessing, what does the chapter say you may do?
Capture it or call animal control or FWC
Call a nuisance trapper and leave the scene
Wait for the owner to remove it from the pool
Shoot it to protect the family and the public
Next you may try to capture it or call animal control or the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC), weighing your experience and training before handling any animal.
A raccoon keeps getting into a home's attic. Which resources does the chapter say you may request?
Wildlife rehabilitators or nuisance animal trappers
Animal control or nuisance animal trappers only
FWC or the county's livestock inspectors
Wildlife rehabilitators or domestic animal shelters
You may request wildlife rehabilitators or nuisance animal trappers.
A dog hit by a car is badly injured and suffering. What does the chapter allow?
Equipment only, never force
Force only if FWC approves
Appropriate equipment and force
Force only if the owner agrees
Use appropriate equipment and force if an animal endangers personal or public safety or is badly injured.
A trash fire of paper and wood starts next to a building. Which extinguisher does the chapter say works best?
Dry chemical
CO2
Foam
Halon
Foam extinguishers work best on paper or wood fires, while CO2 extinguishers are better for flammable liquids.
A man pulled a fire alarm at a school as a prank. What must you document to charge false alarm of fire?
He spread a false fire alarm on a recorded line
He spread a false fire alarm causing property damage
He spread a false fire alarm causing an evacuation
He spread a false fire alarm without reasonable cause
To charge false alarm of fire, document that the suspect spread a false fire alarm without reasonable cause.
A woman reports losing her phone. What does the chapter say to use?
An offense report with a description and value
A general information report with the serial number only
A property/receipt form with a description and value
A general information report with a description and value
Document lost property on a general information report with a description and estimated value; precise descriptions and unique identifiers like scratches or unique parts aid recovery.
During a traffic stop you see a TV matching a burglary report. Where does the chapter say stolen property may surface?
At traffic stops, arrests, on patrol or from a resident
At traffic stops, arrests or pawnshops only
Only after a victim files a lost property report
Only through FCIC hits on serial numbers
Stolen property may surface on routine patrol, at traffic stops or arrests, or from a resident.
A recovered laptop has no forensic value and the owner is known. What does the chapter say to do?
Return it to the owner without documenting
Give it to the property clerk as evidence
Submit it as evidence for latent prints
Return it to the owner and document that

It also includes photographing the item, processing it for latent prints and touch DNA, returning it to the owner if it has no forensic value (and documenting that), or submitting it as evidence if the owner cannot be found or it has forensic value.
A burglary victim asks where her stolen jewelry may have gone. What does the chapter say?
Stolen property is often sold to pawnbrokers
Stolen property is often reported by a resident
Stolen property is often held by pawnbrokers
Stolen property is often recovered at traffic stops
Stolen property is often sold to pawnbrokers.
A pawnbroker is told an officer wants a second hold order on the same ring. What does the chapter say?
A second order needs the pawnbroker's consent
A second order may extend the first by 30 days
Only one hold order may be placed on the property
Two hold orders are allowed for up to 90 days
The official may rescind a hold order in writing, and only one hold order may be placed on the property.
Two neighbors argue over where their property line is. What does the chapter say to do?
Refer them to civil court
Refer them to county court
Refer them to mediation
Refer them to the clerk
Boundary disputes are civil matters handled outside the criminal justice process; refer the parties to civil court.
A hotel guest refuses to leave after checkout. Does the landlord-tenant Act apply?
No; it applies only to RV parks and campgrounds
No; it does not apply to public lodging like hotels
Yes; it applies to anyone who rents a room
Yes; but the hotel must give a 3-day notice
The Act does not apply to public lodging such as hotels and motels; medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar residency facilities; or recreational vehicle parks.
A customer and a mechanic argue over a bill at an auto shop. Which dispute does the chapter call this?
A landlord-tenant dispute
A civil standby
A boundary dispute
A repair bill dispute
Disputes over repair bills arise at auto repair shops.
You are sent to a child custody exchange. What does the chapter say about calls like this?
Criminal calls are the only confrontational ones
Civil calls can become highly confrontational
Civil calls are handled only by civil court
Civil calls rarely become confrontational
Civil calls such as landlord-tenant disputes or child custody issues can become highly confrontational.
Before arriving at a landlord-tenant call, how does the chapter say to gauge the threat?
Dispatch information, the lease and the court file
The landlord's account and the tenant's account
The address's call history and the eviction notice
Dispatch information, call history and what you know
Gauge the threat from dispatch information, the address's call history, what you know about the people and what you see; stay alert and request backup to match the threat.
Before a civil standby, what does the chapter say to query in FCIC/NCIC?
Hold orders or warrants
Injunctions or hold orders
Injunctions or warrants
Licenses or registrations
Query FCIC/NCIC for injunctions or warrants.
During a civil standby, the ex-wife insists you take her side. What does the chapter say?
Remain impartial and use conflict management skills
Enforce the ex-wife's request if she called
Leave until the parties settle the dispute
Side with the party who has the court order
Remain impartial and use conflict management skills so the situation does not escalate.
A resident asks for a civil standby but has no court order. What does the chapter say?
A court order is always required in Florida
Agencies differ, so know your agency's policy
A court order is never needed for a standby
Only the sheriff may do a standby without one
Agencies differ on whether a court order must exist before a civil standby, so know your agency's policy.
A peaceful protest march turns into people breaking windows. What does the chapter say?
When an assembly has no permit, police resolve it
When an assembly is no longer peaceful, police resolve it
A permit protects the assembly until it ends
The First Amendment protects it until it disperses
The First Amendment protects peaceful assembly; when an assembly is no longer peaceful, law enforcement resolves the disturbance.
A group gathers quietly in a park without a permit. How does the chapter say you decide if it's lawful?
Under federal law and the First Amendment only
Under state law and county and city ordinances
Under the permit rules for large planned events
Under agency policy on crowd size and mood
People may gather if they cause no disturbance and stay within the law; you decide whether a gathering is lawful under state law and county and city ordinances.
At 2 a.m. a large crowd forms in the street. What does the chapter say can cause sudden crowds?
Leaders agitating a planned rally
Bars closing or venues letting out
Gang members displaying colors
Permits for planned large events
Florida may require permits for planned events expecting large crowds; sudden crowds can come from bars closing or venues letting out.
A crowd forms after a fight; you see people wearing the same colors. What does the chapter say to identify?
Whether it has a permit and who is leading or agitating
Whether it's organized and who is leading or agitating
Whether it's peaceful and who is leading or watching
Whether it's lawful and who called the police
Identify whether the crowd is organized and whether anyone is leading or agitating it; some crowds involve gang members displaying colors, symbols and weapons.
Monitoring a crowd, you see people picking up broken bottles. What does the chapter say to do?
Relay it once backup arrives on the scene
Relay it only after the crowd disperses
Relay it often to dispatch or assisting agencies
Relay it to the crowd's leader to settle it
Relay information often to dispatch or assisting agencies: crowd size and movement, weapons such as broken bottles, property damage and any escalation or de-escalation.
You're watching a large, angry crowd. What does the chapter say to keep?
A vantage point so the crowd can't see you
A position at the crowd's center to watch all
A show of force with your weapon drawn
An exit strategy so the crowd can't corner you
A crowd's anonymity can provoke aggressive individuals; attacks can come from any direction, so keep an exit strategy and do not let the crowd corner you.
A crowd grows tense. What does the chapter say can help settle it?
Showing force or presence in numbers
Relaying crowd size to dispatch
Separating the leader before backup
Withdrawing all officers from view
Showing force or presence in numbers can help settle a crowd.
You don't know why a crowd has gathered. How does the chapter say to learn why?
Wait for the crowd to break up and ask then
Look at signs and symbols and listen to chants
Ask dispatch to check the event permit
Ask the crowd's leader in front of the group
Learn why the group gathered by looking at signs and symbols on clothing and listening to what people say or chant.
Backup has arrived at a protest. What does the chapter say to do with the leader?
Interview the leader in front of the whole group
Separate the leader and interview without the group
Separate the leader and arrest him for agitating
Ask the leader to address the crowd before talking
After backup arrives, separate the leader from the crowd and interview the leader without the group's influence.
Dispatch sends you to an alarm at a jewelry store at night. What does the chapter say your tactics depend on?
The alarm's type and location
The alarm's brand and location
The alarm's type and history
The key holder's response time
Some alarms are false; your response and tactics depend on the alarm's type and location, considering threats to life, danger to the public or major property loss.
You arrive alone at an alarm call. What does the chapter say about a second officer?
Some agencies require a canine unit on every alarm call
Every agency requires at least two officers on alarm calls
No agency sends a second officer unless a crime is found
Some agencies require at least two officers on alarm calls
Some agencies require at least two officers on alarm calls; others send a second officer in certain circumstances or on request.
At an alarm call, the key holder tells dispatch the system has been faulty. What is this information helping you do?
Set a large perimeter
Choose a room-entry method
Plan to apprehend suspects
Find the alarm's cause
Find the alarm's cause by observing, interviewing people present and getting dispatch information such as a suspect description, false alarm notice or the key holder's response.
At an alarm, you see someone moving inside a closed store. What does the chapter say to plan?
To apprehend, with a perimeter and maybe a canine
To leave and report it as a false alarm
To clear the building alone before backup arrives
To wait for the key holder to unlock the door
If suspects are present, plan to apprehend them: decide on a perimeter, whether they know police are there, whether a building search is needed and whether to call a canine or tactical team.
Before entering a dark building to search, your keys jingle. What does the chapter say to do?
Secure loose items and lower volumes
Turn off your flashlight and radio
Secure loose items and raise volumes
Hold your keys and leave radios on
Jingling keys, change, phones and radios can reveal where you are, so secure loose items and lower volumes; never put your flashlight beam on other officers.
Two deputies search a warehouse together. How does the chapter say they lower the risk of crossfire?
Talk by radio from different rooms
Use hand signals and stay together
Shine flashlights on each other
Split up and search opposite ends
Use hand signals, work together and stay together so you cover each other and lower the risk of crossfire.
Searching a building after a burglary alarm, what does the chapter call the biggest danger?
Jingling keys revealing your position
Crossfire between searching officers
A flashlight lighting up other officers
A hidden, possibly armed suspect
In a building search the biggest danger is a hidden, possibly armed suspect, so search carefully and completely.
You're deciding how to enter a room. How does the chapter say to tell which way a door opens?
Find the handle
Find the frame
Find the lock
Find the hinges
Decide how to enter by how doors and windows open, for example finding the hinges to see which way a door opens; most entries are through doorways.
Halfway through a large office building, you lose track of which rooms are done. What does the chapter say?
Search systematically and track cleared areas
Search the largest rooms first, then the rest
Search only rooms with open doors
Search quickly and re-clear any doubtful rooms
Search systematically and keep track of cleared rooms or areas.
Before entering a room, you and your partner pick crisscross. What does the chapter say about room-entry methods?
Coordinate with other officers whichever you use
Use buttonhook only when you are alone
Only one method is approved for patrol
Use crisscross for doors and buttonhook for windows
Two common room-entry methods are crisscross and buttonhook; coordinate with other officers whichever you use.
During a building search you see an unlocked desk drawer. What does the chapter say about searching it?
The search covers anything large enough to hold a weapon
The search covers any place a suspect left evidence
The search covers drawers only with the owner's consent
The search is limited to finding persons
The search is limited to finding persons; after each room, close the door or keep it under observation, and return the building to the responsible person once cleared.
A burglar fled into a neighborhood. How does the chapter say to start the perimeter?
Start at the last known location and stay there
Start where the canine unit tells you to
Start small and widen it as backup arrives
Start large and adjust as the situation changes
Start with a large perimeter and adjust it as the situation changes; the primary officer or a supervisor decides the need and resources from knowledge of the area.
A suspect has hidden somewhere in a large wooded park. Which resource does the chapter say may be used?
More staff or FWC officers
A helicopter or canines
A helicopter or fire rescue
Canines or animal control
Use resources to protect the public while limiting contained suspects' movement; choice depends on incident type, time elapsed and geography, and may include more staff, a helicopter or canines.
You have been on a perimeter post for three hours. When does the chapter say you may leave?
When the primary officer clears the building
When the canine unit arrives and begins tracking
When six hours have passed or you are relieved
When relieved, relocated or the situation is resolved
Stay at your post until relieved or relocated or the situation is resolved; good planning and positioning make perimeters work even with limited resources.
You and a partner search a field for a suspect. Which ground search technique does the chapter list?
Work with a partner; light your partner's way
Work with a partner; move only as fast as is safe
Work with a partner; move as fast as you can
Work alone; move only as fast as is safe
Ground search techniques: work with a partner, do not expose yourself, use cover and concealment, mind your noise and move only as fast as is safe, coordinate to avoid crossfire.
A suspect fled into a neighborhood of pools and fences. Why does the chapter say this is harder than a building search?
Exterior ground searches are easier to contain
Exterior ground searches are harder to contain
Building searches are harder to contain
Exterior ground searches need more canines
Exterior ground searches are harder to contain than building searches; fences, pools, vehicles, dead ends and barriers affect tactics.
A shoplifter runs at dusk in the rain. Which pursuit safety factor does the chapter list?
The value of the property
The suspect's age and dress
Time of day and weather
Time of day and the store

Pursuit safety factors: chance the suspect is armed, seriousness of the offense, threat to officers and public, location and ambush potential, time of day and weather, and whether the suspect is known and can be caught later.
Three suspects run from you and your partner. Which pursuit factor does the chapter list?
The number of officers versus witnesses
The number of officers versus suspects
The number of canines versus suspects
The number of suspects versus bystanders
More factors: officers versus suspects, physical limits of each, available resources (canine, air support, SWAT), ability to secure the patrol car, and familiarity with the area.
You lose sight of a suspect and don't know where he went. What does the chapter say about the pursuit?
You or a supervisor may end it
Only dispatch may end the pursuit
Only a supervisor may end it
You must keep going until caught

You or a supervisor may end a pursuit at any time, including when the suspect's location is unknown, you cannot continue from injury, fatigue or unfamiliarity, or the suspect is identified and no longer a threat.
After an arrest, you start asking the arrestee where he hid the gun. What applies?
Miranda requirements
Hold order rules
Booking procedures
BTAM guidelines
Miranda requirements apply whenever you conduct an interrogation.
The arrestee's mother asks you what happened. What does the chapter say?
Give no information until the case is closed
Give full details since she is the family
Give general information when reasonably possible
Give general information only to the victim
Victims, witnesses and the arrestee's family may have a direct interest; give general information whenever reasonably possible, since this may be their only contact with an officer.
A reporter asks for details of an arrest. What governs what you may release?
Federal law and agency policy
Agency policy and the victim
State law and agency policy
State law and the judge's order
What may be released to the public is governed by state law and agency policy.
You are arresting a woman who is visibly pregnant. How may you restrain her?
You may not use any restraints
You may use leg restraints only
You may place restraints in front
You may restrain her behind her back
For a pregnant arrestee, you may place restraints in front.
An inmate is in labor at the hospital. When does the Act allow restraining her?
Only for a substantial flight risk or extraordinary reason
Only for a substantial flight risk, not medical reasons
Only when she was charged or adjudicated as an adult
Only when she is moved to a medical facility by car

The Healthy Pregnancy for Incarcerated Women Act bars restraining an incarcerated pregnant person during labor, delivery or postpartum recovery unless she is a substantial flight risk or another extraordinary medical or security reason requires it.
You arrive at the jail with an arrestee. Where does the chapter say to put your weapons?
Lock them in the trunk or keep them holstered
Lock them in the patrol car's back seat
Hand them to the booking officer to lock up
Lock them in the trunk, a locker or a lockbox
At the detention facility, lock up your weapons in the patrol car trunk, a weapons locker or a lockbox at the drop-off point; the agency and facility set which places are acceptable.
At the jail drop-off, your arrestee's codefendant is in the hall. What does the chapter say?
You're responsible until staff receive the arrestee
Responsibility passes when you get clearance
Facility staff are responsible once you arrive
Codefendants must wait in the patrol car
You are responsible for the arrestee until facility staff receive them; watch for hazards such as codefendants or other arrestees.
You bring a 15-year-old to the jail for prints and photos. What does the chapter require?
The juvenile must be held in a separate jail
The juvenile must be held for at least six hours
Adult arrestees cannot see or hear the juvenile
Adult arrestees cannot be in the same building

A juvenile may be kept in a jail's secure booking area or an adult jail for temporary custody of six hours or less, or for prints and photos, as long as adult arrestees cannot see or hear the juvenile.
A 16-year-old is held in an adult jail. Which exception does the chapter list?
Juveniles waiting for a parent to arrive
Juveniles charged with any violent felony
Juveniles arrested with adult codefendants
Juveniles charged as adults or emancipated
Most juveniles in adult jails or lockups are awaiting transport or in pre- or post-court holding; exceptions are juveniles charged as adults or emancipated or adjudicated as adults.
A 17-year-old says he was adjudicated as an adult. How can you confirm it?
DJJ, court records or criminal histories
DJJ, court records or his parents
DCF, court records or criminal histories
DJJ, DAVID records or criminal histories
Confirm a juvenile's legal adult status with the Department of Juvenile Justice, court records or criminal histories.
A juvenile you arrested appears high. Until when are you responsible?
Until you have notified the juvenile's parents
Until the juvenile is booked into the jail
Until a booking officer takes the affidavit
Until a parent, guardian or DCF takes responsibility
You are responsible for a juvenile with a medical condition, mental illness or substance effects, and until a parent, guardian or DCF representative takes responsibility.
You arrest a 14-year-old at 2 a.m. What does the chapter say about his parents?
Tell them only when he is released from custody
Tell them only if DCF is involved or taking custody
Make a thorough effort within a reasonable time
Tell them only after he is booked and photographed
Make a thorough effort to tell a juvenile's parents within a reasonable time after the arrest.
A juvenile asks to be released and walk home. What does the chapter say?
A juvenile may leave once his parents are notified
A juvenile may leave after six hours in custody
A juvenile may be released on his own recognizance
A qualified adult or organization must take custody
A juvenile cannot be released on their own recognizance; an adult relative, qualified adult or organization must take custody and sign booking forms or charging documents.
You bring an arrestee to a county jail you haven't used before. What does the chapter say?
Leave the arrestee with any jail staff
Follow your own agency's booking policy only
Book the arrestee yourself at the jail
Know and follow the booking officers' policies
Many agencies have booking or intake officers (law enforcement or correctional) at the county jail, and you must know and follow their policies.
You turn over an arrestee to the booking officer at the jail. What must go with him?
The FCIC printout
The search warrant
The arrest affidavit
Your field notes
The arresting officer must fill out an arrest affidavit that goes with the arrestee to the booking officer.
You're completing a fingerprint card at booking. Why does accuracy matter?
The court uses it in place of the report
FCIC/NCIC builds criminal history data from it
DAVID uses it to update the license photo
The booking officer uses it as the affidavit
FCIC/NCIC builds criminal history data from fingerprint cards and arrest and correctional reports, so fill them out accurately.
The jail already has a booking photo from an arrest last month. What does the chapter say?
Many facilities can use photos from past arrests
Facilities use DAVID license photos instead
Families can supply photos for booking
Every arrest needs a new booking photo
Booking photos give a visual record; many facilities can use photos from past arrests instead of taking new ones.
A deputy writes a short, vague arrest report. Why does the chapter say to document completely?
So the arrestee can be released sooner
So the booking photo can be reused
So the facts clearly support prosecution
So FDLE can create the arrestee's CCH
Document arrests completely and accurately so the facts clearly support prosecution.
Responding alone, a deputy sees a crowd of 300 growing restless outside a stadium. Why does the chapter say to call for help and wait for backup?
Crowds of this size need a permit before police step in
Sheer numbers can overwhelm officers and make arrests hard
Officers must interview the leader before backup arrives
Non-hostile crowds turn violent only when backup is late

Any large gathering can be dangerous; officer safety is the first consideration when engaging a crowd. Sheer numbers can overwhelm responding officers and make it hard to remove or arrest members of a large group, so call for help and wait for backup.
A new deputy asks what she will spend most of her working day doing once she is on her own. What does the chapter say?
Attending roll call
Writing reports
Patrolling
Answering calls
Patrol is the main daily activity of an officer; its primary purposes are keeping a public presence, enforcing laws and ordinances, and deterring crime.
A deputy on a quiet call stops paying attention once the man calms down. What does the chapter say about awareness during an encounter?
Stay aware of the whole situation as it evolves
Stay aware of the person's hands and nothing else
Stay aware until the person is calm and talking
Stay aware only on calls for service and stops
To protect the public you must keep yourself safe; assess officer safety constantly, stay alert and keep situational awareness.
A veteran says he uses the same approach on every call. What does the chapter say decides your tactics?
The circumstances of the situation
The time of day of the call
The policy for that type of call
The number of officers present
The circumstances dictate the tactics; always stay alert and use observation to spot dangers.
A deputy skips the gym for months and gets winded on a short foot chase. Who does the chapter say poor shape puts in danger?
Only you, since it is your choice
You and your partner on the call
You, other officers and the public
You and the suspect you are chasing
Poor physical condition endangers you, other officers and the public; enough sleep and an exercise and wellness program are part of fitness for duty.
A deputy treats a barking-dog call as routine and walks up with her hands full. What does the chapter warn?
The wrong mindset breeds complacency on felony calls
Routine calls need less alertness than crimes in progress
Barking-dog calls should be left to animal control
The wrong mindset breeds complacency on a deadly call
Never assume a call is routine; going in without the right mindset breeds complacency in a potentially deadly situation.
A deputy texts a joke about a suspect from her work phone. Why does the chapter say to stay professional in every electronic message?
All computer activity is shared with the suspect's lawyer
All computer activity is recorded and can be reviewed
All texts are read by a supervisor before they are sent
Only radio traffic is recorded, so texts are private
Every computer action is logged under the FBI's security policy and can be reviewed under public records law, so keep texts, emails and radio traffic professional.
Your laptop freezes as you need backup on a traffic stop. Which device does the chapter say you rely on most?
The body camera
The laptop
The radio
The cell phone
The radio is the device officers use most; it carries vital information to and from dispatch and other officers, calls for backup and helps identify suspects or wanted persons.
At the end of a shift, a deputy drives home without telling dispatch. Why does checking in and out matter?
It records your hours so payroll can pay your overtime correctly
It tells FDLE that your FCIC terminal access has now ended
It lets your supervisor plan the next shift's roll call notes
It keeps you safer and lets dispatch send calls and track you
Agency policy may require telling dispatch when you start or end duty; checking in and out keeps you safer and lets dispatch send calls and track your status.
Another unit's radio goes quiet in the middle of a traffic stop. Why does the chapter say to stay aware of all radio traffic?
Another officer may be in trouble
You may need a records check
Dispatch may call your number
You may hear a BOLO update
When dispatch calls you, answer with your assigned identification and current location.
A deputy wants to query a database in a way his agency doesn't allow. What does the chapter say to follow?
FDLE's policies when adding or querying data
The dispatcher's direction on every query
Your own judgment when querying for safety
Your agency's policies when adding or querying data

Records are only reliable if entered accurately, so arrest reports and fingerprint cards must be correct, from suspects' name spellings to the laws violated; the original report and supplements are needed for FCIC/NCIC entry.
A neighbor asks a deputy to run a car's tag because it blocks her driveway. What does the chapter say about database information?
It may be shared with the vehicle's owner
It may be shared with any towing company
It is strictly for law enforcement use
It may be shared to settle parking problems
Database information is for law enforcement use only, with one exception: registration and lien information may be given to towing companies.
A new deputy wonders which databases she can use and how to log in. Where does the chapter say she will find this?
The FCIC user access agreement
Her agency's policies and procedures
The dispatcher working her shift
The FDLE CJIS certification course

CJNet (Criminal Justice Network) gives access to databases such as InSite (statewide crime intelligence), FALCON (Florida's Integrated Criminal History System), CART (Child Abduction Response Team) and the Florida Sexual Offender and Predator database.
At a burglary call, a deputy sees a car pulling away from the block. Why report it to dispatch?
The description may help when arresting suspects
The description is needed before backup can respond
The description replaces a written statement
The description may help find the property owner
Check the area around the car and report suspicious vehicles or people leaving; watch for parked cars with engines running and hidden suspects or a lookout accomplice.
After reaching a burglarized warehouse, how does the chapter say to treat its entrances?
Survey entrances once, then focus on the alarm panel
Survey only the entrance where the alarm went off
Survey entrances after the key holder arrives
Constantly survey entrances and the area around them
Checking a building's exterior, take care at corners, windows and doors and watch for animals, clotheslines, garbage cans, sprinkler heads and swimming pools.
A suspect you are questioning keeps changing his story. What does the chapter say to keep doing?
Keep interviewing and observing the suspect
Keep the questions to his name and birthdate
Keep him in the patrol car until backup arrives
Keep him handcuffed until he tells the truth
With a justifiable reason to think the suspect is a threat or may run, you may handcuff at the start of contact; if you think the suspect has a dangerous weapon, do a pat down.
A man resists your commands and curses at you. What does the chapter say you are still obligated to do?
Stay silent until he calms down and complies
Stay back until a supervisor takes over
Stay firm and stop explaining your commands
Stay professional and treat him with respect
Ask for voluntary compliance first, then give a verbal command; if neither works, you may make the subject comply using Defensive Tactics techniques, staying professional and respectful.
A man gives you a fake name and birth date during a stop. What is he trying to do, according to the chapter?
Disguise his criminal record
Disguise his vehicle's owner
Disguise his real identity
Disguise his home address
Giving false identification happens when someone under arrest or lawful detention gives the officer a false name or otherwise lies about who they are.
Most people you meet on non-criminal calls behave a certain way. What does the chapter say?
Most of the time they resist at first
Most of the time they need first aid
Most of the time they are compliant
Most of the time they need a referral
You may need bystanders' help, usually in emergencies such as rescuing a victim, giving first aid or overcoming a suspect's resistance.
At a vehicle fire you need fire rescue and EMS fast. What can dispatch do?
Close the road and reroute all traffic
Help contact available emergency resources
Shut off power to downed lines nearby
Notify the vehicle's owner and insurer
Judge fire intensity and request fire rescue if you cannot put it out; survey for victims and hazards such as hazmat and downed power lines.
At a large vehicle fire, other agencies arrive. What does the chapter say you may be required to do?
Take command of the fire scene yourself
Interview the driver for the fire report
Leave once fire rescue takes command
Assist the other responding resources
You may be asked to give incident details, control traffic, hold a perimeter or give first aid; a fire caused by a crash must be preserved for evidence.
A crowd grows large and loud. Why does the chapter warn about arresting members of a large group?
It is never allowed until the crowd disperses
It is sometimes difficult to remove or arrest them
It always requires a supervisor's approval first
It is only allowed for the group's leader
A crowd's anonymity can provoke aggressive individuals; attacks can come from any direction, so keep an exit strategy and do not let the crowd corner you.
A crowd is angry and shouting. Which skill does the chapter call essential to resolving it?
Effective communication
A show of force
Crowd dispersal orders
Physical control tactics
Speak professionally with dignity and respect, tell the leader why officers are there, and ask the leader to comply with the law; the leader's cooperation is a major factor.
You see underage drinking inside a large, tense crowd. What does the chapter say about enforcement?
Use discretion; enforce only when it is feasible
Enforce at once, since crimes in crowds can't wait
Ignore it until the crowd has fully dispersed
Enforce only if the crowd's leader agrees to it
Separate crimes inside a crowd, such as underage drinking or drug use, must be dealt with, but use discretion for safety and have enough backup before making a physical arrest.
Arriving alone at a building where a burglar may be inside, what does the chapter say about searching it?
Do not search it alone; use other officers and a canine
Search it alone if the key holder unlocks the door
Wait for the alarm company to search it first
Search it alone only after setting a perimeter
Never search a building alone; use other officers and a canine if available, and plan with your partner how to search and secure it.
Searching a store with a partner, you pass a door that opens toward you. What does the chapter warn?
Knock and announce before each doorway
Be cautious of anyone hiding behind doors
Close every door to keep suspects contained
Leave doors open so your partner can see
Have a plan before going in and never rush: stop, look and listen, and watch for anyone behind doors.
During a foot pursuit, why does the chapter say to keep updating dispatch?
So your supervisor can write the incident report
So responding officers can support you and set a perimeter
So dispatch can end the pursuit if it runs too long
So dispatch can enter the suspect into FCIC at once
In a foot pursuit, radio your location, direction of travel, suspect description and possible charges, and keep updating dispatch so others can support and set a perimeter.
After an arrest, the victim's mother asks how things went. Why does the chapter say to give general information when you can?
This is required before the case goes to court
This keeps her from calling the media about it
This keeps her from filing a complaint later
This may be her only contact with law enforcement
Victims, witnesses and the arrestee's family may have a direct interest; give general information whenever reasonably possible, since this may be their only contact with an officer.
Two days after an arrest, a detective is still interviewing witnesses. What does the chapter say about the investigation?
It does not necessarily stop at the arrest
It continues only if the arrestee confesses
It ends once the arrest affidavit is filed
It ends once the arrestee is booked
What may be released to the public is governed by state law and agency policy.
During an arrest, a crowd films you on their phones. What should you keep in mind?
They may be recording you as well as the arrest
They must stop if you ask, since it is evidence
They need your consent to record the arrest
They may record only from a distance you set
People recording you on personal devices are not committing a crime, and you cannot interfere unless they are actively obstructing the investigation.
Your agency wants a record of what happens on the way to the jail. What does the chapter say some policies require?
Calling the jail when you leave
A written log of every stop made
Audiotaping or videotaping the transport
A second officer in the back seat
If required, give dispatch your destination and beginning and ending mileage; some agencies require audio or video recording of transports, which protects against unfounded misconduct claims.
You have three arrestees to move after a long scene. What does the chapter say about the transport?
Transport them after the scene is fully cleared
Make every effort to transport them in a timely manner
